Hamiltonicity of graphs of acyclic orientations
and acyclic polynomials

Leonie Mühlherr and Germain Poullot
Date: September 17, 2026
Abstract.

We study the graph 𝒜​𝒪​(G){\mathcal{AO}}(G) of acyclic orientations of a graph GG. Two acyclic orientations are adjacent in this graph if they disagree on the orientation of a single arc. In particular, we focus on the Hamiltonicity of the graphs 𝒜​𝒪​(G){\mathcal{AO}}(G).

Using two methods of pattern lacing which generalize the zig-zag method of Brenner, Cardinal, McConville, Merino and Mütze, we characterize which multipaths are 𝒜​𝒪{\mathcal{AO}}-Hamiltonian. Moreover, we give a criterion for the gluing of a multipath on a given graph to preserve 𝒜​𝒪{\mathcal{AO}}-Hamiltonicity. Building towards an inductive certification of 𝒜​𝒪{\mathcal{AO}}-Hamiltonicity via the (open) ear decomposition of 2-connected graphs, we propose three ways of gluing several multipaths to a given graph.

In addition, we define the acyclic polynomials to encapsulate both the number of acyclic orientations of a graph and the “parity problem” proposed by Savage, Squire and West: if −1-1 is not a root of the acyclic polynomial of GG, then GG is not 𝒜​𝒪{\mathcal{AO}}-Hamiltonian. We explore numerous properties of the acyclic polynomials, proving that they are not instances of the famous Tutte–Whitney polynomials, but that they too exhibit a partial deletion-contraction phenomenon.

Use of AI declaration

The only use we made of AI (namely ChatGPT using GPT-5.5) was to correct mistakes in English writing, to search the literature and to improve some minor explanations of the existing literature (e.g. replacing “the number of maximal cones at a given distance from a base maximal cone in the dual graph of a hyperplane arrangement” by “the Whitney numbers”), to improve the readability of the table in Appendix D, and to parallelize our implementation of the acyclic signature in order to obtain the results of Example 3.13. All statements, proofs, concepts, notations, figures, references to the literature, etc., were made by us, as humans, using non-AI-powered tools (as far as we are aware). Notably, computations of Hamiltonian cycles and acyclic polynomials were run using SageMath [36] and our own pieces of code, not relying on AI-powered computations, except for the parallelization required in Example 3.13 for graphs of more than 2222 edges.

1. Introduction

The motivation for this article spans across various mathematical disciplines. At its core, the question we want to answer is for which graphs the acyclic orientations can be enumerated in a nice way. One can make this statement more precise by formulating it via Gray codes, which are enumerations where consecutive objects differ only by a small change. The original and most common example is the enumeration of binary strings, see [23] for more background. Acyclic orientations of a graph can be encoded as binary strings, each bit coding for an edge, and 00, 11 representing its two possible orientations. Yet, in this representation, it is hard to check whether a binary string encodes an acyclic orientation or not. We are interested in the following problem.

Formulation 1.

Classify the graphs GG for which the list of acyclic orientations admits a Gray code.

The reader unfamiliar with this version of the problem may take a look at Tables 2 and 3 for some typical examples. In this article, the main perspective on this question is the graph-theoretical one: We study the graph of acyclic orientations 𝒜​𝒪​(G){\mathcal{AO}}(G) whose nodes are the acyclic orientations of a graph GG, and where two orientations are neighboring if and only if they differ in flipping the orientation of exactly one arc. We can restate our problem:

Formulation 2.

Classify the graphs GG whose graph of acyclic orientations 𝒜​𝒪​(G){\mathcal{AO}}(G) is Hamiltonian.

This is the research angle of Savage, Squire and West in their seminal work [37]. They achieved a classification for some notable example classes, such as cycles, wheel-graphs, ladder-graphs, and chordal graphs (see [37] or here below Example 2.7). This quest for efficient ways to produce all the acyclic orientations of a graph was then pursued by numerous authors, see e.g. Squire [39] and Barbosa–Szwarcfiter [3] for generating problems. Most prominently, Pruesse and Ruskey [34] showed that the prism over the graph of acyclic orientations of any graph is Hamiltonian. Furthermore, Pilaud [32] studied the properties of the poset obtained from the graph of acyclic orientations of GG by orienting it away from a base (acyclic) orientation DD. Remarkably, he determined under which conditions on GG and DD it is a lattice. In particular, the rank function of this poset gives the coefficients of the acyclic polynomials that we study in Section 3. We also refer to Savage’s survey [38] for a presentation of the famous Steinhaus–Johnson–Trotter algorithm [22] which produces a Hamiltonian cycle in the graph of acyclic orientations for the complete graph. The interested reader may consult [9, Figure 5] for a comprehensive survey on algorithms and Hamiltonicity of graphs of acyclic orientations of combinatorial families beyond graphs.

The results of Savage, Squire and West strongly suggest that parity considerations (such as “Is CnC_{n} a cycle with nn even or odd?”) play a key role in determining whether 𝒜​𝒪​(G){\mathcal{AO}}(G) is Hamiltonian or not. In particular, they establish a simple yet powerful criterion for deciding that 𝒜​𝒪​(G){\mathcal{AO}}(G) is not Hamiltonian: fixing any orientation DD of GG, if 𝒜​𝒪​(G){\mathcal{AO}}(G) is Hamiltonian, then the number of acyclic orientations of GG disagreeing with DD on the orientation of an even number of arcs is equal to the number of acyclic orientations of GG disagreeing with DD on an odd number of arcs. When a graph does not satisfy this condition, Savage, Squire and West [37] speak of a parity problem (see also Lemma 2.9).

As a tribute to their foundational work, we extend their methods in Section 3.1 to study Cartesian products of graphs, and prove:

Theorem A (Corollary 3.10).

The following graphs are not 𝒜​𝒪{\mathcal{AO}}-Hamiltonian:

  1. (1)

    Ladder graphs Ln≔Pn×K2L_{n}\coloneqq P_{n}\times K_{2} for any nn even

  2. (2)

    Book graphs Bn≔K1,n×K2B_{n}\coloneqq K_{1,n}\times K_{2} for any nn odd

  3. (3)

    Prism graphs Prn≔Cn×K2\mathrm{Pr}_{n}\coloneqq C_{n}\times K_{2} for any nn even

  4. (4)

    Toroidal grid graphs T4,m≔C4×CmT_{4,m}\coloneqq C_{4}\times C_{m} for any mm even

  5. (5)

    Cube graphs Qn=K2×⋯×K2Q_{n}=K_{2}\times\dots\times K_{2}, with nn copies of K2K_{2}, for any n≥2n\geq 2,

  6. (6)

    More generally, the graph T×QnT\times Q_{n} for any tree TT where either n≥2n\geq 2 or TT has an even number of nodes,

  7. (7)

    Thick wheel graphs TWn≔Wn×K2\mathrm{TW}_{n}\coloneqq W_{n}\times K_{2} for any nn odd, where WnW_{n} is CnC_{n} together with a node adjacent to all nodes of CnC_{n},

  8. (8)

    Any (T,n1,…,ns)(T,\,n_{1},\dots,n_{s})-tree of cycles for any tree TT and any n1,…,ns≥1n_{1},\dots,n_{s}\geq 1, if there is some i∈[d]i\in[d] such that nin_{i} is even and if ∑i=1s(ni−1)\sum_{i=1}^{s}(n_{i}-1) is odd.

This result motivates us to define the rank with respect to DD of an acyclic orientation AA, denoted rkD⁡A\rank_{D}A, as the number of arcs on the orientation of which AA and DD disagree. We encapsulate the numbers of acyclic orientations of each rank in a polynomial Ψ⁡(D,t)≔∑A∈𝒜​𝒪​(G)trkD⁡A\Psi(D;t)\coloneqq\sum_{A\in{\mathcal{AO}}(G)}t^{\rank_{D}A} called the acyclic polynomial (Section 3). In particular, constructing the acyclic signature as σ⁡(D)≔Ψ⁡(D,−1)\sigma(D)\coloneqq\Psi(D;-1) (and σ⁡(G)≔|σ⁡(D)|\sigma(G)\coloneqq|\sigma(D)| for any orientation DD of GG), we can rephrase the parity problem as deciding whether σ⁡(D)=0\sigma(D)=0 or not. See Table 1 for an overview, and Section 3.3 for various properties of the acyclic signature.

Our acyclic polynomial should not be confused with the acyclic orientation polynomial recently defined in [21]: there, the authors assign a variable to each node of a graph, and associate each acyclic orientation to the product of the variables assigned to the sinks of the orientation.

Stanley [40] famously proved that the number of acyclic orientations of a graph GG can be recovered from its chromatic polynomial χ⁡(G,x)\chi(G;x) by evaluating it at −1-1, i.e. Ψ⁡(D,1)=χ⁡(G,−1)\Psi(D;1)=\chi(G;-1) for any orientation DD of GG (see Remark 3.19 for a discussion of this relation). Since then, the study of the chromatic polynomial itself has grown into a branch of Combinatorics, and the focus on the evaluation of this polynomial at −1-1 together with the combinatorial reciprocity theorems it suggests [20, 17, 18, 25, 4] is of particular relevance for our work.

As the chromatic polynomial can be computed exploiting a deletion-contraction phenomenon, it is natural to ask whether the acyclic polynomial also admits one. The main objective of Section 3.2 is to show that the acyclic polynomials partially admit a deletion-contraction phenomenon (Propositions 3.54 and 3.58) which extends to the acyclic signatures (Theorem 3.64), allowing for an algorithm that computes the acyclic signatures of some graphs (Remark 3.66). Furthermore, we prove in Remark 3.18 that the acyclic polynomial is not an evaluation of the famous Tutte–Whitney polynomial (see [45, 44, 12] for the original articles, or [29] for a comprehensive presentation in the broader context of matroids). Yet, it seems that there is more to this story, since recent results show that properties of acyclic orientations, besides counting, are encoded in the Tutte–Whitney polynomial, see e.g. the work of Backman [2].

The question of acyclic orientations of graphs also recently arose in the field of hyperplane arrangements [BrennerCardinalMcConvilleMerinoMutze25-CombinatorialGenerationVII, KorberSchniedersStrickerWalizadeth25-HamiltonianCyclesSupersolvable], where the acyclic orientations of a graph are in one-to-one correspondence with the chambers of the corresponding graphic arrangement, that is the arrangement of hyperplanes 𝒜G:={𝒙∈ℝN;xi=xj}\mathcal{A}_{G}:=\{{\boldsymbol{x}}\in\mathbb{R}^{N}~;~x_{i}=x_{j}\} for {i,j}\{i,j\} an edge of GG with node set NN.

The graph of acyclic orientations 𝒜​𝒪​(G){\mathcal{AO}}(G) is known in this context as the tope graph of the graphic arrangement, describing the neighboring structure of the chambers. Equivalently 𝒜​𝒪​(G){\mathcal{AO}}(G) is also the vertex-edge graph of the zonotope associated to the arrangement, known under the names acyclotopes [47] and graphical zonotopes [33, 30, 31]. The interested reader may consult [41, Section 2] or [6, Section 1.1] for a detailed presentation. The interplay of properties of the tope graph, the arrangement and the zonotope is an active field of research [24, 1]. (Note that our question need not be restricted to the graphic case in this setting.)

Formulation 3.

Classify all (graphic) arrangements whose tope graph admits a Hamiltonian cycle. Equivalently, classify all graphs such that the vertex-edge graph of the associated graphical zonotope (a.k.a. acyclotope) is Hamiltonian.

For example, it is known that the tope graph of so-called reflection arrangements, of which 𝒜Kℓ\mathcal{A}_{K_{\ell}} is an example, admits a Hamiltonian cycle [11]. Recently, there has been another development for this more general setting as two groups of researchers independently found that the tope graph of so-called supersolvable arrangements are Hamiltonian [BrennerCardinalMcConvilleMerinoMutze25-CombinatorialGenerationVII, KorberSchniedersStrickerWalizadeth25-HamiltonianCyclesSupersolvable]. Applying this result to graphic arrangements recovers the result for chordal graphs from Savage, Squire and West [37, Section 4.1]. Furthermore, some of the observations we make in this work about the evaluations of the acyclic polynomial for graphs are already known in this more general hyperplane setting, employing different names and arguments (see Remark 3.24).

In the second main part of our work, Section 4, we prove that some operations can be performed on a graph whose graph of acyclic orientations is Hamiltonian, preserving this property. We introduce two methods of pattern lacing (Corollaries 4.4 and 4.5) which can be seen as generalizing the zig-zag method described in [BrennerCardinalMcConvilleMerinoMutze25-CombinatorialGenerationVII]. This way, we prove that, under a certain parity condition, adding a path of even length (or two paths of odd lengths) between nodes uu and vv preserves having a Hamiltonian graph of acyclic orientations. A graph consisting of several paths between two nodes uu and vv is called a multipath. Using these path gluings together with our results on the acyclic signature, we establish (“GG is 𝒜​𝒪{\mathcal{AO}}-Hamiltonian” means “𝒜​𝒪​(G){\mathcal{AO}}(G) is Hamiltonian”):

Theorem B (Corollaries 4.13 and 4.14).

We have the following positive results:

  1. (1)

    A multipath GG is 𝒜​𝒪{\mathcal{AO}}-Hamiltonian if and only if the number of edges of GG is odd.

  2. (2)

    Any 22-sum of two cycle graphs CnC_{n} and CmC_{m} is 𝒜​𝒪{\mathcal{AO}}-Hamiltonian if and only if n+mn+m is even.

  3. (3)

    For a tree T=([s],E)T=([s],E) and numbers n1,…,ns≥3n_{1},\dots,n_{s}\geq 3, a (T,n1,…,ns)(T,\,n_{1},\dots,n_{s})-tree of cycles is any graph isomorphic to a 22-sum H⊕2CnsH\oplus_{2}C_{n_{s}} where HH is a (T∖s,n1,…,ns−1)(T\smallsetminus s,\,n_{1},\dots,n_{s-1})-tree of cycles. If npn_{p} is odd for all p∈[s]p\in[s], then any (T,n1,…,ns)(T,\,n_{1},\dots,n_{s})-tree of cycles is 𝒜​𝒪{\mathcal{AO}}-Hamiltonian, for any tree TT.

  4. (4)

    If u​v∈Euv\in E is an edge of a 𝒜​𝒪{\mathcal{AO}}-Hamiltonian graph G=(N,E)G=(N,E), and CnC_{n} is a cycle graph, then the 22-sum G⊕2CnG\oplus_{2}C_{n} is 𝒜​𝒪{\mathcal{AO}}-Hamiltonian if and only if nn is odd.

This theorem subsumes the one of Savage, Squire and West: “For a cycle CnC_{n} on nn nodes, 𝒜​𝒪​(Cn){\mathcal{AO}}(C_{n}) is Hamiltonian if and only if nn is odd” [37, below Lemma 3.1 & Theorem 4.2]. The above Theorem B is a specialization of the more general Corollary 4.11 made easier for the introduction.

The motivation behind considering this type of operation arises from the fact that if 𝒜​𝒪​(H){\mathcal{AO}}(H) is Hamiltonian for all the 22-connected components of GG, then 𝒜​𝒪​(G){\mathcal{AO}}(G) is also Hamiltonian. Moreover, it is well-known (see [13, Section 3.1] for details and figures) that 22-connected graphs admit an (open) ear decomposition, i.e. we can construct any 22-connected graph by starting with a cycle and subsequently adding paths between pairs of nodes. Therefore, exploring all the ways of adding paths to a graph that are compatible with the 𝒜​𝒪{\mathcal{AO}}-Hamiltonicity of said graph means iteratively constructing a large example class with hopes of reaching a complete classification. We show (recall that a node is simplicial if all its neighbors pairwise share an edge, i.e. form a clique):

Theorem C (Simplified version Corollary 4.18).

Let GG be a graph such that 𝒜​𝒪​(G){\mathcal{AO}}(G) is Hamiltonian. If G′G^{\prime} is obtained from GG by either

  1. (1)

    the addition of a simplicial node x∘x_{\circ} on a clique of odd cardinality in GG and the (optional) gluing of a multipath of even cardinality at some nodes u,vu,v with u≠x∘u\neq x_{\circ} and v≠x∘v\neq x_{\circ}; or

  2. (2)

    the (optional) addition of a simplicial node and the gluing of a multipath of even cardinality at some nodes u,vu,v that share an edge in GG;

Then 𝒜​𝒪​(G′){\mathcal{AO}}(G^{\prime}) is Hamiltonian.

A more flexible yet notation-heavy version of Theorem C is proven in Corollary 4.18. We also detail a third way of gluing several multipaths on different pairs of nodes in Section 4.4.

This article is organized as follows: In Section 2, we summarize all the graph-theoretic preliminaries that are needed for the present work, especially on orientations, acyclic orientations, but also the usual examples of the Gray code for binary sequences and the Steinhaus–Johnson–Trotter algorithm for permutations. In Section 3 we introduce the acyclic polynomial and explain its fundamental properties. Notably, we decompose it into partial acyclic polynomials (Proposition 3.43), and prove a deletion-contraction formula in certain cases (Propositions 3.54 and 3.58). This allows us to better understand the acyclic signature of graphs (Section 3.3) and to compute the acyclic signature of multipaths (Theorem 3.69), exemplifying how to certify that 𝒜​𝒪​(G){\mathcal{AO}}(G) is not Hamiltonian for some graph GG. On the constructive side of Hamiltonicity considerations, in Section 4, we give explicit constructions of Hamiltonian cycles for graphs obtained via graph operations such as path gluings or addition of a simplicial node.

Generalizations of strategies of pattern lacing can be found in Appendix A, while Appendix B is devoted to complete bipartite graphs, and Appendix C proposes an alternative proof that multipaths of even total length are not 𝒜​𝒪{\mathcal{AO}}-Hamiltonian using a counting argument. In Appendix D, we give 2222 explicit examples of well-known graphs and the properties of their graph of acyclic orientations, for the reader to enjoy.

2. Preliminaries

We denote [n]≔{1,…,n}{[n]}\coloneqq\{1,\dots,n\}, and [i,j]={i,i+1,…,j}[i,j]=\{i,i+1,\dots,j\}. Moreover, let 2X≔{Y;Y⊆X}{2^{X}}\coloneqq\{Y~;~Y\subseteq X\} and (Xk)≔{Y∈2X;|Y|=k}{\binom{X}{k}}\coloneqq\{Y\in 2^{X}~;~|Y|=k\}, where |Y||Y| is the size (i.e. cardinality) of the set YY. For two sets X,YX,Y we denote X⊔Y{X\sqcup Y} for X∪YX\cup Y when XX and YY are disjoint sets. The Cartesian product of XX and YY is X×Y≔{(x,y);x∈X,y∈Y}{X\times Y}\coloneqq\{(x,y)~;~x\in X,y\in Y\}, and the symmetric difference of XX and YY is X​△​Y≔(X∪Y)∖(X∩Y)=(X∖Y)⊔(Y∖X){X\triangle Y}\coloneqq(X\cup Y)\smallsetminus(X\cap Y)=(X\smallsetminus Y)\sqcup(Y\smallsetminus X).

An (undirected) graph G≔(N,E){G}\coloneqq(N,E) is composed of a set of nodes NN, and a set of edges E⊆([n]2)E\subseteq\binom{[n]}{2}. A digraph (or simple directed graph) D≔(N,F){D}\coloneqq(N,F) is composed of a set of nodes NN and a set of arcs (or directed edges) F={(i,j);,i,j∈N}F=\bigl\{(i,j)~;~,i,j\in N\bigr\}, such that {i,j}≠{k,ℓ}\{i,j\}\neq\{k,\ell\} for (i,j),(k,ℓ)∈F(i,j),(k,\ell)\in F. To shorten notation we write i​jij for {i,j}\{i,j\} and (i,j)(i,j) when the context is clear. We denote by N⁡(G),E⁡(G),F⁡(G)N(G),E(G),F(G) the sets of nodes, edges and arcs of a given (di)graph GG. For a given node i∈Ni\in N, the nodes j∈Nj\in N such that i​j∈Eij\in E are called the neighbors of ii.

For a (di)graph G=(N,E)G=(N,E), and some U⊆NU\subseteq N, the associated induced sub(di)graph is defined as G⁡[U]≔(U,{i​j∈E;i,j∈U}){G[U]}\coloneqq\bigl(U,\{ij\in E~;~i,j\in U\}\bigr).

For a digraph D=(N,F)D=(N,F), the associated underlying graph is the graph D¯≔(N,E){\underline{D}}\coloneqq(N,E) where E={{i,j};(i,j)∈F}E=\bigl\{\{i,j\}~;~(i,j)\in F\bigr\}; conversely an orientation of GG is a digraph DD such that D¯=G\underline{D}=G. We denote the set of orientations of GG by 𝒪⁡(G){{\mathcal{O}}(G)}. Similarly, for a digraph DD, we call orientations of DD the orientations of D¯\underline{D}, and denote 𝒪⁡(D){\mathcal{O}}(D) for 𝒪⁡(D¯){\mathcal{O}}(\underline{D}).

A (di)graph G=(N,E)G=(N,E) is bipartite if there exists N1,N2⊆NN_{1},N_{2}\subseteq N such that N1⊔N2=NN_{1}\sqcup N_{2}=N and there is no i​j∈Eij\in E with i,j∈N1i,j\in N_{1} nor with i,j∈N2i,j\in N_{2}.

Example 2.1.

The following examples are well-studied in the literature.

  1. (1)

    For n≥1n\geq 1, the nthn^{\text{th}} cube-graph Qn{Q_{n}} is the graph on the set of nodes  2[n]2^{[n]} where X,Y⊆[n]X,Y\subseteq[n] are linked by an edge if and only if |X​△​Y|=1|X\triangle Y|=1. Moreover, the nthn^{\text{th}} Boolean lattice ℬ​o​o​ln{{\mathcal{B}}ool_{n}} is the orientation of QnQ_{n} with arcs (X,Y)(X,Y) for X⊆YX\subseteq Y and |Y∖X|=1|Y\smallsetminus X|=1. Cube-graphs and Boolean lattices are bipartite: XX and YY belong to the same part if and only if |X||X| and |Y||Y| have the same parity. See Figure 1 (top left) for an illustration.

  2. (2)

    For n≥1n\geq 1, the nthn^{\text{th}} complete graph Kn{K_{n}} is the graph on the set of nodes [n][n] where all ii and jj are linked by an edge for i,j∈[n]i,j\in[n]. Complete graphs are not bipartite. A subset of nodes U⊆NU\subseteq N is a clique in a graph G=(N,E)G=(N,E) if its induced subgraph G⁡[U]G[U] is isomorphic to a complete graph; and a node  ii is simplicial if its set of neighbors is a clique.

  3. (3)

    For n≥1n\geq 1, the nthn^{\text{th}} permutahedral graph Πn{\Pi_{n}} whose nodes are the permutations of [n][n], where σ\sigma and σ′\sigma^{\prime} are linked by an edge if there exists i∈[n−1]i\in[n-1] such that σ′=σ∘(i​i+1)\sigma^{\prime}=\sigma\circ(i~\,~i+1). Moreover, the nthn^{\text{th}} weak (Bruhat) order 𝒲​e​a​kn{{\mathcal{W}}eak_{n}} is the orientation of Πn\Pi_{n} with arcs (σ,σ′)(\sigma,\sigma^{\prime}) if σ′=σ∘(i​i+1)\sigma^{\prime}=\sigma\circ(i~\,~i+1) and σ⁡(i)<σ⁡(i+1)\sigma(i)<\sigma(i+1). Permutahedral graphs and weak orders are bipartite.

2.1. On general orientations

For any fixed orientation D=(N,F)D=(N,F) of G=(N,E)G=(N,E), the set of orientations of GG is in natural bijection with 2E2^{E}: Namely, for ω⊆E\omega\subseteq E, let Fω≔{i​jif ​i​j∈ωj​iif ​i​j∉ω;i​j∈F}{F^{\omega}}\coloneqq\left\{\begin{array}[]{cl}ij&\text{if }ij\in\omega\\ ji&\text{if }ij\notin\omega\\ \end{array}~;~ij\in F\right\}.

The re-orientation of DD with respect to ω\omega is Dω≔(N,Fω){D^{\omega}}\coloneqq(N,F^{\omega}), and it is immediate that ω↦Dω\omega\mapsto D^{\omega} defines a bijection 2E→𝒪⁡(G)2^{E}\to{\mathcal{O}}(G). We define the (re-orientation) rank rkD⁡(Dω)≔|ω|{\rank_{D}(D^{\omega})}\coloneqq|\omega|, see Figure 1 for orientations drawn in ranked posets. With respect to DD, for two orientations D1D_{1} and D2D_{2} of GG, we can find ω1,ω2⊆E\omega_{1},\omega_{2}\subseteq E such that D1=Dω1D_{1}=D^{\omega_{1}} and D2=Dω2D_{2}=D^{\omega_{2}} and we write D1⪯DD2{D_{1}\preceq_{D}D_{2}} if ω1⊆ω2\omega_{1}\subseteq\omega_{2}.

When we choose a fixed orientation DD of GG in order to express all the other orientations of GG as a re-orientation of DD, we call DD a base orientation and denote the set of orientations of some rank k≥0k\geq 0 by 𝒪k​(D)≔{D′∈𝒪⁡(G);rkD⁡(D′)=k}{{\mathcal{O}}_{k}(D)}\coloneqq\{D^{\prime}\in{\mathcal{O}}(G)~;~\rank_{D}(D^{\prime})=k\}. Using the bijection ω↦Dω\omega\mapsto D^{\omega}, we get |𝒪k​(D)|=|(Ek)|=(|E|k)|{\mathcal{O}}_{k}(D)|=\left|\binom{E}{k}\right|=\binom{|E|}{k}, for any base orientation DD and any kk.

Remark 2.2.

Using Newton’s binomial formula, one has, for m≥1m\geq 1:

(∑k​ even(mk))−(∑k​ odd(mk))=∑k=0m(mk)​(−1)k=(1−1)m=0\left(\sum_{k\text{ even}}\binom{m}{k}\right)-\left(\sum_{k\text{ odd}}\binom{m}{k}\right)=\sum_{k=0}^{m}\binom{m}{k}(-1)^{k}=(1-1)^{m}=0

Hence, ∑k​ even(mk)=∑k​ odd(mk)=2m−1\sum_{k\text{ even}}\binom{m}{k}=\sum_{k\text{ odd}}\binom{m}{k}=2^{m-1} for any m≥1m\geq 1. We emphasize that this implies that

∑k​ even|𝒪k​(D)|=∑k​ odd|𝒪k​(D)|=2|E|−1,\sum_{k\text{ even}}|{\mathcal{O}}_{k}(D)|=\sum_{k\text{ odd}}|{\mathcal{O}}_{k}(D)|=2^{|E|-1},

for any base orientation DD of GG. This will prove useful in the following sections, e.g. Section 3.3.

Besides, note that for any D1=Dω1D_{1}=D^{\omega_{1}} and D2=Dω2D_{2}=D^{\omega_{2}}, we can define the difference between D1D_{1} and D2D_{2} as D1​△​D2≔ω1​△​ω2{D_{1}\triangle D_{2}}\coloneqq\omega_{1}\triangle\omega_{2} which does not depend on the base orientation DD: these are the edges of D¯\underline{D} which are not oriented the same way in D1D_{1} as in D2D_{2}. Two orientations D1,D2D_{1},D_{2} of GG are adjacent if |D1​△​D2|=1|D_{1}\triangle D_{2}|=1. The graph of orientations (respectively digraph of orientations with respect to some base orientation DD) of GG is the graph whose nodes  are the orientations of GG, and where two orientations are linked by an edge (resp. arc) if they are adjacent (resp. adjacent with D1⊆DD2D_{1}\subseteq_{D}D_{2}), see Figure 1 (top left). We denote 𝒪⁡(G){{\mathcal{O}}(G)} (resp. 𝒪⁡(D){{\mathcal{O}}(D)}) this (di)graph, where we slightly abuse notation and reuse the notation used for the set of orientations. Fixing any base orientation D∈𝒪⁡(G)D\in{\mathcal{O}}(G), the bijection ω↦Dω\omega\mapsto D^{\omega} defines an isomorphism of graphs from the graph of orientations 𝒪⁡(G){\mathcal{O}}(G) to the cube-graph Q|E|Q_{|E|}, and from the digraph of orientations 𝒪⁡(D){\mathcal{O}}(D) to the Boolean lattice ℬ​o​o​l|E|{\mathcal{B}}ool_{|E|}. Note that each base orientation D∈𝒪⁡(G)D\in{\mathcal{O}}(G) defines a different isomorphism 𝒪⁡(G)→Q|E|{\mathcal{O}}(G)\to Q_{|E|}, and a different orientation 𝒪⁡(D){\mathcal{O}}(D) of 𝒪⁡(G){\mathcal{O}}(G).

2.2. Cycles, Hamiltonian graphs

A (directed) path in a (di)graph GG is a sequence of different nodes  i1,…,ir∈N⁡(G)i_{1},\dots,i_{r}\in N(G) such that ip​ip+1i_{p}i_{p+1} is a (directed) edge in GG for all p∈[r−1]p\in[r-1]. A (directed) cycle is a (directed) path i1,…,ir∈Ni_{1},\dots,i_{r}\in N such that ir​i1i_{r}i_{1} is a (directed) edge in GG. A graph is Hamiltonian (resp. path-Hamiltonian) if it admits a cycle (resp. a path) containing all its nodes. Clearly, a Hamiltonian graph is path-Hamiltonian.

We state here a well-known proposition concerning Hamiltonicity of bipartite graphs and give a short proof for the sake of self-containment.

Proposition 2.3.

Let G=(N,E)G=(N,E) be a graph admitting a bipartition N=N1⊔N2N=N_{1}\sqcup N_{2}.

  1. (1)

    If GG is Hamiltonian, then |N1|=|N2||N_{1}|=|N_{2}|;

  2. (2)

    If GG is path-Hamiltonian with path i1,…,iri_{1},\dots,i_{r} where i1∈N1i_{1}\in N_{1}, then either |N1|=|N2||N_{1}|=|N_{2}| and ir∈N2i_{r}\in N_{2}, or |N1|=|N2|+1|N_{1}|=|N_{2}|+1 and ir∈N1i_{r}\in N_{1}.

Proof.

1 If GG is Hamiltonian, let i1,…,iri_{1},\dots,i_{r} be a cycle with N={i1,…,ir}N=\{i_{1},\dots,i_{r}\}. As ip​ip+1∈Ei_{p}i_{p+1}\in E for all p∈[r−1]p\in[r-1], we get that ip∈N1i_{p}\in N_{1} if and only if ip+1∈N2i_{p+1}\in N_{2} and conversely, by definition of the bipartition. So ip↦ip+1i_{p}\mapsto i_{p+1} for p∈[r−1]p\in[r-1] and ir↦i1i_{r}\mapsto i_{1} defines an involution of NN mapping N1N_{1} onto N2N_{2} Thus, |N1|=|N2||N_{1}|=|N_{2}|.

2 If ir∈N1i_{r}\in N_{1}, then ip↦ip+1i_{p}\mapsto i_{p+1} for p∈[r−1]p\in[r-1] defines an involution of N∖{ir}N\smallsetminus\{i_{r}\} mapping N1∖{ir}N_{1}\smallsetminus\{i_{r}\} onto N2N_{2}, hence |N1|=|N2|+1|N_{1}|=|N_{2}|+1. Else, ip↦ip+1i_{p}\mapsto i_{p+1} for p∈[r−1]p\in[r-1] and ir↦i1i_{r}\mapsto i_{1} defines an involution of NN mapping N1N_{1} onto N2N_{2}, hence |N1|=|N2|+1|N_{1}|=|N_{2}|+1. ∎

Example 2.4.

The cube-graph is bipartite and Hamiltonian. As it is a fundamental example supporting the constructions of Section 4, we detail the properties of Hamiltonian cycles of the cube-graphs.

There are two ways to encode the nodes of QnQ_{n}, either as subsets X⊆[n]X\subseteq[n], or as strings of bits 𝜺=(ε1,…,εn)∈{0,1}n{\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}}=(\varepsilon_{1},\dots,\varepsilon_{n})\in\{0,1\}^{n}. The bijection is given by X⁡(𝜺)={i∈[n];εi=1}X({\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}})=\{i\in[n]~;~\varepsilon_{i}=1\}, and reciprocally, ε​(X)i=1\varepsilon(X)_{i}=1 if and only if i∈Xi\in X.

The bipartition of QnQ_{n} is given by the parts {X⊆[n];|X|​ is even}≃{𝜺∈{0,1}n;∑iεi​ is even}\{X\subseteq[n]~;~|X|\text{ is even}\}\simeq\{{\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}}\in\{0,1\}^{n}~;~\sum_{i}\varepsilon_{i}\text{ is even}\} and {X⊆[n];|X|​ is odd}≃{𝜺∈{0,1}n;∑iεi​ is odd}\{X\subseteq[n]~;~|X|\text{ is odd}\}\simeq\{{\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}}\in\{0,1\}^{n}~;~\sum_{i}\varepsilon_{i}\text{ is odd}\}. In particular, the nodes ∅≃(0,…,0)\varnothing\simeq(0,\dots,0) and [n]≃(1,…,1)[n]\simeq(1,\dots,1) belong to the same part if and only if nn is even.

There are many ways to construct Hamiltonian cycles in QnQ_{n}, see [27, A066037] for a count of them for small nn. First, note that Q2Q_{2} is a cycle on 44 elements, so it trivially admits a Hamiltonian cycle. Then, by induction, given two Hamiltonian cycles 𝑪=(X1,…,X2n){\boldsymbol{C}}=(X_{1},\dots,X_{2^{n}}) and 𝑪′=(Y1,…,Y2n){\boldsymbol{C}}^{\prime}=(Y_{1},\dots,Y_{2^{n}}) of QnQ_{n} with a shared arc (X2n,X1)=(Y2n,Y1)(X_{2^{n}},X_{1})=(Y_{2^{n}},Y_{1}) (e.g. 𝑪=𝑪′{\boldsymbol{C}}={\boldsymbol{C}}^{\prime}), one can construct a Hamiltonian cycle of Qn+1Q_{n+1} as:

(X1,X2,…,X2n,Y2n∪{n+1},Y2n−1∪{n+1},…,Y1∪{n+1}).\bigl(X_{1},\,X_{2},\,\dots,\,X_{2^{n}},\,\,Y_{2^{n}}\cup\{n+1\},\,Y_{2^{n}-1}\cup\{n+1\},\,\dots,\,Y_{1}\cup\{n+1\}\bigr)\,.

In term of sequences of bits, one constructs a highly symmetric Hamiltonian cycle (ε(1),…,ε(2n))\bigl(\varepsilon^{(1)},\dots,\varepsilon^{(2^{n})}\bigr) as follows. For each i∈[n]i\in[n], the sequence (εi(1),εi(2),…,εi(2n))\bigl(\varepsilon_{i}^{(1)},\varepsilon_{i}^{(2)},\dots,\varepsilon_{i}^{(2^{n})}\bigr) starts with a sequence of 2n−i2^{n-i} copies of 00, then alternates between 2n−i+12^{n-i+1} copies of 11 and 2n−i+12^{n-i+1} copies of 00, until it ends with again 2n−i2^{n-i} copies of 00. Such a construction is illustrated by the columns of Table 2.

Example 2.5.

The permutahedral graph Πn\Pi_{n} is bipartite and Hamiltonian. On the one hand, since two adjacent permutations in Πn\Pi_{n} differ by a transposition, the usual signature of permutation provides a bipartition of Πn\Pi_{n}: no two even (resp. odd) permutations share an edge in Πn\Pi_{n}.

We shortly present the famous Steinhaus–Johnson–Trotter algorithm [22] which yields a Hamiltonian cycle of the permutahedral graph. See the survey of Savage [38, Section 3] for a more detailed presentation of the subject.

First, for a permutation τ\tau of nn elements and i∈[n+1]i\in[n+1], we define the permutation τ(i)\tau^{(i)} of n+1n+1 elements by

τ(i)​(j)={τ⁡(j)if ​j<in+1if ​j=iτ⁡(j−1)if ​j>i.\tau^{(i)}(j)=\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}\tau(j)&\text{if }j<i\\ n+1&\text{if }j=i\\ \tau(j-1)&\text{if }j>i\end{array}\right.\,.

The graph Π3\Pi_{3} trivially admits a Hamiltonian cycle since it is a cycle-graph on 66 elements, e.g. 123−132−312−321−231−213123-132-312-321-231-213. By induction, let (σ1,…,σn!)(\sigma_{1},\dots,\sigma_{n!}) be a Hamiltonian cycle of Πn\Pi_{n}, then the following is a Hamiltonian cycle of Πn+1\Pi_{n+1}, see Table 3:

(σ1(n+1),…,σ1(1),σ2(1),…,σ2(n+1),σ3(n+1),…,σ3(1),…,σn!(1),…,σn!(n+1)).\bigl(\sigma_{1}^{(n+1)},\dots,\sigma_{1}^{(1)},\,\sigma_{2}^{(1)},\dots,\sigma_{2}^{(n+1)},\,\sigma_{3}^{(n+1)},\dots,\sigma_{3}^{(1)},\,\dots,\,\sigma_{n!}^{(1)},\dots,\sigma_{n!}^{(n+1)}\bigr)\,.

2.3. Graph of acyclic orientations

A directed graph is acyclic if it contains no directed cycles, otherwise it is cyclic. For a (di)graph GG, its graph of acyclic orientations 𝒜​𝒪​(G){{\mathcal{AO}}(G)} is the subgraph of its graph of orientations 𝒪⁡(G){\mathcal{O}}(G) induced on the set of acyclic orientations of GG, see Figure 1. Correspondingly, fixing a base orientation DD of GG, the associated digraph of acyclic orientations 𝒜​𝒪​(D){{\mathcal{AO}}(D)} is the subdigraph of its digraph of orientations 𝒪⁡(D){\mathcal{O}}(D) induced on the set of acyclic orientations of GG. As sub(di)graphs of bipartite (di)graphs, 𝒜​𝒪​(G){\mathcal{AO}}(G) and 𝒜​𝒪​(D){\mathcal{AO}}(D) are bipartite. They are graded by the rank functions rkD\rank_{D}. We denote 𝒜​𝒪k​(D)≔{A∈𝒜​𝒪​(G);rkD⁡A=k}{{\mathcal{AO}}_{k}(D)}\coloneqq\{A\in{\mathcal{AO}}(G)~;~\rank_{D}A=k\}.

We denote 𝒞​𝒪​(G){{\mathcal{CO}}(G)}, 𝒞​𝒪​(D){{\mathcal{CO}}(D)} and 𝒞​𝒪k​(D){{\mathcal{CO}}_{k}(D)} the counterparts for cyclic orientations.

Example 2.6.

For n≥1n\geq 1, the acyclic orientations of the complete graph KnK_{n} are in bijection with the permutations of [n][n]. Indeed, any orientation DD of KnK_{n} yields a reflexive and transitive relation: i≤ji\leq j if and only if there is a directed path from ii to jj in DD. If this orientation is acyclic, then this relation is anti-symmetric, i.e. it is a permutation of [n][n]. Two acyclic orientations of KnK_{n} are adjacent if they differ on the orientation of a single arc, that is if the associated permutations differ on the order of two consecutive elements. Hence the graph of acyclic orientations of the complete graph 𝒜​𝒪​(Kn){\mathcal{AO}}(K_{n}) is isomorphic to the permutahedral graph Πn\Pi_{n}. Furthermore, choosing any base acyclic orientation DD of KnK_{n}, the digraph of acyclic orientations 𝒜​𝒪​(D){\mathcal{AO}}(D) is isomorphic to the weak Bruhat order 𝒲​e​a​kn{\mathcal{W}}eak_{n}.

Our main motivation in the following sections is analyzing Formulation 2, thus we say that GG is 𝒜​𝒪{\mathcal{AO}}-Hamiltonian if 𝒜​𝒪​(G){\mathcal{AO}}(G) is Hamiltonian.

Example 2.7.

The following are well-known:

  1. (1)

    Trees are 𝒜​𝒪{\mathcal{AO}}-Hamiltonian, see Figure 1 (top left): Since cube-graphs are Hamiltonian, and no orientation of a tree TT can be cyclic, we have that 𝒜​𝒪​(T)≃Qn{\mathcal{AO}}(T)\simeq Q_{n} is Hamiltonian.

  2. (2)

    Complete graphs are 𝒜​𝒪{\mathcal{AO}}-Hamiltonian: The permutahedral graph is Hamiltonian since the Steinhaus–Johnson–Trotter algorithm yields a Hamiltonian cycle on Πn\Pi_{n}, see Example 2.5 (or [22] or the survey [38, Section 3]); and the graph of acyclic orientations of the complete graph KnK_{n} is isomorphic to Πn\Pi_{n}, see Example 2.6.

  3. (3)

    The cycle graph CnC_{n} (see Figure 1 (bottom), the wheel graph WnW_{n} (a cycle graph together with a node connected to all others), and the ladder graph LnL_{n} (two disjoint paths on (a1,…,an)(a_{1},\dots,a_{n}) and (b1,…,bn)(b_{1},\dots,b_{n}) together with edges ai​bia_{i}b_{i} for i∈[n]i\in[n]) are 𝒜​𝒪{\mathcal{AO}}-Hamiltonian  if and only if nn is odd, see [37].

  4. (4)

    Chordal graphs (see Figure 1 (top right)) are 𝒜​𝒪{\mathcal{AO}}-Hamiltonian, see [37, Theorem 4.1] and [BrennerCardinalMcConvilleMerinoMutze25-CombinatorialGenerationVII, KorberSchniedersStrickerWalizadeth25-HamiltonianCyclesSupersolvable].

  5. (5)

    Complete bipartite graphs Km,nK_{m,n} (disjoint sets of nodes (a1,…,am)(a_{1},\dots,a_{m}) and (b1,…,bn)(b_{1},\dots,b_{n}) with edges ai​bja_{i}b_{j} for all i∈[m]i\in[m] and j∈[n]j\in[n]) are not 𝒜​𝒪{\mathcal{AO}}-Hamiltonian if either mm or nn is even. The authors of [37] proved it using a parity argument, see Lemma 2.9. As we will discuss further in Appendix B, the case where nn and mm are both odd is open.

  6. (6)

    We give 2222 examples of small graphs in Appendix D, deciding 𝒜​𝒪{\mathcal{AO}}-Hamiltonicity for some of them.

We are especially interested in operations on graphs that preserve 𝒜​𝒪{\mathcal{AO}}-Hamiltonicity. In particular, we repeatedly use the following lemma, called the parity problem in [37]:

Definition 2.8.

For a graph GG, and DD an acyclic orientation of GG, the associated acyclic signature is σ⁡(D)≔∑k(−1)k⋅|𝒜​𝒪k​(D)|{\sigma(D)}\coloneqq\sum_{k}(-1)^{k}\cdot|{\mathcal{AO}}_{k}(D)|.

Lemma 2.9.

Let DD be an orientation of a graph GG. If σ⁡(D)≠0\sigma(D)\neq 0, then GG is not 𝒜​𝒪{\mathcal{AO}}-Hamiltonian.

Proof.

If two orientations are adjacent, then their ranks differ by 11. Hence a bipartition of 𝒜​𝒪​(G){\mathcal{AO}}(G) is given by the parts ⋃k​ even𝒜​𝒪k​(D)\bigcup_{k\text{ even}}{\mathcal{AO}}_{k}(D) and ⋃k​ odd𝒜​𝒪k​(D)\bigcup_{k\text{ odd}}{\mathcal{AO}}_{k}(D). The contrapositive of Proposition 2.3 1 and the definition of the acyclic signature yield the claim. ∎

Remark 2.10.

We can state a similar lemma for cyclic orientations: If ∑k(−1)k⋅|𝒞​𝒪k​(D)|≠0\sum_{k}(-1)^{k}\cdot|{\mathcal{CO}}_{k}(D)|\neq 0, then GG is not 𝒜​𝒪{\mathcal{AO}}-Hamiltonian.

Indeed, for all kk, we have 𝒪k​(D)=𝒜​𝒪k​(D)⊔𝒞​𝒪k​(D){\mathcal{O}}_{k}(D)={\mathcal{AO}}_{k}(D)\sqcup{\mathcal{CO}}_{k}(D), and by Remark 2.2, we know that ∑k(−1)k⋅|𝒪k​(D)|=0\sum_{k}(-1)^{k}\cdot|{\mathcal{O}}_{k}(D)|=0, so applying Lemma 2.9 gives the claim.

Section 3.3 is devoted to the properties and the computation of acyclic signatures.

For the convenience of the reader, we recall here the principal operations that we will use on (di)graphs. For (di)graphs G=(N,E),G′=(N′,E′)G=(N,E),G^{\prime}=(N^{\prime},E^{\prime}), we define:

For some {e1,…,er}⊆(N2)\{e_{1},\dots,e_{r}\}\subseteq\binom{N}{2}, we define the contraction G/Y≔(…(G/e1)/e2…)/er{G/_{Y}}\coloneqq(\dots(G/_{e_{1}})/_{e_{2}}\dots)/_{e_{r}}. The isomorphism class of G/YG/_{Y} does not depend on the order of the pairs of nodes.

    The union G∪G′≔(N⊔N′,E⊔E′){G\cup G^{\prime}}\coloneqq(N\sqcup N^{\prime},E\sqcup E^{\prime}).

    G×G′{G\times G^{\prime}} the Cartesian product on the node set N×N′N\times N^{\prime} and edge set

    {((x,x′),(x,y′));x′​y′∈E′,x∈N}∪{((x,x′),(y,x′));x​y∈E,x′∈N′}.\Bigl\{\bigl((x,x^{\prime}),(x,y^{\prime})\bigr)~;~x^{\prime}y^{\prime}\in E^{\prime},\,x\in N\Bigr\}\cup\Bigl\{\bigl((x,x^{\prime}),(y,x^{\prime})\bigr)~;~xy\in E,\,x^{\prime}\in N^{\prime}\Bigr\}\,.
