When r=1r=1, the gluing of GG and G′G^{\prime} on KK and K′K^{\prime} with respect to φ\varphi is called a kk-sum where k≔|K|=|K′|k\coloneqq|K|=|K^{\prime}|, denoted G⊕φG′{G\oplus_{\varphi}G^{\prime}} or G⊕kG′{G\oplus_{k}G^{\prime}} when K,K′,φK,K^{\prime},\varphi are clear from the context.

3. Non-𝒜​𝒪{\mathcal{AO}}-Hamiltonicity criteria: modularity, and acyclic polynomials

3.1. Prelude: Expanding on the modularity criterion of Savage, Squire and West

The following Lemmas 3.3 and 3.4 are directly inspired from the method employed in the proof of [37, Theorem 3.2] where Savage, Squire and West showed that ladder graphs Ln≔Pn×K2L_{n}\coloneqq P_{n}\times K_{2} are not 𝒜​𝒪{\mathcal{AO}}-Hamiltonian if nn is even. They prove the reciprocal in [37, Section 4.2], but this is not the purpose of the present section, rather its aim is to develop a useful tool out of the ideas around the number of acyclic orientations modulo 44. In particular, we want to understand the 𝒜​𝒪{\mathcal{AO}}-Hamiltonicity of the Cartesian product G×QnG\times Q_{n} where QnQ_{n} is the nthn^{\text{th}} cube-graph.

The reader inclined to learn more about classes of graphs which are not 𝒜​𝒪{\mathcal{AO}}-Hamiltonian is invited to jump directly to Corollary 3.10. We will need the following two lemmata which are already proven in [37]. We will discuss their proofs in Section 3.2.

Lemma 3.1.

For any graph GG, the number of acyclic orientations ψ⁡(G)\psi(G) is even.

Lemma 3.2 ([37, Lemma 3.1]).

If GG has an even number of edges and ψ⁡(G)\psi(G) is not divisible by 44, then GG is not 𝒜​𝒪{\mathcal{AO}}-Hamiltonian.

Lemma 3.3.

Let G=(N,E)G=(N,E) be a graph with an edge u​v∈Euv\in E and ℓ≥2\ell\geq 2. Then:

ψ(⊕u,vℓG)=(2ℓ−1)⋅ψ(G).\psi\bigl(\oplus_{u,v}^{\ell}G\bigr)=\bigl(2^{\ell}-1\bigr)\cdot\psi(G)\,.

In particular, ψ⁡(G)\psi(G) is divisible by 44 if and only if ψ(⊕u,vℓG)\psi\bigl(\oplus_{u,v}^{\ell}G\bigr) is divisible by 44.

Proof.

Let xx be the node neighboring uu on the induced path of length ℓ\ell of ⊕u,vℓG\oplus_{u,v}^{\ell}G. We perform a deletion-contraction on the edge u​xux. By Stanley’s formula, we get the following (where Pℓ−1P_{\ell-1} denotes a path of length ℓ−1\ell-1), see Figure 2 (left):

ψ(⊕u,vℓG)=ψ(G⊕1Pℓ−1)+ψ(⊕u,vℓ−1G)\psi\bigl(\oplus_{u,v}^{\ell}G\bigr)=\psi(G\oplus_{1}P_{\ell-1})+\psi\bigl(\oplus_{u,v}^{\ell-1}G)

Recall that ψ(H⊕1H′)=ψ(H)⋅ψ(H′)\psi(H\oplus_{1}H^{\prime})=\psi(H)\cdot\psi(H^{\prime}). We get ψ(G⊕1Pℓ−1)=ψ(G)⋅2ℓ−1\psi(G\oplus_{1}P_{\ell-1})=\psi(G)\cdot 2^{\ell-1}. We proceed by induction, until ℓ=2\ell=2, where the contraction ⊕u,vℓ−1G\oplus_{u,v}^{\ell-1}G is just GG itself since u​v∈Euv\in E. Hence, we get:

ψ(⊕u,vℓG)=(∑k=1ℓ−12k)⋅ψ(G)+ψ(G)=(2ℓ−1)⋅ψ(G)\psi\bigl(\oplus_{u,v}^{\ell}G\bigr)=\left(\sum_{k=1}^{\ell-1}2^{k}\right)\cdot\psi(G)+\psi(G)=\bigl(2^{\ell}-1\bigr)\cdot\psi(G)

Note that (2ℓ−1)\bigl(2^{\ell}-1\bigr) is odd for ℓ≥2\ell\geq 2, so it is co-prime with 44. Thus, by Euclid’s lemma, 44 divides ψ(⊕u,vℓG)\psi\bigl(\oplus_{u,v}^{\ell}G\bigr) if and only if 44 divides ψ⁡(G)\psi(G). ∎

Recall that K2K_{2} is the graph with two nodes and one edge.

Theorem 3.4.

Let TT be a tree. We have ψ⁡(T×K2)≡2mod4\psi(T\times K_{2})\equiv 2\mod 4. Moreover, if TT has an even number of nodes (i.e. an odd number of edges), then T×K2T\times K_{2} is not 𝒜​𝒪{\mathcal{AO}}-Hamiltonian.

Proof.

Let nn be the number of nodes of TT (so that n−1n-1 is its number of edges). Consider a leaf uu of TT, and vv its neighboring node in TT. We denote T′T^{\prime} and T′′T^{\prime\prime} the two copies of TT in T×K2T\times K_{2}. Hence, there is an edge v′​v′′v^{\prime}v^{\prime\prime} in T×K2T\times K_{2}, and the graph T×K2T\times K_{2} is isomorphic to ⊕v′​v′′3(T∖{u})×K2\oplus_{v^{\prime}v^{\prime\prime}}^{3}(T\smallsetminus\{u\})\times K_{2}, see Figure 2 (right). By Lemma 3.3, we get that if ψ⁡((T∖{u})×K2)\psi\bigl((T\smallsetminus\{u\})\times K_{2}\bigr) is not divisible by 44, then neither is ψ⁡(T×K2)\psi(T\times K_{2}). By iteratively stripping TT of its leaves, we obtain that if 44 does not divide ψ⁡({x}×K2)\psi(\{x\}\times K_{2}) where xx denotes any arbitrarily chosen node of TT, then 44 does not divide ψ⁡(T×K2)\psi(T\times K_{2}). Since ψ⁡({x}×K2)=ψ⁡(K2)=2\psi(\{x\}\times K_{2})=\psi(K_{2})=2, and the number of acyclic orientations of a graph is always even, we get the first claim.

Moreover, the number of edges of T×K2T\times K_{2} is 3​n−23n-2 which is even if and only if nn is even. We deduce by Lemma 3.2 that if nn is even, then T×K2T\times K_{2} is not 𝒜​𝒪{\mathcal{AO}}-Hamiltonian. ∎

Proposition 3.5.

Let ee be an edge of a graph GG, and Q=Km1×⋯×KmsQ=K_{m_{1}}\times\dots\times K_{m_{s}} be a Cartesian product of cliques where mi=2kim_{i}=2^{k_{i}} for some ki≥1k_{i}\geq 1 for all i∈[s]i\in[s]. Then, we have:

ψ(G×Q)≡ψ((G/e)×Q)+ψ((G∖e)×Q)mod4.\psi(G\times Q)\equiv\psi\bigl((G/_{e})\times Q\bigr)+\psi\bigl((G\smallsetminus e)\times Q\bigr)\mod 4\,.
Proof.

Let m≔2km\coloneqq 2^{k} for some k≥1k\geq 1. We start by proving the case s=1s=1, that is ψ(G×Km)≡ψ((G/e)×Km)+ψ((G∖e)×Km)mod4\psi(G\times K_{m})\equiv\psi\bigl((G/_{e})\times K_{m}\bigr)+\psi\bigl((G\smallsetminus e)\times K_{m}\bigr)\mod 4. For u∈N⁡(Km)u\in N(K_{m}), we denote G×uG\times u the copy of GG associated to the node uu. Pick an edge i​jij of GG, and, for u∈N⁡(Km)u\in N(K_{m}), let i​j×uij\times u be the copy the edge i​jij in G×uG\times u. We are going to apply Stanley’s deletion-contraction formula to all the copies of i​jij. Since i​j×uij\times u and i​j×vij\times v do not share any node as long as u≠vu\neq v, contracting or deleting i​j×uij\times u leaves i​j×vij\times v unaltered. Consequently, we can delete or contract all the copies of i​jij independently, leading to an expression of ψ⁡(G×Km)\psi(G\times K_{m}) as a sum of |2N⁡(Km)|=2m|2^{N(K_{m})}|=2^{m} terms. For X⊆N⁡(Km)X\subseteq N(K_{m}), we denote H⁡(X)H(X) the graph obtained from G×KmG\times K_{m} by contracting all i​j×uij\times u for u∈Xu\in X and deleting all i​j×vij\times v for v∉Xv\notin X. Using Stanley’s formula, we get:

(3.1) ψ⁡(G×Km)=∑X⊆N⁡(Km)ψ⁡(H⁡(X))\psi(G\times K_{m})=\sum_{X\subseteq N(K_{m})}\psi(H(X))

So far, we have not yet used the fact that KmK_{m} is a complete graphs. The group of automorphisms of the complete graph KmK_{m} is the symmetric group on N⁡(Km)=[m]N(K_{m})=[m]. In particular, for any X,Y⊆N⁡(Km)X,Y\subseteq N(K_{m}) such that |X|=|Y||X|=|Y|, there exists an automorphism σ\sigma of KmK_{m} that σ⁡(X)=Y\sigma(X)=Y. This extends to an automorphism on G×KmG\times K_{m} by defining σ¯:i×u↦i×σ⁡(u)\overline{\sigma}:i\times u\mapsto i\times\sigma(u). Moreover, we have σ¯​(H​(X))=H​(Y)\overline{\sigma}(H(X))=H(Y), so the graphs H⁡(X)H(X) and H⁡(Y)H(Y) are isomorphic. In particular, ψ⁡(H⁡(X))=ψ⁡(H⁡(Y))\psi(H(X))=\psi(H(Y)) as long as |X|=|Y||X|=|Y|. Consequently, we denote H⁡(k)H(k) the graph H⁡(X)H(X) for any X⊆N⁡(Km)X\subseteq N(K_{m}) with |X|=k|X|=k. Note that H(0)=(G/i​j)×KmH(0)=(G/_{ij})\times K_{m} since all the copies of i​jij are contracted in H⁡(0)H(0), while H⁡(m)=(G∖i​j)×KmH(m)=(G\smallsetminus ij)\times K_{m} since all the copies of i​jij are deleted in H⁡(m)H(m). Thus, grouping subsets by sizes, Equation 3.1 simplifies to:

ψ⁡(G×Km)=∑k=0m(mk)⋅ψ⁡(H⁡(k))\psi(G\times K_{m})=\sum_{k=0}^{m}\binom{m}{k}\cdot\psi(H(k))

It remains to use the fact that m=2km=2^{k} and that ψ⁡(G)\psi(G) is an even number for any graph GG, by Lemma 3.1. By Lucas’s theorem [26], for any k∉{0,2k}k\notin\{0,2^{k}\}, the binomial coefficient (2kk)\binom{2^{k}}{k} is even. So, for any k∉{0,2k}k\notin\{0,2^{k}\}, the term (mk)⋅ψ⁡(H⁡(k))\binom{m}{k}\cdot\psi(H(k)) is divisible by 44: all the terms of the above sum except for k=0k=0 and k=2kk=2^{k} are equal to 00 modulo 44. We obtain:

ψ(G×K2k)≡ψ((G∖ij)×K2k)+ψ((G/i​j)×K2k)mod4\psi(G\times K_{2^{k}})\equiv\psi\bigl((G\smallsetminus ij)\times K_{2^{k}}\bigr)+\psi\bigl((G/_{ij})\times K_{2^{k}}\bigr)\mod 4

This proves that the function f:G↦(ψ⁡(G×K2k)mod4)f:G\mapsto\bigl(\psi(G\times K_{2^{k}})\mod 4\bigr) defined from the set of graphs towards ℤ/4​ℤ\mathbb{Z}/4\mathbb{Z} satisfies the same deletion-contraction formula as the function g:G↦(ψ⁡(G)mod4)g:G\mapsto\bigl(\psi(G)\mod 4\bigr), i.e. both f(G)=f(G/e)+f(G∖e)f(G)=f(G/_{e})+f(G\smallsetminus e) and g(G)=g(G/e)+g(G∖e)g(G)=g(G/_{e})+g(G\smallsetminus e) for any edge ee of GG. Now fix Q=Km1×⋯×KmsQ=K_{m_{1}}\times\dots\times K_{m_{s}} to be a Cartesian product of cliques where mi=2kim_{i}=2^{k_{i}} for some ki≥1k_{i}\geq 1 for all i∈[s]i\in[s]. Since we have only used the deletion-contraction formula for gg (not the initialization for this recursive formula), one can apply the exact same reasoning to ff inductively in order to prove that ψ(G×Q)≡ψ((G/e)×Q)+ψ((G∖e)×Q)mod4\psi(G\times Q)\equiv\psi\bigl((G/_{e})\times Q\bigr)+\psi\bigl((G\smallsetminus e)\times Q\bigr)\mod 4. ∎

Theorem 3.6.

For any n≥1n\geq 1, the n​thn\textsuperscript{th} cube graph Qn≔K2×⋯×K2Q_{n}\coloneqq K_{2}\times\dots\times K_{2} satisfies ψ⁡(Qn)≡2mod4\psi(Q_{n})\equiv 2\mod 4. Consequently, QnQ_{n} is not 𝒜​𝒪{\mathcal{AO}}-Hamiltonian.

Proof.

The argument boils down to applying Lemma 3.2 using the first part of the theorem, since QnQ_{n} has an even number of edges. It remains to prove the first claim.

Recall that K2K_{2} is just an edge. For n=1n=1, we have ψ⁡(Q1)=ψ⁡(K2)=2\psi(Q_{1})=\psi(K_{2})=2.

For n≥2n\geq 2, note that Qn=K2×K2×⋯×K2=K2×Qn−1Q_{n}=K_{2}\times K_{2}\times\dots\times K_{2}=K_{2}\times Q_{n-1}. We denote ee the edge of this distinguished “first” copy of K2K_{2}. By Proposition 3.5, we have:

ψ(Qn)≡ψ((K2/e)×Qn−1)+ψ((K2∖e)×Qn−1)≡ψ(Qn−1)+ψ(Qn−1⊔Qn−1)mod4.\psi(Q_{n})\equiv\psi\bigl((K_{2}/_{e})\times Q_{n-1}\bigr)+\psi\bigl((K_{2}\smallsetminus e)\times Q_{n-1}\bigr)\equiv\psi(Q_{n-1})+\psi(Q_{n-1}\sqcup Q_{n-1})\mod 4\,.

Last, remark that ψ⁡(H⊔H′)=ψ⁡(H)⋅ψ⁡(H′)\psi(H\sqcup H^{\prime})=\psi(H)\cdot\psi(H^{\prime}) when HH and H′H^{\prime} are node-disjoint graphs. As ψ⁡(H)\psi(H) is divisible by 22 for all graph HH, by Lemma 3.1, we get that 44 divides ψ⁡(H⊔H′)\psi(H\sqcup H^{\prime}) when HH and H′H^{\prime} are node-disjoint graphs. Thus, we get: ψ⁡(Qn)≡ψ⁡(Qn−1)mod4\psi(Q_{n})\equiv\psi(Q_{n-1})\mod 4. By induction, we get ψ⁡(Qn)≡2mod4\psi(Q_{n})\equiv 2\mod 4 for all n≥1n\geq 1. ∎

For the sake of completeness, we also prove the following:

Proposition 3.7.

Let Q=Kp×Km1×⋯×KmsQ=K_{p}\times K_{m_{1}}\times\dots\times K_{m_{s}} be a Cartesian product of cliques where mi=2kim_{i}=2^{k_{i}} for some ki≥1k_{i}\geq 1 for all i∈[s]i\in[s] with s≥1s\geq 1. If p≥3p\geq 3, then ψ⁡(Q)≡0mod4\psi(Q)\equiv 0\mod 4.

Proof.

Let uu be a node of KpK_{p}, and let e1,…,ep−1e_{1},\dots,e_{p-1} be the edges adjacent to uu in KpK_{p}. Note that Kp/eiK_{p}/_{e_{i}} is isomorphic to Kp−1K_{p-1}, while eje_{j} is an edge in Kp∖eiK_{p}\smallsetminus e_{i} as long as i≠ji\neq j. Furthermore, (Kp∖X)/ei(K_{p}\smallsetminus X)/_{e_{i}} is isomorphic to Kp−1K_{p-1} for any X⊆{e1,…,ep−1}∖{ei}X\subseteq\{e_{1},\dots,e_{p-1}\}\smallsetminus\{e_{i}\}. Hence, we can perform p−1p-1 deletion-contractions on the edges e1,…,ep−1e_{1},\dots,e_{p-1} using Proposition 3.5. We get, modulo 44 (where we denote Q′≔Km1×⋯×KmsQ^{\prime}\coloneqq K_{m_{1}}\times\dots\times K_{m_{s}}):

ψ⁡(Kp×Q′)\displaystyle\psi(K_{p}\times Q^{\prime}) ≡ψ((Kp/e1×Q′)+ψ((Kp∖e1×Q′)\displaystyle\equiv\psi\bigl((K_{p}/_{e_{1}}\times Q^{\prime}\bigr)+\psi\bigl((K_{p}\smallsetminus{e_{1}}\times Q^{\prime}\bigr)
≡ψ(Kp−1×Q′)+ψ(((Kp∖e1)/e2)×Q′)+ψ((Kp∖{e1,e2})×Q′)\displaystyle\equiv\psi\bigl(K_{p-1}\times Q^{\prime}\bigr)+\psi\bigl(((K_{p}\smallsetminus{e_{1}})/_{e_{2}})\times Q^{\prime}\bigr)+\psi\bigl((K_{p}\smallsetminus\{e_{1},e_{2}\})\times Q^{\prime}\bigr)
≡2⋅ψ(Kp−1×Q′)+ψ(((Kp∖{e1,e2})/e3)×Q′)+ψ((Kp∖{e1,e2,e3})×Q′)\displaystyle\equiv 2\cdot\psi\bigl(K_{p-1}\times Q^{\prime}\bigr)+\psi\bigl(((K_{p}\smallsetminus\{e_{1},e_{2}\})/_{e_{3}})\times Q^{\prime}\bigr)+\psi\bigl((K_{p}\smallsetminus\{e_{1},e_{2},e_{3}\})\times Q^{\prime}\bigr)
≡…\displaystyle\equiv\ldots
≡(p−1)⋅ψ⁡(Kp−1×Q′)+ψ⁡((Kp−1⊔{u})×Q′)\displaystyle\equiv(p-1)\cdot\psi\bigl(K_{p-1}\times Q^{\prime}\bigr)+\psi((K_{p-1}\sqcup\{u\})\times Q^{\prime})

Recall that ψ⁡(H)\psi(H) is divisible by 22 for any graph HH by Lemma 3.1. Since Kp−1⊔{u}K_{p-1}\sqcup\{u\} is a disconnected graph, ψ⁡((Kp−1⊔{u})×Q′)\psi((K_{p-1}\sqcup\{u\})\times Q^{\prime}) is divisible by 44 (because ψ⁡(H⊔H′)=ψ⁡(H)⋅ψ⁡(H′)\psi(H\sqcup H^{\prime})=\psi(H)\cdot\psi(H^{\prime}) when HH and H′H^{\prime} are node-disjoint graphs). Besides, if p=3p=3, then 44 divides (p−1)⋅ψ⁡(Kp−1×Q′)(p-1)\cdot\psi\bigl(K_{p-1}\times Q^{\prime}\bigr) as a product of even numbers; whereas if p≥4p\geq 4, then 44 divides (p−1)⋅ψ⁡(Kp−1×Q′)(p-1)\cdot\psi\bigl(K_{p-1}\times Q^{\prime}\bigr) by induction on pp. This gives the claim. ∎

Corollary 3.8.

Let GG be a graph and n≥1n\geq 1, then ψ⁡(G×K2)≡ψ⁡(G×Qn)mod4\psi(G\times K_{2})\equiv\psi(G\times Q_{n})\mod 4.

Moreover, if ψ⁡(G×K2)\psi(G\times K_{2}) is not divisible by 44 and if either n≥2n\geq 2 or GG has an even number of nodes, then G×QnG\times Q_{n} is not 𝒜​𝒪{\mathcal{AO}}-Hamiltonian.

Proof.

Consider the two functions on graphs with values in ℤ/4​ℤ\mathbb{Z}/4\mathbb{Z} defined by f:G↦(ψ⁡(G×K2)mod4)f:G\mapsto\bigl(\psi(G\times K_{2})\mod 4\bigr) and g:G↦(ψ⁡(G×Qn)mod4)g:G\mapsto\bigl(\psi(G\times Q_{n})\mod 4\bigr). By Proposition 3.5, the functions ff and gg satisfy the same inductive formula: f(G)=f(G/e)+f(G∖e)f(G)=f(G/_{e})+f(G\smallsetminus e) and g(G)=g(G/e)+g(G∖e)g(G)=g(G/_{e})+g(G\smallsetminus e) for any edge ee of GG. Hence, to prove that ff and gg are equal, it is enough to show that they are equal for the initialization graphs, i.e. for any graph GG which is composed of isolated nodes with no edge.

Let mm be the number of nodes of such GG. If m≥2m\geq 2, then both G×K2G\times K_{2} and G×QnG\times Q_{n} have several connected components, so ψ⁡(G×K2)\psi(G\times K_{2}) and ψ⁡(G×Qn)\psi(G\times Q_{n}) are divisible by 44 because ψ⁡(H⊔H′)=ψ⁡(H)⋅ψ⁡(H′)\psi(H\sqcup H^{\prime})=\psi(H)\cdot\psi(H^{\prime}) when HH and H′H^{\prime} are node-disjoint graphs, and ψ⁡(H)\psi(H) is divisible by 22 for any graph HH by Lemma 3.1. If m=1m=1, then ψ⁡(G×K2)=ψ⁡(K2)=2\psi(G\times K_{2})=\psi(K_{2})=2, and, by Theorem 3.6, ψ⁡(G×Qn)=ψ⁡(Qn)≡2mod4\psi(G\times Q_{n})=\psi(Q_{n})\equiv 2\mod 4. Thus f=gf=g by induction, as claimed.

The “moreover” part boils down to using Lemma 3.2 together with the first part of the corollary, where the condition that n≥2n\geq 2 or GG has an even number of nodes ensures that condition ensures that G×QnG\times Q_{n} has an even number of edges. ∎

Remark 3.9.

Let Q=Km1×⋯×KmsQ=K_{m_{1}}\times\dots\times K_{m_{s}} with mi=2kim_{i}=2^{k_{i}} for some ki≥1k_{i}\geq 1 for all i∈[s]i\in[s]. The proof of Corollary 3.8 suggest that we can explicitly compute (ψ⁡(G×Q)mod4)\bigl(\psi(G\times Q)\mod 4\bigr) running the deletion-contraction algorithm on GG itself, instead of running it on G×QG\times Q. Indeed, the functions with values in ℤ/4​ℤ\mathbb{Z}/4\mathbb{Z} defined as f:G↦(ψ⁡(G×Q)mod4)f:G\mapsto\bigl(\psi(G\times Q)\mod 4\bigr) and g:G↦(ψ⁡(G)mod4)g:G\mapsto\bigl(\psi(G)\mod 4\bigr) satisfy the same recursion, i.e. f(G)=f(G/e)+f(G∖e)f(G)=f(G/_{e})+f(G\smallsetminus e) and g(G)=g(G/e)+g(G∖e)g(G)=g(G/_{e})+g(G\smallsetminus e) for any edge ee of GG. However, it is false to say that ψ⁡(G×Q)≡ψ⁡(G)mod4\psi(G\times Q)\equiv\psi(G)\mod 4 because ff and gg do not have the same value for initialization graphs: If GG consists in mm isolated nodes and no edge, then f⁡(G)≡f⁡(Q)f(G)\equiv f(Q) if m=1m=1 and f⁡(G)=0f(G)=0 if m≥2m\geq 2, but g⁡(G)=1g(G)=1 for all m≥1m\geq 1.

For the case Q=K2Q=K_{2}, and more generally for the cube-graph Q=QnQ=Q_{n}, one can compute recursively ψ⁡(G×K2)mod4\psi(G\times K_{2})\mod 4 as follows. Fix a graph GG. Running the deletion-contraction algorithm on GG until we get forests, means if GG is a forest we do nothing, and otherwise we choose an edge ee of GG, then run the deletion-contraction algorithm on G/eG/_{e} and on G∖eG\smallsetminus e until we get forests. Let tt be the number of trees produced by running the deletion-contraction algorithm on GG until we obtain forests, then ψ⁡(G×K2)≡ψ⁡(G×Qn)≡2⋅tmod4\psi(G\times K_{2})\equiv\psi(G\times Q_{n})\equiv 2\cdot t\mod 4. Hence, ψ⁡(G×K2)\psi(G\times K_{2}) and ψ⁡(G×Qn)\psi(G\times Q_{n}) are divisible by 44 if and only if tt is even. To prove this claim, note that, by Propositions 3.5 and 3.8, we have ψ(G×Qn)≡ψ(G×K2)≡ψ((G/e)×K2)+ψ((G∖e)×K2)\psi(G\times Q_{n})\equiv\psi(G\times K_{2})\equiv\psi\bigl((G/_{e})\times K_{2}\bigr)+\psi\bigl((G\smallsetminus e)\times K_{2}\bigr), and by Theorem 3.4, we have ψ⁡(G×K2)≡2mod4\psi(G\times K_{2})\equiv 2\mod 4 when GG is a tree, while ψ⁡(G×K2)≡0mod4\psi(G\times K_{2})\equiv 0\mod 4 when GG is disconnected.

On the other hand, let k1≥2k_{1}\geq 2 and Q=Km1×⋯×KmsQ=K_{m_{1}}\times\dots\times K_{m_{s}} with mi=2kim_{i}=2^{k_{i}} for some ki≥1k_{i}\geq 1 for all i≥2i\geq 2. By the same reasoning as in the proof of Corollary 3.8, ψ⁡(G×Q)\psi(G\times Q) is equivalent modulo 44 to a certain multiple of ψ⁡(Q)\psi(Q). Since ψ⁡(Q)≡0mod4\psi(Q)\equiv 0\mod 4 by Proposition 3.7, this implies ψ⁡(G×Q)≡0mod4\psi(G\times Q)\equiv 0\mod 4 for all GG, and yields no conclusion on whether G×QG\times Q is 𝒜​𝒪{\mathcal{AO}}-Hamiltonian or not.

We can now prove Theorem A by listing classes of graphs which are not 𝒜​𝒪{\mathcal{AO}}-Hamiltonian. Beyond the usual path on nn nodes PnP_{n}, cycle on nn nodes CnC_{n}, star with nn outer nodes K1,nK_{1,n}, and complete graph on nn nodes KnK_{n}, we need to define the following two classes of graphs.

The wheel graph WnW_{n} is the cycle CnC_{n} together with a central node adjacent to all nodes of CnC_{n}.

For a tree T=([s],E)T=([s],E) and numbers n1,…,ns≥3n_{1},\dots,n_{s}\geq 3, a (T,n1,…,ns)(T,\,n_{1},\dots,n_{s})-tree of cycles is any graph isomorphic to a 22-sum H⊕2CnsH\oplus_{2}C_{n_{s}} where HH is a (T∖s,n1,…,ns−1)(T\smallsetminus s,\,n_{1},\dots,n_{s-1})-tree of cycles (of course for s=1s=1, a (T,n1)(T,\,n_{1})-tree of cycle is just a cycle graph Cn1C_{n_{1}}).

Corollary 3.10.

The following graphs are not 𝒜​𝒪{\mathcal{AO}}-Hamiltonian:

  1. (1)

    Ladder graphs Ln≔Pn×K2L_{n}\coloneqq P_{n}\times K_{2} for any nn even,

  2. (2)

    Book graphs Bn≔K1,n×K2B_{n}\coloneqq K_{1,n}\times K_{2} for any nn odd,

  3. (3)

    Prism graphs Prn≔Cn×K2\mathrm{Pr}_{n}\coloneqq C_{n}\times K_{2} for any nn even,

  4. (4)

    Toroidal grid graphs T4,m≔C4×CmT_{4,m}\coloneqq C_{4}\times C_{m} for any mm even,

  5. (5)

    Cube graphs Qn=K2×⋯×K2Q_{n}=K_{2}\times\dots\times K_{2}, with nn copies of K2K_{2}, for any n≥2n\geq 2,

  6. (6)

    The graph T×QnT\times Q_{n} for any tree TT where either n≥2n\geq 2 or TT has an even number of nodes,

  7. (7)

    Thick wheel graphs TWn≔Wn×K2\mathrm{TW}_{n}\coloneqq W_{n}\times K_{2} for any nn odd,

  8. (8)

    Any (T,n1,…,ns)(T,\,n_{1},\dots,n_{s})-tree of cycles for any tree TT and any n1,…,ns≥1n_{1},\dots,n_{s}\geq 1, if there is some i∈[d]i\in[d] such that nin_{i} is even and if ∑i=1s(ni−1)\sum_{i=1}^{s}(n_{i}-1) is odd.

Proof.

(1) and (2): Ladder and book graphs are of the form T×K2T\times K_{2} where TT is a tree (respectively a path and a star), so by Theorem 3.4, they are not 𝒜​𝒪{\mathcal{AO}}-Hamiltonian when they have an even number of nodes. Ladder graphs already appear in [37, Theorem 3.2].

(3): Let Prn=Cn×K2\mathrm{Pr}_{n}=C_{n}\times K_{2}. We are going to prove by induction that ψ⁡(Prn)\psi(\mathrm{Pr}_{n}) is divisible by 44 if nn is odd, and not divisible by 44 if nn is even. We denote Cn′C_{n}^{\prime} and Cn′′C_{n}^{\prime\prime} the two copies of CnC_{n} in Prn\mathrm{Pr}_{n}. Fix any edge ee of CnC_{n}, and let e′e^{\prime} and e′′e^{\prime\prime} the copies of ee in Cn′C_{n}^{\prime} and Cn′′C_{n}^{\prime\prime}. We denote H′H^{\prime} (resp. H′′H^{\prime\prime}) the graph obtained by contracting e′e^{\prime} and deleting e′′e^{\prime\prime} (resp. by deleting e′e^{\prime} and contracting e′′e^{\prime\prime}) in Prn\mathrm{Pr}_{n}. Note that H′H^{\prime} and H′′H^{\prime\prime} are isomorphic. By deletion-contraction on the edges e′e^{\prime} and e′′e^{\prime\prime}, we have (using Cn/e≃Cn−1C_{n}/_{e}\simeq C_{n-1}):

ψ⁡(Prn)\displaystyle\psi(\mathrm{Pr}_{n}) =ψ((Cn∖e)×K2)+ψ(H′)+ψ(H′′)+ψ((Cn/e)×K2)\displaystyle=\psi\bigl((C_{n}\smallsetminus e)\times K_{2}\bigr)+\psi(H^{\prime})+\psi(H^{\prime\prime})+\psi\bigl((C_{n}/_{e})\times K_{2}\bigr)
=ψ⁡((Cn∖e)×K2)+2⋅ψ⁡(H′)+ψ⁡(Prn−1)\displaystyle=\psi\bigl((C_{n}\smallsetminus e)\times K_{2}\bigr)+2\cdot\psi(H^{\prime})+\psi(\mathrm{Pr}_{n-1})
≡ψ⁡((Cn∖e)×K2)+ψ⁡(Prn−1)mod4\displaystyle\equiv\psi\bigl((C_{n}\smallsetminus e)\times K_{2}\bigr)+\psi(\mathrm{Pr}_{n-1})\mod 4

Since (Cn∖e)×K2(C_{n}\smallsetminus e)\times K_{2} is a ladder graph on an even number of nodes, 44 does not divide ψ⁡((Cn∖e)×K2)\psi\bigl((C_{n}\smallsetminus e)\times K_{2}\bigr), by the proof of (1), so ψ⁡((Cn∖e)×K2)≡2mod4\psi\bigl((C_{n}\smallsetminus e)\times K_{2}\bigr)\equiv 2\mod 4. Hence, by induction, ψ⁡(Prn)≡2⋅(n−1)mod4\psi(\mathrm{Pr}_{n})\equiv 2\cdot(n-1)\mod 4 because Pr2=C4\mathrm{Pr}_{2}=C_{4} with ψ⁡(C4)=14≡2mod4\psi(C_{4})=14\equiv 2\mod 4. Thus, if nn is even, ψ⁡(Prn)\psi(\mathrm{Pr}_{n}) is not divisible by 44. As the number of edges of Prn\mathrm{Pr}_{n} is 3​n3n, we get the claim.

(4): We just proved that ψ⁡(Cm×K2)≡2mod4\psi(C_{m}\times K_{2})\equiv 2\mod 4. Since C4=K2×K2=Q2C_{4}=K_{2}\times K_{2}=Q_{2}, by Corollary 3.8, we have ψ⁡(Cm×C4)≡ψ⁡(Cm×K2)≢0mod4\psi(C_{m}\times C_{4})\equiv\psi(C_{m}\times K_{2})\not\equiv 0\mod 4, so by Lemma 3.2, we get that T4,m=Cm×C4T_{4,m}=C_{m}\times C_{4} is not 𝒜​𝒪{\mathcal{AO}}-Hamiltonian for all mm even because T4,mT_{4,m} has an even number of edges.

(5): This is Theorem 3.6.

(6): Combine Theorems 3.4 and 3.8 where T×QnT\times Q_{n} has an even number of edges if n≥2n\geq 2 or if TT has an even number of nodes.

(7): We use the same decomposition that Savage, Squire and West applied to the wheel graph WnW_{n} in the proof of [37, Theorem 3.1]. Let ee be and edge of WnW_{n} which does not contain the central node, and let Gn=Wn∖eG_{n}=W_{n}\smallsetminus e and TGn=Gn×K2\mathrm{TG}_{n}=G_{n}\times K_{2}. Note that Wn/e=Wn−1W_{n}/_{e}=W_{n-1}, hence by deletion-contraction and Proposition 3.5, we have: ψ⁡(TWn)≡ψ⁡(TWn−1)+ψ⁡(TGn)mod4\psi(\mathrm{TW}_{n})\equiv\psi(\mathrm{TW}_{n-1})+\psi(\mathrm{TG}_{n})\mod 4. Moreover, let ff be and edge of GnG_{n} not containing the central node xx, then Gn/f=Gn−1G_{n}/_{f}=G_{n-1} and Gn∖fG_{n}\smallsetminus f is a 11-sum of Gn−1G_{n-1} with a single edge. In particular, by Lemma 3.3, ψ⁡((Gn∖f)×K2)≡ψ⁡(TGn−1)mod4\psi\bigl((G_{n}\smallsetminus f)\times K_{2}\bigr)\equiv\psi(\mathrm{TG}_{n-1})\mod 4 since (Gn∖f)×K2(G_{n}\smallsetminus f)\times K_{2} is obtained from TGn−1\mathrm{TG}_{n-1} by gluing a path of length 33 on the edge {x}×K2\{x\}\times K_{2}. Thus, by Lemmas 3.1 and 3.5, we get: ψ⁡(TGn)≡2⋅ψ⁡(TGn−1)≡0mod4\psi(\mathrm{TG}_{n})\equiv 2\cdot\psi(\mathrm{TG}_{n-1})\equiv 0\mod 4. Consequently, ψ⁡(TWn)≡ψ⁡(TWn−1)mod4\psi(\mathrm{TW}_{n})\equiv\psi(\mathrm{TW}_{n-1})\mod 4, and by induction, since ψ⁡(TW1)≡ψ⁡(C4)≡2mod4\psi(\mathrm{TW}_{1})\equiv\psi(C_{4})\equiv 2\mod 4, we obtain ψ⁡(TWn)≡2mod4\psi(\mathrm{TW}_{n})\equiv 2\mod 4. As the wheel graph WnW_{n} has an even number of edges and n+1n+1 nodes, the thick wheel graph has an even number of edges when nn is odd, so we conclude by Lemma 3.2.

(8): Fix a (T,n1,…,ns)(T,n_{1},\dots,n_{s})-tree of cycle GG with nin_{i} even for some i∈[s]i\in[s]. Note that the number of edges of GG, namely 1+∑i=1s(ni−1)1+\sum_{i=1}^{s}(n_{i}-1), is even by hypothesis. Let i1,…,isi_{1},\dots,i_{s} be an enumeration of [s][s], with ni1n_{i_{1}} even, such that Tj=T⁡[{i1,…,ij}]T_{j}=T[\{i_{1},\dots,i_{j}\}] is a tree. In particular, iji_{j} is a leaf in TjT_{j}. Let also GjG_{j} be the (Tj,ni1,…,nij)(T_{j},n_{i_{1}},\dots,n_{i_{j}})-subtree of cycle of GG. As GjG_{j} is obtained from Gj−1G_{j-1} by gluing a path of length nj−1n_{j}-1 on an edge, ψ⁡(Gj)\psi(G_{j}) is divisible by 44 if and only if ψ⁡(Gj−1)mod4\psi(G_{j-1})\mod 4 is divisible by 44, by Lemma 3.3. Since G1G_{1} is an even cycle with ni1n_{i_{1}} nodes, ψ⁡(G1)≡2mod4\psi(G_{1})\equiv 2\mod 4 by Example 3.16, so ψ⁡(G)\psi(G) is not divisible by 44. By Lemma 3.2, GG is not 𝒜​𝒪{\mathcal{AO}}-Hamiltonian. ∎

Remark 3.11.

We have only presented a few possible applications of Lemmas 3.3 and 3.5 together with the usual deletion-contraction formula. The reader is invited to try to compute ψ⁡(G×K2)mod4\psi(G\times K_{2})\mod 4 for their favorite (family of) graphs GG, and conclude on the 𝒜​𝒪{\mathcal{AO}}-Hamiltonicity of G×K2G\times K_{2} if the number of nodes of GG is odd, using Lemma 3.2.

Note that any result proven for G×K2G\times K_{2} immediately extends to G×QnG\times Q_{n} for n≥1n\geq 1 thanks to Corollary 3.8.

We give one last structural result relying on the same ideas. This can be used to start tackling non-22-connected graphs.

Proposition 3.12.

If GG is disconnected, then ψ⁡(G×Qn)≡ψ⁡(G)≡0mod4\psi(G\times Q_{n})\equiv\psi(G)\equiv 0\mod 4 for all n≥1n\geq 1.

Moreover, for any graph GG and any tree TT, we have for all n≥1n\geq 1:

ψ((G⊕1T)×Qn)≡ψ((G⊕1T)×K2)≡ψ(G×K2)mod4.\psi\bigl((G\oplus_{1}T)\times Q_{n}\bigr)\equiv\psi\bigl((G\oplus_{1}T)\times K_{2}\bigr)\equiv\psi(G\times K_{2})\mod 4\,.
Proof.

The first statement comes from ψ⁡(H⊔H′)=ψ⁡(H)⋅ψ⁡(H′)\psi(H\sqcup H^{\prime})=\psi(H)\cdot\psi(H^{\prime}) for node-disjoint graphs HH and H′H^{\prime}, and 22 divides both ψ⁡(H)\psi(H) and ψ⁡(H′)\psi(H^{\prime}) by Lemma 3.1 (note that (H⊔H′)×Qn(H\sqcup H^{\prime})\times Q_{n} is also disconnected).

The first equivalence of the second statement is given by Corollary 3.8. For the second one, let uu be a leaf of TT which is not the one shared by GG in G⊕1TG\oplus_{1}T, let vv be the unique neighbor of uu in TT, and let T′=T∖uT^{\prime}=T\smallsetminus u. Then (G⊕1T)×K2(G\oplus_{1}T)\times K_{2} is obtained from (G⊕1T′)×K2(G\oplus_{1}T^{\prime})\times K_{2} by gluing a path of length 33 on the edge {v}×K2\{v\}\times K_{2}. By Lemma 3.3, we have that ψ((G⊕1T)×K2)≡7⋅ψ((G⊕1T′)×K2)≡ψ((G⊕1T′)×K2)mod4\psi\bigl((G\oplus_{1}T)\times K_{2}\bigr)\equiv 7\cdot\psi\bigl((G\oplus_{1}T^{\prime})\times K_{2}\bigr)\equiv\psi\bigl((G\oplus_{1}T^{\prime})\times K_{2}\bigr)\mod 4. Trimming TT of its leaves recursively, we get the claim. ∎

We conclude by discussing further possible research angles that use the same core idea of counting the number of acyclic orientations of graphs and checking its divisibility by 44.

Example 3.13.

Our computer experiments show that the following graphs GG satisfy ψ⁡(G)≡2mod4\psi(G)\equiv 2\mod 4, and hence are not 𝒜​𝒪{\mathcal{AO}}-Hamiltonian since they have an even number of edges:

  1. (1)

    The octahedral graph;

  2. (2)

    The Franklin graph;

  3. (3)

    The Herschel graph;

  4. (4)

    The Möbius–Kantor graph;

  5. (5)

    The Desargues graph;

  6. (6)

    The triangular grid graphs Trn,m\mathrm{Tr}_{n,m} for (n,m)∈{(3,3),(3,5)}(n,m)\in\{(3,3),(3,5)\};

  7. (7)

    The graph of the antiprisms AnA_{n} for n∈{3,6}n\in\{3,6\} but not for n∈{4,5,7,8}n\in\{4,5,7,8\};

  8. (8)

    The grid graphs Grn,m=Pn×Pm\mathrm{Gr}_{n,m}=P_{n}\times P_{m} for (n,m)∈{(3,3),(3,5),(3,7)}(n,m)\in\{(3,3),(3,5),(3,7)\} but not for n=m=4n=m=4;

  9. (9)

    The complete tripartite graphs Km,n,pK_{m,n,p} for n=m=2n=m=2 and 2≤p≤72\leq p\leq 7 and for (n,m,p)=(2,3,4)(n,m,p)=(2,3,4)

  10. (10)

    The generalized Petersen graphs Pet⁡(n,k)\mathrm{Pet}(n,k) for (n,k)∈{(6,1),(8,1),(8,3),(10,1),(10,3)}(n,k)\in\{(6,1),(8,1),(8,3),(10,1),(10,3)\} but not for (n,k)∈{(6,2),(8,2),(10,2),(10,4)}(n,k)\in\{(6,2),(8,2),(10,2),(10,4)\}.

The reader must be careful: each “but not” means that ψ⁡(G)≡0mod4\psi(G)\equiv 0\mod 4, it does not imply that GG is 𝒜​𝒪{\mathcal{AO}}-Hamiltonian. Note also that the number of acyclic orientations of Chvátal graphs is divisible by 44, yet it is not 𝒜​𝒪{\mathcal{AO}}-Hamiltonian, see Table 5: we will need the notion of acyclic signature studied in Section 3.3 to understand this case.

In view of the previous example list, we conjecture the following.

Conjecture 1.

For the following graphs GG, we have ψ⁡(G)≡2mod4\psi(G)\equiv 2\mod 4, and consequently GG is not 𝒜​𝒪{\mathcal{AO}}-Hamiltonian since GG has an even number of edges:

  1. (1)

    The grid graphs Grn,m=Pn×Pm\mathrm{Gr}_{n,m}=P_{n}\times P_{m} for m,n≥3m,n\geq 3 both odd;

  2. (2)

    The triangular grid graphs Trn,m\mathrm{Tr}_{n,m} for m,n≥3m,n\geq 3 both odd;

  3. (3)

    The generalized Petersen graphs Pet⁡(n,k)\mathrm{Pet}(n,k) for nn even and kk odd;

  4. (4)

    The complete tripartite graphs Km,n,pK_{m,n,p} for nn, mm, pp not all odd.

We believe that methods similar to the one studied above for path gluing and Cartesian products may be developed in these cases. Note that the ladder graphs (i.e. grid graphs Gr2,m\mathrm{Gr}_{2,m}) and the complete bipartite graphs were already dealt with by Savage, Squire and West [37].

3.2. The acyclic polynomial in general

For graphs, using a deletion-contraction recursion proven by Stanley [40], one can compute the number ψ⁡(G)\psi(G) of acyclic orientations of the graph G=(N,E)G=(N,E): for all u​v∈Euv\in E, we have ψ(G)=ψ(G/u​v)+ψ(G∖uv)\psi(G)=\psi(G/_{uv})+\psi(G\smallsetminus uv). This yields a counting algorithm with time complexity O⁡(φ|N|+|E|)O\bigl(\varphi^{|N|+|E|}\bigr) where φ≔1+52\varphi\coloneqq\frac{1+\sqrt{5}}{2}, see [46, end of Section 2.3]. Our ultimate goal is to present a similar, although incomplete, algorithm for computing the acyclic signature σ⁡(D)\sigma(D) of an orientation of GG. This will be done in Section 3.3. It is natural to count acyclic orientations according to their rank (with respect to a fixed base orientation).

3.2.1. Definition and first examples

For a digraph DD, the acyclic polynomial is defined as

Ψ⁡(D,t)≔∑A∈𝒜​𝒪​(D)trkD⁡A.{\Psi(D;t)}\coloneqq\sum_{A\in{\mathcal{AO}}(D)}t^{\rank_{D}A}\,.

By convention, Ψ⁡(D,t)=1\Psi(D;t)=1 if DD has no edge. Clearly, for any orientation DD of GG, one has ψ⁡(G)=Ψ⁡(D,1)\psi(G)=\Psi(D;1), and σ⁡(D)=Ψ⁡(D,−1)\sigma(D)=\Psi(D;-1).

We give 2222 examples of acyclic polynomials for small, well-known graphs in Appendix D.

Remark 3.14.

The coefficients of Ψ⁡(D,t)\Psi(D;t) are the Whitney numbers of the second kind of the poset of regions of the graphic arrangement with base region given by DD. See [42, Section 3.10], for the general definition and background. We will not make use of this perspective, since our goal is to present graph-theoretic proofs of every claim.

Example 3.15 (Trees).

For a tree TT with mm edges, recall that all orientations are acyclic. Hence, for any orientation DD of TT, we get |𝒜​𝒪k​(D)|=|𝒪k​(D)|=(mk)|{\mathcal{AO}}_{k}(D)|=|{\mathcal{O}}_{k}(D)|=\binom{m}{k}. Thus we get

Ψ⁡(D,t)=∑k(mk)​tk=(1+t)m.\Psi(D;t)=\sum_{k}\binom{m}{k}t^{k}=(1+t)^{m}\,.

We recover that the number of acyclic orientations of TT is ψ⁡(T)=Ψ⁡(D,1)=2m\psi(T)=\Psi(D;1)=2^{m} while its signature is σ⁡(D)=Ψ⁡(D,−1)=0\sigma(D)=\Psi(D;-1)=0.

Example 3.16 (Cycles).

For a cycle Cn=([n],E)C_{n}=([n],E) all orientations except 2 are acyclic. Let DD be one of the cyclic orientations of CnC_{n}, hence DED^{E} is the other cyclic orientation of CnC_{n}.

Thus Ψ⁡(D,t)=(1+t)n−1−tn.\Psi(D;t)=(1+t)^{n}-1-t^{n}\,. We recover that the number of acyclic orientations of CnC_{n} is ψ⁡(Cn)=Ψ⁡(D,1)=2n−2\psi(C_{n})=\Psi(D;1)=2^{n}-2 while its signature is σ⁡(D)=Ψ⁡(D,−1)={0 if ​n​ is odd−2 if ​n​ is even\sigma(D)=\Psi(D;-1)=\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}0&\text{ if }n\text{ is odd}\\ -2&\text{ if }n\text{ is even}\end{array}\right..

Changing the base orientation from a cyclic orientation DD to some acyclic orientation A=DXA=D^{X} with |X|=q|X|=q, we easily get Ψ⁡(A,t)=(1+t)n−tq−tn−q,\Psi(A;t)=(1+t)^{n}-t^{q}-t^{n-q}\,, yielding σ⁡(A)={0 if ​n​ is odd(−1)q+1⋅2 if ​n​ is even\sigma(A)=\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}0&\text{ if }n\text{ is odd}\\ (-1)^{q+1}\cdot 2&\text{ if }n\text{ is even}\end{array}\right..

Example 3.17.

As our running example, the complete bipartite graph K2,3K_{2,3} has 4646 acyclic orientations, and its acyclic signature is ±6\pm 6 depending on the chosen orientation. We depict all the possible acyclic polynomials in Figure 3. Out of the 26=642^{6}=64 orientations of K2,3K_{2,3}, we only get 88 different polynomials: as we will see in Corollary 3.46, reversing the directions of all arcs yield the same acyclic polynomial; and moreover, it is clear that if two base orientations DD and D′D^{\prime} differ by an automorphism of the underlying graph GG, then their associated acyclic polynomials are identical.

Remark 3.18.

Since we will show that the acyclic polynomial admits a deletion-contraction phenomenon (see Section 3.2.6), one might wonder if Ψ⁡(D,t)\Psi(D;t) is a specialization of the famous Tutte–Whitney polynomial of GG for some orientation DD of the graph GG. We conjecture that this is not possible, and we now argue against it.

Let G=K2,3G=K_{2,3}, and DD the orientation of GG of Figure 3. The Tutte–Whitney polynomial of GG is TK2,3​(x,y)=x4+2​x3+3​x2+3​x​y+y2+x+y.T_{K_{2,3}}(x,y)=x^{4}+2x^{3}+3x^{2}+3xy+y^{2}+x+y\,.

On the other hand, Ψ⁡(D,t)=1+6​t+9​t2+14​t3+9​t4+6​t5+1\Psi(D;t)=1+6t+9t^{2}+14t^{3}+9t^{4}+6t^{5}+1 is of degree 66 (since DD has been chosen acyclic), as indicated in Figure 3. There are many ways to interpret “being a specialization of TK2,3T_{K_{2,3}}”; we are going to prove that it is impossible that there exist polynomials A⁡(t),B⁡(t)A(t),B(t) with real coefficients, such that TK2,3​(A⁡(t),B⁡(t))=Ψ⁡(D,t)T_{K_{2,3}}\bigl(A(t),B(t)\bigr)=\Psi(D;t).

Indeed, suppose it is the case, and let aa (resp. bb) be the degree of A⁡(t)A(t) (resp. B⁡(t)B(t)). The degree of TK2,3​(A⁡(t),B⁡(t))T_{K_{2,3}}\bigl(A(t),B(t)\bigr) depends on which of 4​a4a and 2​b2b is the greatest (since a+b<max⁡(4​a,2​b)a+b<\max(4a,2b)). In particular, we need to have max⁡(4​a,2​b)≥6\max(4a,2b)\geq 6.

  • •

    If 4​a>2​b4a>2b, then the degree of TK2,3​(A⁡(t),B⁡(t))T_{K_{2,3}}\bigl(A(t),B(t)\bigr) is 4​a4a which needs to be equal to 66, but cannot.

  • •

    If 4​a<2​b4a<2b, then the degree of TK2,3​(A⁡(t),B⁡(t))T_{K_{2,3}}\bigl(A(t),B(t)\bigr) is 2​b2b which needs to be equal to 66, so b=3b=3 and a≤1a\leq 1. Hence, writing A⁡(t)=α0+α1​tA(t)=\alpha_{0}+\alpha_{1}t and B⁡(t)=β0+β1​t+β2​t2+β3​t3B(t)=\beta_{0}+\beta_{1}t+\beta_{2}t^{2}+\beta_{3}t^{3}, one can develop TK2,3​(A⁡(t),B⁡(t))=Ψ⁡(D,t)T_{K_{2,3}}\bigl(A(t),B(t)\bigr)=\Psi(D;t) to get 77 equations involving the 66 variables α0,α1,β0,β1,β2,β3\alpha_{0},\alpha_{1},\beta_{0},\beta_{1},\beta_{2},\beta_{3}. A tedious computation (or a solver of polynomial systems) shows that this explicit system has no solutions.

  • •

    If 4​a>64a>6 and 2​b>62b>6, then 4​a=2​b4a=2b and the leading coefficients of A​(t)4A(t)^{4} and B​(t)2B(t)^{2} compensate each other (otherwise the degree of TK2,3​(A⁡(t),B⁡(t))T_{K_{2,3}}\bigl(A(t),B(t)\bigr) would not be 66). Yet, since 44 and 22 are even powers, this is not possible.

Consequently, there exists a graph GG (e.g. G=K2,3G=K_{2,3}) and an orientation DD of GG (actually several) such that for all polynomials A⁡(t),B⁡(t)∈ℝ⁡[t]A(t),B(t)\in\mathbb{R}[t], we have TG​(A⁡(t),B⁡(t))≠Ψ⁡(D,t)T_{G}(A(t),B(t))\neq\Psi(D;t). However, this does not rule out the possibility that TG​(A⁡(t),B⁡(t))=Ψ⁡(D,t)T_{G}(A(t),B(t))=\Psi(D;t) for some orientation DD of some graph GG and for some polynomials A⁡(t),B⁡(t)∈ℂ⁡[t]A(t),B(t)\in\mathbb{C}[t]. We still believe this cannot happen except in trivial cases, but cannot (un)prove it.

Remark 3.19.

It is well-known (e.g. see [40]) that ψ⁡(G)=χ⁡(G,−1)\psi(G)=\chi(G;-1) where χ⁡(G,x)\chi(G;x) is the chromatic polynomial of GG, i.e. χ⁡(G,c)\chi(G;c) is the number of ways one can color GG using cc colors, such that no edge has both endpoints of the same color. The chromatic and acyclic polynomials shall not be confused: in general Ψ⁡(D,t)≠χ⁡(D¯,−t)\Psi(D;t)\neq\chi(\underline{D};-t) for a digraph DD. For example, one can compare the results of Figure 3 with: χ⁡(K2,3,x)=7​x−17​x2+15​x3−6​x4+x5\chi(K_{2,3};x)=7x-17x^{2}+15x^{3}-6x^{4}+x^{5}.

We do not know if there exists a polynomial Φ⁡(D,t,x)\Phi(D;t,x), satisfying a deletion-contraction recursion, from which both Ψ⁡(D,t)\Psi(D;t) and χ⁡(D¯,x)\chi(\underline{D};x) can be naturally recovered (e.g. such that Φ⁡(D,t,1)=Ψ⁡(D,t)\Phi(D;t,1)=\Psi(D;t) and Φ⁡(D,1,x)=χ⁡(D¯,x)\Phi(D;1,x)=\chi(\underline{D};x) for all x,tx,t). We saw in Remark 3.18 that if such a polynomial were to exist, it could not be a specification of the Tutte–Whitney polynomial.

Proposition 3.20.

Let GG be a graph and 𝒪⁡(G){\mathcal{O}}(G) the set of all its orientations, then

∑D∈𝒪⁡(G)Ψ⁡(D,t)=(1+t)|E|⋅ψ⁡(G).\sum_{D\in{\mathcal{O}}(G)}\Psi(D;t)=(1+t)^{|E|}\cdot\psi(G).
Proof.

Note that we have rkD⁡A=rkA⁡D\rank_{D}A=\rank_{A}D, by definition (the number of arcs on which AA differs from DD is equal to the number of arcs on which DD differs from AA). We have:

∑D∈𝒪⁡(G)Ψ⁡(D,t)=∑D∈𝒪⁡(G)A∈𝒜​𝒪​(G)trkD⁡A=∑A∈𝒜​𝒪​(G)∑D∈𝒪⁡(G)trkA⁡D=∑A∈𝒜​𝒪​(G)(1+t)|E|=(1+t)|E|⋅ψ⁡(G)\sum_{D\in{\mathcal{O}}(G)}\Psi(D;t)=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}D\in{\mathcal{O}}(G)\\ A\in{\mathcal{AO}}(G)\end{subarray}}t^{\rank_{D}A}=\sum_{A\in{\mathcal{AO}}(G)}\sum_{D\in{\mathcal{O}}(G)}t^{\rank_{A}D}=\sum_{A\in{\mathcal{AO}}(G)}(1+t)^{|E|}=(1+t)^{|E|}\cdot\psi(G)

where for any A∈𝒜​𝒪​(G)A\in{\mathcal{AO}}(G) we have: ∑D∈𝒪⁡(G)trkA⁡D=∑X⊆EtrkA⁡AX=∑X⊆Et|X|=(1+t)|E|\sum_{D\in{\mathcal{O}}(G)}t^{\rank_{A}D}=\sum_{X\subseteq E}t^{\rank_{A}A^{X}}=\sum_{X\subseteq E}t^{|X|}=(1+t)^{|E|}. ∎

Example 3.21.

For the complete bipartite graph K2,3K_{2,3}, Proposition 3.20 gives ∑D∈𝒪⁡(K2,3)Ψ⁡(D,t)=46⋅(1+t)6\sum_{D\in{\mathcal{O}}(K_{2,3})}\Psi(D;t)=46\cdot(1+t)^{6}. This can be checked by summing the polynomials of Figure 3, taking into account the reversion of all the arcs of each orientation and their multiplicities.

3.2.2. Disconnected graphs and 1-sums of graphs

As an easy property of acyclic polynomials, we show that the acyclic polynomial of a disconnected graph is the product of the acyclic polynomials of its connected components, while the acyclic polynomial of a 11-sum of graphs is the product of the acyclic polynomials of the summands.

Proposition 3.22.

Let G=(N,E)G=(N,E) be a disconnected graph with connected components N1,…,NrN_{1},\dots,N_{r}, and DD an orientation of GG, then:

Ψ⁡(D,t)=∏k=1rΨ⁡(D⁡[Nk],t).\Psi(D;t)=\prod_{k=1}^{r}\Psi(D[N_{k}];t)\,.
Proof.

It is trivial that the map A↦(A⁡[N1],…,A⁡[Nr])A\mapsto(A[N_{1}],\dots,A[N_{r}]) is a bijection between 𝒜​𝒪​(G){\mathcal{AO}}(G) and 𝒜​𝒪​(G⁡[N1])×⋯×𝒜​𝒪​(G⁡[Nr]){\mathcal{AO}}(G[N_{1}])\times\dots\times{\mathcal{AO}}(G[N_{r}]). Moreover, given a fixed acyclic orientation DD of GG, we have rkD⁡A=rkD⁡[N1]⁡A⁡[N1]+⋯+rkD⁡[Nr]⁡A⁡[Nr]\rank_{D}A=\rank_{D[N_{1}]}A[N_{1}]+\dots+\rank_{D[N_{r}]}A[N_{r}]. Thus:

Ψ⁡(D,t)=∑A∈𝒜​𝒪​(G)trkD⁡A=∑A1,…,Ar∈𝒜​𝒪​(G⁡[N1])×⋯×𝒜​𝒪​(G⁡[Nr])∏k=1rtrkD⁡[Nk]⁡A⁡[Nk]=∏k=1rΨ⁡(D⁡[Nk],t),\Psi(D;t)=\sum_{A\in{\mathcal{AO}}(G)}t^{\rank_{D}A}=\sum_{A_{1},\dots,A_{r}\in{\mathcal{AO}}(G[N_{1}])\times\dots\times{\mathcal{AO}}(G[N_{r}])}\prod_{k=1}^{r}t^{\rank_{D[N_{k}]}A[N_{k}]}=\prod_{k=1}^{r}\Psi(D[N_{k}];t)\,,

where the last equality comes from exchanging the sum with the product and summing over each 𝒜​𝒪​(G⁡[Nk]){\mathcal{AO}}(G[N_{k}]) independently. ∎

Proposition 3.23.

Let G=H⊕1H′G=H\oplus_{1}H^{\prime} be a 11-sum of graphs. For any orientation DD of GG, one naturally has D=D[H]⊕1D[H′]D=D[H]\oplus_{1}D[H^{\prime}], and obtains Ψ⁡(D,t)=Ψ⁡(D⁡[H],t)⋅Ψ⁡(D⁡[H′],t).\Psi(D;t)=\Psi(D[H];t)\cdot\Psi(D[H^{\prime}];t)\,.

Proof.

The map A↦(A⁡[H],A⁡[H′])A\mapsto(A[H],A[H^{\prime}]) is a bijection between 𝒜​𝒪​(G){\mathcal{AO}}(G) and 𝒜​𝒪​(H)×𝒜​𝒪​(H′){\mathcal{AO}}(H)\times{\mathcal{AO}}(H^{\prime}) since it is impossible to create a (directed) cycle in GG using arcs of both HH and H′H^{\prime}. Moreover, rkD⁡A=rkD⁡[H]⁡A⁡[H]+rkD⁡[H′]⁡A⁡[H′]\rank_{D}A=\rank_{D[H]}A[H]+\rank_{D[H^{\prime}]}A[H^{\prime}]. The claim follows. ∎

Consequently, it is enough to compute acyclic polynomials of 22-connected graphs in order to recover the acyclic polynomials of all graphs.

3.2.3. Simplicial nodes, chordal graphs, complete graphs

A graph GG is chordal if all its induced cycles have length 33. On the other hand, a perfect elimination ordering of a graph G=(N,E)G=(N,E) with |N|=n|N|=n is a bijection θ:[n]→N\theta:[n]\to N such that for all i∈[n]i\in[n] the neighbors of θ⁡(i)\theta(i) in {θ⁡(1),…,θ⁡(i−1)}\{\theta(1),\dots,\theta(i-1)\} form a clique in GG (i.e. are pairwise connected by an edge in GG). We say that θ⁡(i)\theta(i) is simplicial in G⁡[{θ⁡(1),…,θ⁡(i−1)}]G[\{\theta(1),\dots,\theta(i-1)\}]. It is well-known, see [35] that GG is chordal if and only if GG admits a perfect elimination ordering.

Remark 3.24.

For a graph G=(N,E)G=(N,E) with an orientation DD, the coefficients of the acyclic polynomial Ψ⁡(D,t)\Psi(D;t) are the Whitney numbers of the second kind of the graphic hyperplane arrangement ℋG≔({𝒙∈ℝN;xi=xj},i​j∈E){\mathcal{H}}_{G}\coloneqq\bigl(\{{\boldsymbol{x}}\in\mathbb{R}^{N}~;~x_{i}=x_{j}\}~;~ij\in E\bigr) with respect to the base chamber corresponding to DD, i.e. 𝖢D≔{xi≤xj;i​j∈D}\mathsf{C}_{D}\coloneqq\{x_{i}\leq x_{j}~;~ij\in D\}. In particular, the graphic hyperplane arrangement of chordal graphs are known to be supersolvable. In this context, the formula of Proposition 3.26 is already known, see [5, Thm 4.4 & Cor. 4.5].

Moreover, Edelman and Reiner [16] proved that the sequence of exponents of the graphic arrangement associated to a chordal graph is precisely the elimination-degree sequence defined thereafter. As the sequence of exponents is an invariant of the hyperplane arrangement, the independence from a specific base chamber (i.e. from a specific perfect elimination ordering) follows automatically, see [16, Lemma 3.4].

Accordingly, we do not pretend that Propositions 3.26, 3.28 and 3.29 are new, but we give graph-theoretical proofs below for the sake of self-containment, and to showcase how to compute acyclic polynomials. Besides, Lemmas 3.25, 3.31 and 3.32 seem not to appear in the existing literature, although we believe that other authors may have already thought about it. Finally, Theorem 3.36 is new, as far as we are aware.

In order to prove Proposition 3.26, we first state the following more general lemma. A node is called simplicial if its neighbors form a clique.

Lemma 3.25.

Let G=(N,E)G=(N,E) be a graph with a simplicial node v∈Nv\in N with bb neighbors. Let DD be an orientation of GG where all edges u​vuv are directed from uu to vv, and let D′=D∖{v}D^{\prime}=D\smallsetminus\{v\}. Then:

Ψ⁡(D,t)=Ψ⁡(D′,t)⋅(1+t+⋯+tb)=Ψ⁡(D′,t)⋅1−tb+11−t.\Psi(D;t)=\Psi(D^{\prime};t)\cdot(1+t+\dots+t^{b})=\Psi(D^{\prime};t)\cdot\frac{1-t^{b+1}}{1-t}\,.

In particular ψ⁡(G)=Ψ⁡(D,1)=ψ⁡(G∖{v})⋅(b+1)\psi(G)=\Psi(D;1)=\psi(G\smallsetminus\{v\})\cdot(b+1), and if bb is odd then σ⁡(D)=Ψ⁡(D,−1)=0\sigma(D)=\Psi(D;-1)=0, if bb is even, then σ⁡(D)=σ⁡(D′)\sigma(D)=\sigma(D^{\prime}).

Proof.

The rightmost equality is immediate. The values of ψ⁡(G)\psi(G) and σ⁡(D)\sigma(D) come from direct evaluations.

To ease notation, let G′≔G∖{v}G^{\prime}\coloneqq G\smallsetminus\{v\} and U⊆NU\subseteq N be the set of neighbors of vv in GG, and recall that b=|U|b=|U|. For an acyclic orientation AA of GG, let A′=A∖{v}A^{\prime}=A\smallsetminus\{v\} and let jj be the number of neighbors uu of vv with u→vu\to v in AA. The acyclic orientation AA is fully determined by (A′,j)(A^{\prime},j) because since A′A^{\prime} defines a total order on UU (as UU induces a clique in GG) the acyclicity of AA implies that if u→v∈Au\to v\in A for some u∈Uu\in U, then u′→v∈Au^{\prime}\to v\in A for all u′∈Uu^{\prime}\in U with u′→u∈A′u^{\prime}\to u\in A^{\prime}. Hence the sole number of arcs pointing towards vv fully determines these arcs. Reciprocally, for all acyclic orientations A′A^{\prime} of G′G^{\prime} and all j∈{0,…,b}j\in\{0,\dots,b\}, one can construct an acyclic orientation AA of GG by A∖{v}=A′A\smallsetminus\{v\}=A^{\prime} and orienting u→vu\to v for u∈Uu\in U among the jj first nodes of UU according to the total order of UU imposed by A′A^{\prime}, and v→uv\to u for all other u∈Uu\in U. Consequently, A↦(A′,j)A\mapsto(A^{\prime},j) is a bijection between acyclic orientations of GG and pairs of acyclic orientations of G′G^{\prime} and j∈{0,…,bn}j\in\{0,\dots,b_{n}\}. Finally, we have rkD⁡A=rkD′⁡A′+(b−j)\rank_{D}A=\rank_{D^{\prime}}A^{\prime}+(b-j) since (b−j)(b-j) of the edges u​vuv for u∈Uu\in U are not oriented from uu to vv in AA. Thus:

Ψ⁡(D,t)=∑A∈𝒜​𝒪​(G)trkD⁡A=∑j=0b∑A′∈𝒜​𝒪​(G′)trkD′⁡A′⋅tb−j=Ψ⁡(D′,t)⋅(1+t+⋯+tb).∎\Psi(D;t)=\sum_{A\in{\mathcal{AO}}(G)}t^{\rank_{D}A}=\sum_{j=0}^{b}\sum_{A^{\prime}\in{\mathcal{AO}}(G^{\prime})}t^{\rank_{D^{\prime}}A^{\prime}}\cdot t^{b-j}=\Psi(D^{\prime};t)\cdot(1+t+\dots+t^{b})\,.~\qed

For a chordal graph G=(N,E)G=(N,E) and a perfect elimination ordering θ\theta, we denote Dθ{D_{\theta}} the orientation of GG induced by θ\theta, that is the orientation with arcs from θ⁡(i)\theta(i) to θ⁡(j)\theta(j) for all i<ji<j such that θ⁡(i)​θ​(j)∈E\theta(i)\theta(j)\in E. Besides, we define the ithi^{\text{th}} elimination degree as the size of the clique of previous neighbors of θ⁡(i)\theta(i), that is bi≔|{j∈[i−1];θ⁡(i)​θ​(j)∈E}|{b_{i}}\coloneqq\bigl|\{j\in[i-1]~;~\theta(i)\theta(j)\in E\}\bigr|, where by convention b1=0b_{1}=0. We call the sequence (b1,…,bn)\bigr(b_{1},\dots,b_{n}\bigr) the elimination-degree sequence. Note that if GG is connected, then b2=1b_{2}=1.

Proposition 3.26.

Let GG be a connected chordal graph with a perfect elimination ordering θ\theta, and let DθD_{\theta} be its induced orientation, and (b1,…,bn)\bigl(b_{1},\dots,b_{n}\bigr) its elimination-degree sequence. Then:

Ψ⁡(Dθ,t)=∏i=1n(1+t+⋯+tbi)=∏i=1n1−tbi+11−t.\Psi(D_{\theta};t)=\prod_{i=1}^{n}\bigl(1+t+\dots+t^{b_{i}}\bigr)=\prod_{i=1}^{n}\frac{1-t^{b_{i}+1}}{1-t}\,.

In particular, ψ⁡(G)=Ψ⁡(Dθ,1)=∏i=1n(bi+1)\psi(G)=\Psi(D_{\theta};1)=\prod_{i=1}^{n}(b_{i}+1) and σ⁡(Dθ)=Ψ⁡(Dθ,−1)=0\sigma(D_{\theta})=\Psi(D_{\theta};-1)=0.

Proof.

Inductive application of Lemma 3.25 on the sequence of induced subgraphs on {θ⁡(1),…,θ⁡(i)}\{\theta(1),\dots,\theta(i)\} in which θ⁡(i)\theta(i) is a simplicial node with bib_{i} neighbors. For σ⁡(Dθ)\sigma(D_{\theta}), note that b2=1b_{2}=1 is odd. ∎

Example 3.27.

In particular, for the complete graph KnK_{n}, which is a chordal graph, the acyclic orientations are in bijection with the permutations of [n][n]. Fixing DD to be any acyclic orientation of KnK_{n}, the number of acyclic orientations of KnK_{n} of a given rank kk is the number of permutations on nn elements with kk inversions. These are counted by the Mahonian numbers Tn,kT_{n,k} [27, A008302]. In particular, Proposition 3.26 helps us to retrieve the famous formula:

Ψ⁡(D,t)=∑k=0n⁡(n−1)/2Tn,k​tk=∏j=1n1−tj1−t.\Psi(D;t)=\sum_{k=0}^{n(n-1)/2}T_{n,k}\,t^{k}=\prod_{j=1}^{n}\frac{1-t^{j}}{1-t}\,.

We recover that the number of acyclic orientations of KnK_{n} is ψ⁡(Kn)=Ψ⁡(D,1)=n!\psi(K_{n})=\Psi(D;1)=n!, while its signature is σD​(Kn)=Ψ⁡(D,−1)=0\sigma_{D}(K_{n})=\Psi(D;-1)=0 for n≥2n\geq 2.

One may wonder what happens when we change the chosen perfect elimination ordering of a given graph GG. Luckily, the acyclic polynomial remains unchanged.

Proposition 3.28.

Let GG be a connected chordal graph. Up to a permutation, the elimination-degree sequence does not depend on the perfect elimination ordering.

Proof.

For a given G=(N,E)G=(N,E), consider the graph 𝒫⁡(G){\mathcal{P}}(G) whose nodes are the perfect elimination orderings of GG and where two perfect elimination orderings θ\theta and θ′\theta^{\prime} are linked by an edge if θ′=θ∘(j​j+1)\theta^{\prime}=\theta\circ(j~\,~j\!+\!1) where (j​j+1)(j~\,~j\!+\!1) denotes a transposition of [n][n] (i.e. 𝒫⁡(G){\mathcal{P}}(G) is the subgraph of the permutahedral graph induced on the perfect elimination orderings of GG).

According to [10], 𝒫⁡(G){\mathcal{P}}(G) is connected: the authors even prove that 𝒫⁡(G){\mathcal{P}}(G) is a Hamiltonian graph by expliciting a Gray code. Hence, it is enough to prove that if θ\theta and θ′\theta^{\prime} are linked by an edge in 𝒫⁡(G){\mathcal{P}}(G), then their associated elimination degree sequences are the same up to permutation. To this end, fix a perfect elimination ordering θ\theta of GG and j∈[n−1]j\in[n-1] such that θ′=θ∘(j​j+1)\theta^{\prime}=\theta\circ(j~\,~j\!+\!1) is also a perfect elimination ordering. We denote bib_{i} (resp. bi′b^{\prime}_{i}) the ithi^{\text{th}} elimination degree of θ\theta (resp. of θ′\theta^{\prime}). If θ⁡(j)​θ​(j+1)∉E\theta(j)\theta(j+1)\notin E, then bi=bi′b_{i}=b^{\prime}_{i} for all i∉{j,j+1}i\notin\{j,j+1\}, and bj′=bj+1b^{\prime}_{j}=b_{j+1} and bj+1′=bjb^{\prime}_{j+1}=b_{j} since swapping the order of θ⁡(j)\theta(j) and θ⁡(j+1)\theta(j+1) does not change the clique of previous nodes of any node. If θ⁡(j)​θ​(j+1)∈E\theta(j)\theta(j+1)\in E, then bi=bi′b_{i}=b^{\prime}_{i} for all i∈[n]i\in[n] since swapping the order of θ⁡(j)\theta(j) and θ⁡(j+1)\theta(j+1) only changes the cliques of previous nodes of θ⁡(j)\theta(j) (whose size increases by 11) and of θ⁡(j+1)\theta(j+1) (whose size decreases by 11) and their sizes have a difference of 11. In both cases, b′b^{\prime} is a permutation of bb, which proves the claim. ∎

Corollary 3.29.

Let GG be a connected chordal graph with two perfect elimination orderings θ\theta and θ′\theta^{\prime}. Then Ψ⁡(Dθ,t)=Ψ⁡(Dθ′,t)\Psi(D_{\theta};t)=\Psi(D_{\theta^{\prime}};t).

Proof.

Direct application of Propositions 3.26 and 3.28. ∎

Remark 3.30.

For graphic hyperplane arrangements, it is known that the characteristic polynomial of the arrangement coincides with the chromatic polynomial of the graph, see [28, Section 2.4]. Thus, we know that χ⁡(G,x)=∏i=1n(x−bi)\chi(G,x)=\prod_{i=1}^{n}(x-b_{i}) according to the Factorization Theorem [28, Theorem 4.6.21]. In particular, this again shows that the chromatic polynomial and the acyclic polynomials (of perfect elimination orientations) are two different polynomials.

We can further explore the distribution of the coefficients of the polynomial Ψ⁡(Dθ,t)\Psi(D_{\theta};t) for θ\theta a perfect elimination ordering of a chordal graph GG.

A sequence of positive integers 𝒂=(a1,…,as){\boldsymbol{a}}=(a_{1},\dots,a_{s}) is log-concave if for all i∈[s−1]i\in[s-1] we have ai+12≥ai⋅ai+2a_{i+1}^{2}\geq a_{i}\cdot a_{i+2}. Such a sequence is unimodal if there exists m∈[s]m\in[s], called the mode of 𝒂{\boldsymbol{a}}, such that (a1,…,am)(a_{1},\dots,a_{m}) is increasing, while (am,…,as)(a_{m},\dots,a_{s}) is decreasing. A notorious property of log-concave sequences is that they are unimodal. Furthermore, if the polynomial ∑i=1sai​ti\sum_{i=1}^{s}a_{i}t^{i} is real-rooted (i.e. does not have complex non-real roots), then 𝒂{\boldsymbol{a}} is log-concave, and hence unimodal. We refer to Brändén’s handbook [7] for all the “well-known” facts on unimodality, log-concavity, real-rootedness, and, later, 𝜸{\boldsymbol{\gamma}}-vectors.

For chordal graphs endowed with the orientation induced by a perfect elimination ordering, the coefficients of the acyclic polynomial form a log-concave sequence.

Theorem 3.31.

Let G=(N,E)G=(N,E) be a graph with a simplicial node v∈Nv\in N. Let DD be an orientation of GG where all edges u​vuv are directed from uu to vv, and let D′=D∖{v}D^{\prime}=D\smallsetminus\{v\}. If the coefficients of the polynomial Ψ⁡(D′,t)\Psi(D^{\prime};t) form a log-concave (hence unimodal) sequence, then so do the coefficients of the polynomial Ψ⁡(D,t)\Psi(D;t).

Proof.

Recall that if the coefficients of both polynomials p⁡(t)p(t) and q⁡(t)q(t) form log-concave sequences, then the coefficients of the polynomial p⁡(t)⋅q⁡(t)p(t)\cdot q(t) also form a log-concave sequence. Note that, for all bb, the coefficients of 1+t+⋯+tb1+t+\dots+t^{b} are all 11, hence form a log-concave sequence. Consequently, by Lemma 3.25, if the coefficients of Ψ⁡(D′,t)\Psi(D^{\prime};t) form a log-concave sequence, then the coefficients of the product Ψ⁡(D′,t)⋅(1+t+⋯+tb)\Psi(D^{\prime};t)\cdot(1+t+\dots+t^{b}) form a log-concave sequence, whatever the value of bb. ∎

Corollary 3.32.

Let GG be a connected chordal graph with a perfect elimination ordering θ\theta. Then the coefficients of the polynomial Ψ⁡(Dθ,t)\Psi(D_{\theta};t) form a log-concave (hence unimodal) sequence.

Proof.

Inductive application of Theorem 3.31 on the induced subgraphs on {θ⁡(1),…,θ⁡(i)}\{\theta(1),\dots,\theta(i)\}. For i=2i=2, this induced subgraph is an edge whose acyclic polynomial 1+t1+t has a log-concave sequence of coefficients. ∎

Remark 3.33.

The Mahonian numbers Tn,kT_{n,k} seen in Example 3.27 are log-concave (in kk) according to Corollary 3.32 (see [19] for more details), even though the polynomial ∑k=0n⁡(n−1)/2Tn,k​tk=∏j=1n1−tj1−t\sum_{k=0}^{n(n-1)/2}T_{n,k}\,t^{k}=\prod_{j=1}^{n}\frac{1-t^{j}}{1-t} is obviously not real-rooted.

However, note that the coefficients of Ψ⁡(D,t)\Psi(D;t) given by of Figure 3, where GG is the complete bipartite graph K2,3K_{2,3}, do not form a log-concave (not even a unimodal) sequence. This motivates the following question.

Question 3.34.

Classify the graphs GG and orientations DD such that Ψ⁡(D,t)\Psi(D;t) is real-rooted, and the ones whose coefficients form a log-concave sequence, or a unimodal sequence.

Definition 3.35.

If 𝒂=(a0,…,ad){\boldsymbol{a}}=(a_{0},\dots,a_{d}) is a palindromic sequence of length dd, then one can rewrite the associated polynomial in the so-called γ\gamma-basis, that is:

∑k=0dak​tk=∑j=0⌊d2⌋γj​tj​(1+t)d−2​j,\sum_{k=0}^{d}a_{k}t^{k}=\sum_{j=0}^{\left\lfloor\frac{d}{2}\right\rfloor}\gamma_{j}t^{j}(1+t)^{d-2j}\,,

where 𝜸≔(γ0,…,γ⌊d2⌋){{\boldsymbol{\gamma}}}\coloneqq(\gamma_{0},\dots,\gamma_{\left\lfloor\frac{d}{2}\right\rfloor}) is called the γ\gamma-vector associated to 𝒂{\boldsymbol{a}}.

It is well-known that if 𝒂{\boldsymbol{a}} is γ\gamma-positive, that is if γj≥0\gamma_{j}\geq 0 for all j∈{0,…,⌊d2⌋}j\in\{0,\dots,\left\lfloor\frac{d}{2}\right\rfloor\}, then 𝒂{\boldsymbol{a}} is unimodal. Besides, if ∑k=0dak​tk\sum_{k=0}^{d}a_{k}t^{k} is real-rooted, then 𝒂{\boldsymbol{a}} is γ\gamma-positive.

The coefficients of Ψ⁡(Dθ,t)\Psi(D_{\theta};t) are palindromic for a chordal graph GG with a perfect elimination ordering θ\theta, as can be seen from Proposition 3.26, and we will prove that this actually holds for any directed graph in Corollary 3.44. Hence, one can wonder whether the coefficients of Ψ⁡(D,t)\Psi(D;t) form a γ\gamma-positive sequence for some digraph DD. We give a negative but surprising answer in the case of chordal graphs: We say that a sequence 𝒂{\boldsymbol{a}} is γ\gamma-alternating if the sign of (−1)j⋅γj(-1)^{j}\cdot\gamma_{j} does not depend on j∈{0,…,⌊d2⌋}j\in\{0,\dots,\left\lfloor\frac{d}{2}\right\rfloor\}.

Theorem 3.36.

Let GG be a connected chordal graph with a perfect elimination ordering θ\theta. Then the sequence of coefficients of the polynomial Ψ⁡(Dθ,t)\Psi(D_{\theta};t) is γ\gamma-alternating.

Proof.

We first prove that the γ\gamma-coefficients of the sequence (1,1,…,1)(1,1,\dots,1) of length bb is γj=(−1)j⋅(b−jj)\gamma_{j}=(-1)^{j}\cdot\binom{b-j}{j} and that products of γ\gamma-alternating sequences are γ\gamma-alternating. Then we conclude the proof using Proposition 3.26.

Let Fn​(s,x)F_{n}(s,x) be the nthn^{\text{th}} bivariate Fibonacci polynomial, that is F⁡(s,x)=s⋅Fn−1​(s,x)+x⋅Fn−2​(s,x)F(s,x)=s\cdot F_{n-1}(s,x)+x\cdot F_{n-2}(s,x), and F0​(s,x)=0F_{0}(s,x)=0, F1​(s,x)=1F_{1}(s,x)=1. Using the Binet formula, we get Fn​(s,x)=α​(s,x)n−β​(s,x)nα⁡(s,x)−β⁡(s,x)F_{n}(s,x)=\frac{\alpha(s,x)^{n}-\beta(s,x)^{n}}{\alpha(s,x)-\beta(s,x)} where α⁡(s,x)\alpha(s,x) and β⁡(s,x)\beta(s,x) are the roots of Z2−s​Z−xZ^{2}-sZ-x. The usual “sum of diagonals” argument on the Fibonacci numbers yields Fb+1​(s,x)=∑j=0⌊b/2⌋(b−jj)​sb−2​j​xjF_{b+1}(s,x)=\sum_{j=0}^{\lfloor b/2\rfloor}\binom{b-j}{j}s^{b-2j}x^{j}. In particular

∑j=0⌊b/2⌋(−1)j​(b−jj)​tj​(1+t)b−2​j=(1+t)b​∑j=0⌊b/2⌋(b−jj)​1b−2​j​(−t(1+t)2)j=(1+t)b​Fb+1​(1,−t(1+t)2).\sum_{j=0}^{\lfloor b/2\rfloor}(-1)^{j}\binom{b-j}{j}t^{j}(1+t)^{b-2j}=(1+t)^{b}\sum_{j=0}^{\lfloor b/2\rfloor}\binom{b-j}{j}1^{b-2j}\left(\frac{-t}{(1+t)^{2}}\right)^{j}=(1+t)^{b}F_{b+1}\left(1,\frac{-t}{(1+t)^{2}}\right).

Using α⁡(1,−x)=1+1−4​x2\alpha(1,-x)=\frac{1+\sqrt{1-4x}}{2} and β⁡(1,−x)=1−1−4​x2\beta(1,-x)=\frac{1-\sqrt{1-4x}}{2}, and evaluating for x=t(1+t)2x=\frac{t}{(1+t)^{2}}, we get (after several simplifications): (1+t)b​Fb+1​(1,−t(1+t)2)=1−tb+11−t=1+t+t2+⋯+tb(1+t)^{b}F_{b+1}\left(1,\frac{-t}{(1+t)^{2}}\right)=\frac{1-t^{b+1}}{1-t}=1+t+t^{2}+\dots+t^{b}. Hence, γj=(−1)j⋅(b−jj)\gamma_{j}=(-1)^{j}\cdot\binom{b-j}{j} is indeed the γ\gamma-vector of the sequence (1,1,…,1)(1,1,\dots,1) of length bb. This sequence is thus γ\gamma-alternating.

Besides, if (−1)j​γj≥0(-1)^{j}\gamma_{j}\geq 0 and (−1)k​δk≥0(-1)^{k}\delta_{k}\geq 0 for all j,k≥0j,k\geq 0, then

(∑jγj​tj​(1+t)b−2​j)⋅(∑kγk​tk​(1+t)c−2​k)=∑p(∑j=0pγj⋅δp−j)​tp​(1+t)b+c−2​p,\left(\sum_{j}\gamma_{j}t^{j}(1+t)^{b-2j}\right)\cdot\left(\sum_{k}\gamma_{k}t^{k}(1+t)^{c-2k}\right)=\sum_{p}\left(\sum_{j=0}^{p}\gamma_{j}\cdot\delta_{p-j}\right)t^{p}(1+t)^{b+c-2p}\,,

where for all j∈{0,…,p}j\in\{0,\dots,p\}, (−1)p​γj⋅δp−j≥0(-1)^{p}\gamma_{j}\cdot\delta_{p-j}\geq 0, so (−1)p⋅(∑j=0pγj⋅δp−j)≥0(-1)^{p}\cdot\left(\sum_{j=0}^{p}\gamma_{j}\cdot\delta_{p-j}\right)\geq 0. Hence if two sequences are γ\gamma-alternating, then their product is also γ\gamma-alternating.

By Proposition 3.26, the sequence of coefficients of Ψ⁡(Dθ,t)\Psi(D_{\theta};t) is a product of γ\gamma-alternating sequences: it is γ\gamma-alternating. ∎

Remark 3.37.

Note that we are not the first to describe a γ\gamma-alternating behavior: in [14, Corollary 7.10], the authors show that for a (d−1)(d-1)-dimensional Cohen–Macaulay sphere Δ\Delta with positive hh-vectors, the ring RΔR_{\Delta} they define is γ\gamma-alternating.

Question 3.38.

Classify the graphs GG and orientations DD such that the coefficients of Ψ⁡(D,t)\Psi(D;t) form a γ\gamma-positive or a γ\gamma-alternating sequence.

3.2.4. Decomposition of the acyclic polynomial and reversion of the direction of all arcs

In order to propose some deletion-contraction formulas, we will need to split the acyclic polynomial according to the following notion:

Definition 3.39.

For two distinct nodes  u,v∈Nu,v\in N in a graph G=(N,E)G=(N,E), and an acyclic orientation AA of GG, we define the direction between uu and vv in AA as:

A⁡(u,v)≔{+1 if there exists a directed path from ​u​ to ​v​ in ​A,−1 if there exists a directed path from ​v​ to ​u​ in ​A,0 otherwise {A(u,v)}\coloneqq\left\{\begin{array}[]{cl}+1&\text{ if there exists a directed path from }u\text{ to }v\text{ in }A,\\ -1&\text{ if there exists a directed path from }v\text{ to }u\text{ in }A,\\ 0&\text{ otherwise }\end{array}\right.

We allow such a directed path to be composed of a single edge. Besides: A⁡(v,u)=−A⁡(u,v)A(v,u)=-A(u,v). For a sequence of acyclic orientations 𝑨=(A1,…,Ar){\boldsymbol{A}}=(A_{1},\dots,A_{r}), let 𝑨⁡(u,v)≔(A1​(u,v),…,Ar​(u,v)){{\boldsymbol{A}}(u,v)}\coloneqq\bigl(A_{1}(u,v),\dots,A_{r}(u,v)\bigr).

Let G=H⊔H′G=H\sqcup H^{\prime} be a bipartition of the edges of the graph GG. Fix an orientation of GG, say D⊔D′D\sqcup D^{\prime} where DD is an orientation of HH, and D′D^{\prime} is an orientation of H′H^{\prime}. If D⊔D′D\sqcup D^{\prime} is acyclic, then both DD and D′D^{\prime} are acyclic. Moreover, if D⊔D′D\sqcup D^{\prime} is acyclic, then for any nodes u,vu,v of GG, we have D⁡(u,v)⋅D′​(u,v)≠−1D(u,v)\cdot D^{\prime}(u,v)\neq-1. The reciprocal is straightforward:

Lemma 3.40.

Let G=H⊔H′G=H\sqcup H^{\prime} be a bipartition of the edges of the graph GG. The map (A,A′)↦A⊔A′(A,A^{\prime})\mapsto A\sqcup A^{\prime} is a bijection from the pairs of acyclic orientations of HH and H′H^{\prime} such that A⁡(u,v)⋅A′​(u,v)≠−1A(u,v)\cdot A^{\prime}(u,v)\neq-1 for all nodes u,vu,v of GG, and the acyclic orientations of GG.

Moreover, 𝒜​𝒪​(G){\mathcal{AO}}(G) is the subgraph of the Cartesian product 𝒜​𝒪​(H)×𝒜​𝒪​(H′){\mathcal{AO}}(H)\times{\mathcal{AO}}(H^{\prime}) induced on these pairs of acyclic orientations, that is A⊔A′A\sqcup A^{\prime} and B⊔B′B\sqcup B^{\prime} are adjacent in 𝒜​𝒪​(G){\mathcal{AO}}(G) if and only if either A=BA=B, and A′A^{\prime} and B′B^{\prime} are adjacent in 𝒜​𝒪​(H′){\mathcal{AO}}(H^{\prime}), or A′=B′A^{\prime}=B^{\prime}, and AA and BB are adjacent in 𝒜​𝒪​(H){\mathcal{AO}}(H).

Proof.

Clearly, (A,A′)↦A⊔A′(A,A^{\prime})\mapsto A\sqcup A^{\prime} is an injection, since this is just a standard operation between sets. Moreover, A⊔A′A\sqcup A^{\prime} is acyclic if and only if for all u,v∈Nu,v\in N there is no path from uu to vv and from vv to uu in A⊔A′A\sqcup A^{\prime}, which is equivalent to: for all u,v∈Nu,v\in N there is no path from uu to vv and from vv to uu both in AA (i.e. AA is acyclic), and there is no path from uu to vv and from vv to uu both in A′A^{\prime} (i.e. A′A^{\prime} is acyclic), and there is no path from uu to vv and from vv to uu, one in AA and the other in A′A^{\prime} (i.e. A⁡(u,v)⋅A′​(u,v)≠−1A(u,v)\cdot A^{\prime}(u,v)\neq-1). This proves the bijection.

Besides, A⊔A′A\sqcup A^{\prime} and B⊔B′B\sqcup B^{\prime} are adjacent if and only if they differ on exactly 1 edge: due to the bipartition of the edges of GG, this edge is either in HH or in H′H^{\prime} not in both. This proves the adjacency relation. ∎

Some fundamental properties of the acyclic polynomial come from understanding what happens when we reverse the direction of all the arcs of an orientation at once. We will often use the following straightforward lemma:

Lemma 3.41.

Fix a (di)graph G=(N,E)G=(N,E), any u,v∈Nu,v\in N, and any orientation DD of GG. The map X↦E∖XX\mapsto E\smallsetminus X satisfies rkD⁡DE∖X=|E|−rkD⁡DX\rank_{D}D^{E\smallsetminus X}=|E|-\rank_{D}D^{X}, and it is:

  1. (1)

    an involution without fixed point on 𝒪⁡(G){\mathcal{O}}(G), and

  2. (2)

    an involution without fixed point on 𝒜​𝒪​(G){\mathcal{AO}}(G), and

  3. (3)

    an involution without fixed point on {A∈𝒜​𝒪​(G);A⁡(u,v)=0}\{A\in{\mathcal{AO}}(G)~;~A(u,v)=0\}, and

  4. (4)

    a bijection between {A∈𝒜​𝒪​(G);A⁡(u,v)=+1}\{A\in{\mathcal{AO}}(G)~;~A(u,v)=+1\} and {A∈𝒜​𝒪​(G);A⁡(u,v)=−1}\{A\in{\mathcal{AO}}(G)~;~A(u,v)=-1\}, and

  5. (5)

    if |E||E| is even, an involution without fixed point on {A∈𝒜​𝒪​(G);rkD⁡A​ is even}\{A\in{\mathcal{AO}}(G)~;~\rank_{D}A\text{ is even}\}, and an involution without fixed point on {A∈𝒜​𝒪​(G);rkD⁡A​ is odd}\{A\in{\mathcal{AO}}(G)~;~\rank_{D}A\text{ is odd}\}, and

  6. (6)

    if |E||E| is odd, a bijection between the set {A∈𝒜​𝒪​(G);rkD⁡A​ is even}\{A\in{\mathcal{AO}}(G)~;~\rank_{D}A\text{ is even}\} and the set{A∈𝒜​𝒪​(G);rkD⁡A​ is odd}\{A\in{\mathcal{AO}}(G)~;~\rank_{D}A\text{ is odd}\}.

Proof.

It is immediate that X↦E∖XX\mapsto E\smallsetminus X is an involution of 2E2^{E}. For (1), note that 𝒪⁡(G){\mathcal{O}}(G) is isomorphic to 2E2^{E}. For (2), note that reversing the directions of all the arcs at once does not change whether the orientation is acyclic or not. For (3) and (4), note that reversing the directions of all the arcs at once changes a directed path from uu to vv into a directed path from vv to uu, i.e. DE∖X​(u,v)=−DX​(u,v)D^{E\smallsetminus X}(u,v)=-D^{X}(u,v) for all orientations DD of GG.

The claimed rank equality is by definition: rkD⁡DE∖X=|E∖X|=|E|−|X|=|E|−rkD⁡DX\rank_{D}D^{E\smallsetminus X}=|E\smallsetminus X|=|E|-|X|=|E|-\rank_{D}D^{X}. This immediately implies (5) and (6). ∎

Using the fundamental involution, we can re-prove one of the powerful results of [37] that they repeatedly use in order to show that some graphs are not 𝒜​𝒪{\mathcal{AO}}-Hamiltonian. Our proof is essentially the same as theirs, but written with our language.

Theorem 3.42 ([37, Lemma 3.1]).

If a graph with an even number of edges is 𝒜​𝒪{\mathcal{AO}}-Hamiltonian, then its number of acyclic orientations is divisible by 44.

Proof.

Let GG be such a graph, and DD some orientation of GG. Since |E||E| is even, Lemma 3.41 (5) shows that X↦E∖XX\mapsto E\smallsetminus X induces an involution without fixed point on {A∈𝒜​𝒪​(G);rkD⁡A​ is even}\{A\in{\mathcal{AO}}(G)~;~\rank_{D}A\text{ is even}\}. This implies that the latter set is of even size.

By Lemma 2.9, we have σ⁡(D)=Ψ⁡(D,−1)=0\sigma(D)=\Psi(D;-1)=0. So writing Ψ⁡(D,t)=∑k=0dpk​tk\Psi(D;t)=\sum_{k=0}^{d}p_{k}t^{k} we get that ∑k​ evenpk=∑k​ oddpk\sum_{k\text{ even}}p_{k}=\sum_{k\text{ odd}}p_{k}. Since ∑k​ evenpk=|{A∈𝒜​𝒪​(G);rkD⁡A​ is even}|\sum_{k\text{ even}}p_{k}=\bigl|\{A\in{\mathcal{AO}}(G)~;~\rank_{D}A\text{ is even}\}\bigr| is even, we finally get that ψ⁡(G)=Ψ⁡(D,1)=∑kpk\psi(G)=\Psi(D;1)=\sum_{k}p_{k} is divisible by 44. ∎

Thanks to the notion of direction and the fundamental involution, we can isolate two sub-polynomials hidden inside the acyclic polynomial. The core idea is to split the edges of GG between two subgraphs HH and H′H^{\prime} which meet on exactly two nodes uu and vv: in an acyclic orientation of GG, either there is no directed path between uu and vv inside the induced orientation of HH, or there is a directed path from uu to vv, or from vv to uu. The set of possible acyclic orientations of H′H^{\prime} depends only on which of these three cases we are in, not on the exact acyclic orientation of HH. In Figure 3, we illustrate the particular case where H′H^{\prime} is the subgraph of K2,3K_{2,3} with nodes u,vu,v and no edge.

Proposition 3.43.

Let G=H⊔H′G=H\sqcup H^{\prime} be a bipartition of the edges of GG such that N⁡(H)∩N⁡(H′)={u,v}N(H)\cap N(H^{\prime})=\{u,v\} for two nodes u,vu,v. Then: Ψ⁡(D⊔D′,t)=Ψu↮v​(D⊔D′,t)+Ψu→v​(D⊔D′,t)+t|E|⋅Ψu→v​(D⊔D′,1t)\Psi(D\sqcup D^{\prime};t)=\Psi^{u\not\leftrightarrow v}(D\sqcup D^{\prime};t)+\Psi^{u\to v}(D\sqcup D^{\prime};t)+t^{|E|}\cdot\Psi^{u\to v}(D\sqcup D^{\prime};\tfrac{1}{t}), where:

Ψu↮v​(D⊔D′,t)≔∑A⊔A′∈𝒜​𝒪​(G)A⁡(u,v)=0trkD⊔D′⁡A⊔A′ and Ψu→v​(D⊔D′,t)≔∑A⊔A′∈𝒜​𝒪​(G)A⁡(u,v)=1trkD⊔D′⁡A⊔A′{\Psi^{u\not\leftrightarrow v}(D\sqcup D^{\prime};t)}\coloneqq\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}A\sqcup A^{\prime}\in{\mathcal{AO}}(G)\\ A(u,v)=0\end{subarray}}t^{\rank_{D\sqcup D^{\prime}}A\sqcup A^{\prime}}\hskip 14.22636pt\text{ and }\hskip 14.22636pt{\Psi^{u\to v}(D\sqcup D^{\prime};t)}\coloneqq\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}A\sqcup A^{\prime}\in{\mathcal{AO}}(G)\\ A(u,v)=1\end{subarray}}t^{\rank_{D\sqcup D^{\prime}}A\sqcup A^{\prime}}
Proof.

Clearly, for any D⊔D′D\sqcup D^{\prime}, and tt, we have:

Ψ⁡(D⊔D′,t)=∑A⊔A′∈𝒜​𝒪​(G)A⁡(u,v)=0trkD⊔D′⁡A⊔A′+∑A⊔A′∈𝒜​𝒪​(G)A⁡(u,v)=1trkD⊔D′⁡A⊔A′+∑A⊔A′∈𝒜​𝒪​(G)A⁡(u,v)=−1trkD⊔D′⁡A⊔A′\Psi(D\sqcup D^{\prime};t)=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}A\sqcup A^{\prime}\in{\mathcal{AO}}(G)\\ A(u,v)=0\end{subarray}}t^{\rank_{D\sqcup D^{\prime}}A\sqcup A^{\prime}}~+~\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}A\sqcup A^{\prime}\in{\mathcal{AO}}(G)\\ A(u,v)=1\end{subarray}}t^{\rank_{D\sqcup D^{\prime}}A\sqcup A^{\prime}}~+~\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}A\sqcup A^{\prime}\in{\mathcal{AO}}(G)\\ A(u,v)=-1\end{subarray}}t^{\rank_{D\sqcup D^{\prime}}A\sqcup A^{\prime}}

Thus, we only need to prove that ∑A⊔A′∈𝒜​𝒪​(G)A⁡(u,v)=−1trkD⊔D′⁡A⊔A′=t|E|⋅Ψu→v​(D⊔D′,1t)\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}A\sqcup A^{\prime}\in{\mathcal{AO}}(G)\\ A(u,v)=-1\end{subarray}}t^{\rank_{D\sqcup D^{\prime}}A\sqcup A^{\prime}}=t^{|E|}\cdot\Psi^{u\to v}(D\sqcup D^{\prime};\frac{1}{t}). Using the bijection X↦E∖XX\mapsto E\smallsetminus X on the graph GG from Lemma 3.41 (4), we get:

∑A⊔A′∈𝒜​𝒪​(G)A⁡(u,v)=−1trkD⊔D′⁡A⊔A′=∑A⊔A′∈𝒜​𝒪​(G)A⁡(u,v)=+1t|E|−rkD⊔D′⁡A⊔A′=t|E|⋅∑A⊔A′∈𝒜​𝒪​(G)A⁡(u,v)=+1(1t)rkD⊔D′⁡A⊔A′=t|E|⋅Ψu→v​(D⊔D′,1t)∎\begin{array}[]{rcl}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}A\sqcup A^{\prime}\in{\mathcal{AO}}(G)\\ A(u,v)=-1\end{subarray}}t^{\rank_{D\sqcup D^{\prime}}A\sqcup A^{\prime}}&=&\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}A\sqcup A^{\prime}\in{\mathcal{AO}}(G)\\ A(u,v)=+1\end{subarray}}t^{|E|-\rank_{D\sqcup D^{\prime}}A\sqcup A^{\prime}}\\ &=&t^{|E|}\cdot\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}A\sqcup A^{\prime}\in{\mathcal{AO}}(G)\\ A(u,v)=+1\end{subarray}}\left(\frac{1}{t}\right)^{\rank_{D\sqcup D^{\prime}}A\sqcup A^{\prime}}\\ &=&t^{|E|}\cdot\Psi^{u\to v}(D\sqcup D^{\prime};\tfrac{1}{t})~\qed\end{array}

As a special case, we define the partial acyclic polynomials Ψu↮v​(D,t){\Psi^{u\not\leftrightarrow v}(D;t)} and Ψu→v​(D,t){\Psi^{u\to v}(D;t)} to the polynomials associated to the bipartition of edges G=H⊔H′G=H\sqcup H^{\prime} where H′H^{\prime} is the graph with nodes u,vu,v and no edge between them. The polynomial Ψu↮v​(D,t)\Psi^{u\not\leftrightarrow v}(D;t) (resp. Ψu→v​(D,t)\Psi^{u\to v}(D;t)) counts the number of acyclic orientations of GG containing no directed path from uu to vv nor from vv to uu (resp. containing a directed path from uu to vv), according to their rank with respect to the orientation DD.

Recall that a polynomial P⁡(t)=∑k=0dpk​tkP(t)=\sum_{k=0}^{d}p_{k}t^{k} is palindromic of length dd if its coefficients satisfy pk=pd−kp_{k}=p_{d-k} for all k∈[d]k\in[d], or equivalently if P⁡(t)=td⋅P⁡(1t)P(t)=t^{d}\cdot P(\tfrac{1}{t}).

Corollary 3.44.

The acyclic polynomial Ψ⁡(D,t)\Psi(D;t) is palindromic of length |E||E|.

Furthermore, if G=H⊔H′G=H\sqcup H^{\prime} is a bipartition of the edges of GG with N⁡(H)∩N⁡(H′)={u,v}N(H)\cap N(H^{\prime})=\{u,v\}, then the polynomial Ψu↮v​(D⊔D′,t)\Psi^{u\not\leftrightarrow v}(D\sqcup D^{\prime};t) is palindromic of length |E||E|.

Proof.

Using the involution X↦E∖XX\mapsto E\smallsetminus X from Lemma 3.41 (3), we get:

Ψu↮v​(D⊔D′,t)=∑A⊔A′∈𝒜​𝒪​(G)A⁡(u,v)=0trkD⊔D′⁡A⊔A′=∑A⊔A′∈𝒜​𝒪​(G)A⁡(u,v)=0t|E|−rkD⊔D′⁡A⊔A′=t|E|⋅Ψu↮v​(D⊔D′,1t)\Psi^{u\not\leftrightarrow v}(D\sqcup D^{\prime};t)=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}A\sqcup A^{\prime}\in{\mathcal{AO}}(G)\\ A(u,v)=0\end{subarray}}t^{\rank_{D\sqcup D^{\prime}}A\sqcup A^{\prime}}=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}A\sqcup A^{\prime}\in{\mathcal{AO}}(G)\\ A(u,v)=0\end{subarray}}t^{|E|-\rank_{D\sqcup D^{\prime}}A\sqcup A^{\prime}}=t^{|E|}\cdot\Psi^{u\not\leftrightarrow v}(D\sqcup D^{\prime};\tfrac{1}{t})

Hence, the polynomial Ψu↮v​(D,t)\Psi^{u\not\leftrightarrow v}(D;t) is palindromic. Consequently, by Proposition 3.43, Ψ⁡(D,t)\Psi(D;t) is also palindromic, as it is the sum of a palindromic polynomial Ψu↮v​(D,t)\Psi^{u\not\leftrightarrow v}(D;t) with another palindromic polynomial Ψu→v​(D,t)+t|E|⋅Ψu→v​(D,1t)\Psi^{u\to v}(D;t)+t^{|E|}\cdot\Psi^{u\to v}(D;\tfrac{1}{t}). ∎

Remark 3.45.

Note that Ψ⁡(D,t)\Psi(D;t) is not necessarily of degree |E||E| (nor does it need to have a non-zero constant term), especially when DD is not acyclic, see the example of cycles CnC_{n} in Example 3.16, or of K2,3K_{2,3} in Examples 3.17 and 3.

For two orientations DD and D′D^{\prime} of the same graph G=(N,E)G=(N,E), it is not evident how to determine Ψ⁡(D′,t)\Psi(D^{\prime};t) given Ψ⁡(D,t)\Psi(D;t). However, for an orientation DD, we can easily express the acyclic polynomial of the reverse orientation DED^{E}:

Corollary 3.46.

For any digraph D=(N,E)D=(N,E), we have: Ψ⁡(DE,t)=Ψ⁡(D,t)\Psi(D^{E};t)=\Psi(D;t).

Furthermore, if G=H⊔H′G=H\sqcup H^{\prime} is a bipartition of the edges of GG with N⁡(H)∩N⁡(H′)={u,v}N(H)\cap N(H^{\prime})=\{u,v\}, then we have Ψu↮v​((D⊔D′)E,t)=Ψu↮v​(D⊔D′,t)\Psi^{u\not\leftrightarrow v}((D\sqcup D^{\prime})^{E};t)=\Psi^{u\not\leftrightarrow v}(D\sqcup D^{\prime};t), and also Ψu→v​((D⊔D′)E,t)=t|E|⋅Ψu→v​(D⊔D′,1t)\Psi^{u\to v}((D\sqcup D^{\prime})^{E};t)=t^{|E|}\cdot\Psi^{u\to v}(D\sqcup D^{\prime};\tfrac{1}{t}).

Proof.

Note that rkDE⁡DX=|E∖X|=|E|−rkD⁡DX\rank_{D^{E}}D^{X}=|E\smallsetminus X|=|E|-\rank_{D}D^{X}. Using the involution X↦E∖XX\mapsto E\smallsetminus X from Lemma 3.41 (2), we get

Ψ⁡(DE,t)=∑A∈𝒜​𝒪​(DE)trkDE⁡A=∑A∈𝒜​𝒪​(D)t|E|−rkD⁡A=t|E|⋅Ψ⁡(D,1t).\Psi(D^{E};t)=\sum_{A\in{\mathcal{AO}}(D^{E})}t^{\rank_{D^{E}}A}=\sum_{A\in{\mathcal{AO}}(D)}t^{|E|-\rank_{D}A}=t^{|E|}\cdot\Psi(D;\tfrac{1}{t}).

Since Ψ⁡(D,t)\Psi(D;t) is palindromic of length |E||E| by Corollary 3.44, the latter is equal to Ψ⁡(D,t)\Psi(D;t).

The proof is the same for Ψu↮v\Psi^{u\not\leftrightarrow v}. From the equality on Ψ\Psi and on Ψu↮v\Psi^{u\not\leftrightarrow v}, we deduce the one of Ψu→v\Psi^{u\to v} via the decomposition of Proposition 3.43. ∎

Example 3.47.

By Corollary 3.46, we can deduce from Figure 3 the acyclic polynomials (and their decomposition) of the orientations obtained by reversing the direction of all the arcs in the drawn orientations.

3.2.5. Automorphisms of (di)graphs and palindromicity of Ψu→v​(D⊔D′,t)\Psi^{u\to v}(D\sqcup D^{\prime};t)

It is straightforward to show that if two orientations DD and D′D^{\prime} of GG are isomorphic (as digraphs, i.e. if there exists φ:N→N\varphi:N\to N such that x​y∈Dxy\in D if and only if φ⁡(x)​φ​(y)∈D′\varphi(x)\varphi(y)\in D^{\prime}), then their acyclic polynomials are the same. We can go one step further by considering automorphisms of digraphs.

Definition 3.48.

For a (directed) graph G=(N,E)G=(N,E), an automorphism is a bijection φ:N→N\varphi:N\to N such that GG has the (directed) edge u​v∈Euv\in E if and only if GG has the (directed) edge φ⁡(u)​φ​(v)\varphi(u)\varphi(v).

The set of automorphisms of a (directed) graph together with the composition of functions forms a group, which is denoted Aut⁡(G){\Aut(G)}.

Theorem 3.49.

Let G=H⊔H′G=H\sqcup H^{\prime} be a graph with a bipartition of the edges of GG such that N⁡(H)∩N⁡(H′)={u,v}N(H)\cap N(H^{\prime})=\{u,v\}, and D⊔D′D\sqcup D^{\prime} an orientation of GG. If the directed graph D⊔D′D\sqcup D^{\prime} admits an automorphism φ\varphi which induces an automorphism of DD and such that φ⁡(u)=v\varphi(u)=v and φ⁡(v)=u\varphi(v)=u, then Ψu→v​(D⊔D′,t)\Psi^{u\to v}(D\sqcup D^{\prime};t) is palindromic of length |E||E|.

Proof.

Fix GG, D⊔D′D\sqcup D^{\prime}, u,v∈Nu,v\in N and φ\varphi as above. For an acyclic orientation A⊔A′A\sqcup A^{\prime} of GG, we denote φ⁡(A⊔A′)\varphi(A\sqcup A^{\prime}) the orientation whose arcs are from φ⁡(x)\varphi(x) to φ⁡(y)\varphi(y) for all arcs from xx to yy in A⊔A′A\sqcup A^{\prime}.

First, if there is a directed path x0→x1→…→xℓx_{0}\to x_{1}\to\dots\to x_{\ell} in A⊔A′A\sqcup A^{\prime}, then there is a directed path φ⁡(x0)→φ⁡(x1)→…→φ⁡(xℓ)\varphi(x_{0})\to\varphi(x_{1})\to\dots\to\varphi(x_{\ell}) in φ⁡(A⊔A′)\varphi(A\sqcup A^{\prime}). Hence, since φ\varphi is a bijection, A⊔A′A\sqcup A^{\prime} is acyclic if and only if φ⁡(A⊔A′)\varphi(A\sqcup A^{\prime}) is acyclic. Moreover, since φ⁡(u)=v\varphi(u)=v and φ⁡(v)=u\varphi(v)=u, there is a path from uu to vv in AA if and only if there is a path from vv to uu in φ⁡(A)\varphi(A) because φ\varphi is also an automorphism of DD. Second, let X⊆EX\subseteq E be such that A⊔A′=(D⊔D′)XA\sqcup A^{\prime}=(D\sqcup D^{\prime})^{X}, i.e. XX is the set of edges x​y∈Exy\in E such that we have an arc from xx to yy in D⊔D′D\sqcup D^{\prime} but an arc from yy to xx in A⊔A′A\sqcup A^{\prime}. For such x​y∈Exy\in E, we have φ⁡(x)→φ⁡(y)\varphi(x)\to\varphi(y) in D⊔D′D\sqcup D^{\prime} because φ\varphi is an automorphism of D⊔D′D\sqcup D^{\prime}, and φ⁡(x)→φ⁡(y)\varphi(x)\to\varphi(y) in A⊔A′A\sqcup A^{\prime} by definition. Hence, if A⊔A′=(D⊔D′)XA\sqcup A^{\prime}=(D\sqcup D^{\prime})^{X}, then φ⁡(A⊔A′)=(D⊔D′){φ⁡(x)​φ​(y);x​y∈E}\varphi(A\sqcup A^{\prime})=(D\sqcup D^{\prime})^{\{\varphi(x)\varphi(y)~;~xy\in E\}}. In particular, we get: rkD⊔D′⁡φ⁡(A⊔A′)=rkD⊔D′⁡A⊔A′\rank_{D\sqcup D^{\prime}}\varphi(A\sqcup A^{\prime})=\rank_{D\sqcup D^{\prime}}A\sqcup A^{\prime}.

Now, we mix both φ\varphi and the reversion of all arcs. Note that if AA admits a directed path from uu to vv, then φ⁡(A)\varphi(A) admits a directed path from vv to uu, so φ​(A)E\varphi(A)^{E} admits a directed path from uu to vv again. Consequently, the map A⊔A′↦φ​(A⊔A′)EA\sqcup A^{\prime}\mapsto\varphi(A\sqcup A^{\prime})^{E} defines a bijection (whose reciprocal is A⊔A′↦φ−1​((A⊔A′)E)A\sqcup A^{\prime}\mapsto\varphi^{-1}((A\sqcup A^{\prime})^{E})) of the set of acyclic orientations of GG with a directed path from uu to vv in DD, such that rkD⊔D′⁡φ​(A⊔A′)E=|E|−rkD⊔D′⁡φ⁡(A⊔A′)=|E|−rkD⊔D′⁡A⊔A′\rank_{D\sqcup D^{\prime}}\varphi(A\sqcup A^{\prime})^{E}=|E|-\rank_{D\sqcup D^{\prime}}\varphi(A\sqcup A^{\prime})=|E|-\rank_{D\sqcup D^{\prime}}A\sqcup A^{\prime}. This bijection yields the following transformation of the sum:

Ψu→v​(D⊔D′,t)=∑A⊔A′∈𝒜​𝒪​(G)A⁡(u,v)=+1trkD⊔D′⁡A⊔A′=∑B⊔B′∈𝒜​𝒪​(G)B⁡(u,v)=+1trkD⊔D′⁡φ−1​(B⊔B′)E=t|E|⋅∑B⊔B′∈𝒜​𝒪​(D)B⁡(u,v)=+1t−rkD⊔D′⁡B⊔B′=t|E|⋅Ψu→v​(D⊔D′,1t)\begin{array}[]{rcl}\Psi^{u\to v}(D\sqcup D^{\prime};t)&=&\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}A\sqcup A^{\prime}\in{\mathcal{AO}}(G)\\ A(u,v)=+1\end{subarray}}t^{\rank_{D\sqcup D^{\prime}}A\sqcup A^{\prime}}\vskip 7.11317pt=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}B\sqcup B^{\prime}\in{\mathcal{AO}}(G)\\ B(u,v)=+1\end{subarray}}t^{\rank_{D\sqcup D^{\prime}}\varphi^{-1}(B\sqcup B^{\prime})^{E}}\\ &=&t^{|E|}\cdot\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}B\sqcup B^{\prime}\in{\mathcal{AO}}(D)\\ B(u,v)=+1\end{subarray}}t^{-\rank_{D\sqcup D^{\prime}}B\sqcup B^{\prime}}\vskip 7.11317pt=t^{|E|}\cdot\Psi^{u\to v}(D\sqcup D^{\prime};\tfrac{1}{t})\end{array}

This ensures that Ψu→v​(D⊔D′,t)\Psi^{u\to v}(D\sqcup D^{\prime};t) is palindromic of length |E||E|. ∎
