Remark 3.51.

One has to be careful not to confuse automorphisms of graphs and of digraphs. For instance, let G=(N,E)G=(N,E) be a path on ℓ\ell nodes, with ℓ\ell odd, denoted x1,…,xℓx_{1},\dots,x_{\ell} with xi​xi+1∈Ex_{i}x_{i+1}\in E. Let u=x1u=x_{1} and v=xℓv=x_{\ell} be the endpoints of this path. The graph GG admits an automorphism that exchanges uu and vv, namely φ:xi↦xℓ−i\varphi:x_{i}\mapsto x_{\ell-i} for i∈[ℓ]i\in[\ell]. Moreover, this is the only automorphism of GG.

Consequently, there is no orientation DD of GG which admits an automorphism that exchanges uu and vv. Indeed, such an automorphism of DD would induce an automorphism of GG, so it would have to be the above φ\varphi, yet since ℓ\ell is odd, there is an edge x(ℓ−1)/2​x(ℓ+1)/2x_{(\ell-1)/2}x_{(\ell+1)/2} in GG whose image by φ\varphi is x(ℓ+1)/2​x(ℓ−1)/2x_{(\ell+1)/2}x_{(\ell-1)/2}: whatever how we orient this edge in DD, its image by φ\varphi would be the same edge but with the reverse orientation, so it would not be an arc of DD.

3.2.6. Deletion-contraction phenomenon for the acyclic polynomial

By means of the decomposition of Proposition 3.43, we can present a deletion-contraction phenomenon. It will be incomplete since it will fail to handle pairs of nodes which share a neighbor which is of degree 3 or more (see Remark 3.57), but it will still enable us to compute the acyclic signature of new graphs, such as the multipaths (see Section 3.3.3). We start with contraction.

Definition 3.52.

Let G=H⊔H′G=H\sqcup H^{\prime} be a graph with a bipartition of the edges of GG such that N⁡(H)∩N⁡(H′)={u,v}N(H)\cap N(H^{\prime})=\{u,v\}. We say that the nodes uu and vv are suspended over HH if all the common neighbors of uu and vv in HH are of degree 22. Moreover, for an orientation D⊔D′D\sqcup D^{\prime} of GG, if uu and vv are suspended over HH, then we denote by xx the number of directed paths of length 22 from uu to vv or from vv to uu in DD, and let yy be the number of paths of length 22 of HH which are not directed paths in DD, and we denote by D~/u​v\tilde{D}/_{uv} the contraction on {u,v}\{u,v\} of the orientation DD with the common neighbors of uu and vv deleted.

Example 3.53.

In Figure 3, the nodes uu and vv are suspended over K2,3K_{2,3}, while any pair among the three other nodes is not suspended over K2,3K_{2,3}. For orientation , we have x=2x=2 and y=1y=1. The orientation D~/u​v\tilde{D}/_{uv} is just a digraph with a single node, whatever the chosen orientation of K2,3K_{2,3}.

Proposition 3.54.

Let G=H⊔H′G=H\sqcup H^{\prime} be a graph with a bipartition of the edges of GG such that N⁡(H)∩N⁡(H′)={u,v}N(H)\cap N(H^{\prime})=\{u,v\}, and D⊔D′D\sqcup D^{\prime} an orientation of GG. Let also ε=1\varepsilon=1 if u​v∈E⁡(H)uv\in E(H) and ε=0\varepsilon=0 if u​v∉E⁡(H)uv\notin E(H). If uu and vv do not have a common neighbor in HH, then

Ψu↮v(D⊔D′;t)=(1−ε)⋅Ψ(D′;t)⋅Ψ(D/u​v;t).\Psi^{u\not\leftrightarrow v}(D\sqcup D^{\prime};t)=(1-\varepsilon)\cdot\Psi(D^{\prime};t)\cdot\Psi(D/_{uv};t)\,.

More generally, if uu and vv are suspended over HH, then with the notations of Definition 3.52:

Ψu↮v(D⊔D′;t)=(1−ε)⋅(2t)x⋅(1+t2)y⋅Ψ(D′;t)⋅Ψ(D~/u​v;t).\Psi^{u\not\leftrightarrow v}(D\sqcup D^{\prime};t)=(1-\varepsilon)\cdot(2t)^{x}\cdot(1+t^{2})^{y}\cdot\Psi(D^{\prime};t)\cdot\Psi(\tilde{D}/_{uv};t)\,.
Proof.

The second formula implies the first when x=y=0x=y=0, hence, we only prove the second.

If there is an edge between uu and vv in HH, then all acyclic orientations A⊔A′A\sqcup A^{\prime} of G=D⊔D′G=D\sqcup D^{\prime} satisfy A⁡(u,v)=±1A(u,v)=\pm 1, so Ψu↮v​(D⊔D′,t)=0\Psi^{u\not\leftrightarrow v}(D\sqcup D^{\prime};t)=0. The right-hand side for the formula is also 00 since (1−ε)=0(1-\varepsilon)=0 in this case. Hence, we assume that there is no edge u​v∈E⁡(H)uv\in E(H) in the following.

The set of acyclic orientations A⊔A′A\sqcup A^{\prime} of G=D⊔D′G=D\sqcup D^{\prime} such that A⁡(u,v)=0A(u,v)=0 is in bijection with the set of pairs (A,A′)∈𝒜​𝒪​(H)×𝒜​𝒪​(H′)(A,A^{\prime})\in{\mathcal{AO}}(H)\times{\mathcal{AO}}(H^{\prime}) such that A⁡(u,v)=0A(u,v)=0. Consequently, since trkD⊔D′⁡A⊔A′=trkD⁡A⋅trkD′⁡A′t^{\rank_{D\sqcup D^{\prime}}A\sqcup A^{\prime}}=t^{\rank_{D}A}\cdot t^{\rank_{D^{\prime}}A^{\prime}}:

Ψu↮v​(D⊔D′,t)=∑A⊔A′∈𝒜​𝒪​(G)A⁡(u,v)=0trkD⊔D′⁡A⊔A′=(∑A′∈𝒜​𝒪​(D′)trkD′⁡A′)⋅(∑A∈𝒜​𝒪​(D)A⁡(u,v)=0trkD⁡A)\Psi^{u\not\leftrightarrow v}(D\sqcup D^{\prime};t)=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}A\sqcup A^{\prime}\in{\mathcal{AO}}(G)\\ A(u,v)=0\end{subarray}}t^{\rank_{D\sqcup D^{\prime}}A\sqcup A^{\prime}}=\left(\sum_{A^{\prime}\in{\mathcal{AO}}(D^{\prime})}t^{\rank_{D^{\prime}}A^{\prime}}\right)\cdot\left(\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}A\in{\mathcal{AO}}(D)\\ A(u,v)=0\end{subarray}}t^{\rank_{D}A}\right)

The left parenthesis is Ψ⁡(D′,t)\Psi(D^{\prime};t).

For the right parenthesis, consider the map A↦A~/u​vA\mapsto\tilde{A}/_{uv}. This maps an acyclic orientation of DD to an orientation of D~/u​v\tilde{D}/_{uv}. Moreover, if AA is acyclic and A⁡(u,v)=0A(u,v)=0, then A~/u​v\tilde{A}/_{uv} is acyclic too (because a directed path between uu and vv in A~/u​v\tilde{A}/_{uv} yields a directed path between uu and vv in AA). Besides, two orientations AA and BB of DD satisfy A~/u​v=B~/u​v\tilde{A}/_{uv}=\tilde{B}/_{uv} if and only if they only differ on the orientation of the paths of length 22 between uu and vv (if there exist any). Let W⊆NW\subseteq N be the set of nodes ww such that there is a path (u,w,v)(u,w,v) in HH, and let WxW_{x} (resp. WyW_{y}) be the set of all nodes ww such that (u,w,v)(u,w,v) is a path in HH and is (resp. is not) a directed path in DD.

Fix w∈Ww\in W: the orientation AA satisfies A⁡(u,v)=0A(u,v)=0 if and only if ww is either a source or a sink in (u,w,v)(u,w,v). Note that this set of orientations admits an involution η\eta without fixed point that exchanges the roles of II and JJ. Let AA be an acyclic orientation of HH where w∈Ww\in W is either a source or a sink.

  1. (1)

    If w∈Wxw\in W_{x}, then rkD⁡A=rkD⁡(A∖w)+1\rank_{D}A=\rank_{D}(A\smallsetminus w)+1;

  2. (2)

Consequently, up to using the involution η\eta, we assume without loss of generality that all w∈Wyw\in W_{y} are sinks in DD. Therefore, for a fixed a∈𝒜𝒪(D~/u​v)a\in{\mathcal{AO}}(\tilde{D}/_{uv}), we get:

rkDA=(rkD~/u​va)+1⋅|Wx|+0⋅|I∩Wy|+2⋅|J∩Wy|=(rkD~/u​va)+x+2⋅|J∩Wy|.\rank_{D}A=(\rank_{\tilde{D}/_{uv}}a)+1\cdot|W_{x}|+0\cdot|I\cap W_{y}|+2\cdot|J\cap W_{y}|=(\rank_{\tilde{D}/_{uv}}a)+x+2\cdot|J\cap W_{y}|.

∑A∈𝒜​𝒪​(D)A⁡(u,v)=0trkD⁡A=∑a∈𝒜𝒪(D~/u​v)trkD~/u​va⋅tx⋅(∑J⊆Wt2​|J∩Wy|)=tx⋅∑a∈𝒜𝒪(D~/u​v)trkD~/u​va⋅(∑J⊆Wyt2​|J|⋅2|W|−|Wy|)=tx⋅(1+t2)|Wy|⋅2x⋅∑a∈𝒜𝒪(D~/u​v)trkD~/u​va=(2t)x⋅(1+t2)y⋅Ψ(D~/u​v;t)∎\begin{array}[]{rclr}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}A\in{\mathcal{AO}}(D)\\ A(u,v)=0\end{subarray}}t^{\rank_{D}A}&=&\sum_{a\in{\mathcal{AO}}(\tilde{D}/_{uv})}t^{\rank_{\tilde{D}/_{uv}}a}\cdot t^{x}\cdot\left(\sum_{J\subseteq W}t^{2|J\cap W_{y}|}\right)&\\ &=&t^{x}\cdot\sum_{a\in{\mathcal{AO}}(\tilde{D}/_{uv})}t^{\rank_{\tilde{D}/_{uv}}a}\cdot\left(\sum_{J\subseteq W_{y}}t^{2|J|}\cdot 2^{|W|-|W_{y}|}\right)&\\ &=&t^{x}\cdot(1+t^{2})^{|W_{y}|}\cdot 2^{x}\cdot\sum_{a\in{\mathcal{AO}}(\tilde{D}/_{uv})}t^{\rank_{\tilde{D}/_{uv}}a}&\\ &=&(2t)^{x}\cdot(1+t^{2})^{y}\cdot\Psi(\tilde{D}/_{uv};t)&\qed\end{array}
Remark 3.55.

As typical use cases of Proposition 3.54, note that if H′=({u,v},∅)H^{\prime}=(\{u,v\},\varnothing), then Ψ⁡(D′,t)=1\Psi(D^{\prime};t)=1; while if H′H^{\prime} is only the edge between uu and vv, then Ψ⁡(D′,t)=1+t\Psi(D^{\prime};t)=1+t.

Example 3.56.

In Figure 3, with the bipartition K2,3=H⊔H′K_{2,3}=H\sqcup H^{\prime} where H′H^{\prime} is the graph with nodes u,vu,v and no edge, the polynomial Ψu↮v​(D,t)\Psi^{u\not\leftrightarrow v}(D;t) can be deduced directly using the second formula of Proposition 3.54: for each orientation, denoting xx the number of directed paths between uu and vv in DD, we get Ψu↮v​(D,t)=(2​t)x​(1+t2)3−x\Psi^{u\not\leftrightarrow v}(D;t)=(2t)^{x}(1+t^{2})^{3-x} whose value is either 8​t38t^{3}, or 4​t2+4​t44t^{2}+4t^{4}, or 2​t+4​t3+2​t52t+4t^{3}+2t^{5}, or 1+3​t2+3​t4+t61+3t^{2}+3t^{4}+t^{6}.

Remark 3.57.

In Proposition 3.54, the condition that uu and vv are suspended over HH is not artificial. Consider the map δ:A↦A/u​v\delta:A\mapsto A/_{uv} from the acyclic orientations of HH to the acyclic orientations of H/u​vH/_{uv}. If all common neighbors of u,vu,v are of degree 22, then the proof of Proposition 3.54 essentially relies on the fact that the fibers δ−1​(a)\delta^{-1}(a) for a∈𝒜𝒪(H/u​v)a\in{\mathcal{AO}}(H/_{uv}) are well-behaved: they have the same size, and the rank of the pre-images can be controlled easily. However, if there exists a common neighbor to u,vu,v which is connected to other nodes of HH (possibly to other common neighbors of uu and vv), then nothing guarantees that the fibers of δ\delta are well-behaved.

As illustrated in Figure 4, is not even true in general that the polynomial Ψ(D~/u​v;t)\Psi(\tilde{D}/_{uv};t) divides the polynomial Ψu↮v​(D⊔D′,t)\Psi^{u\not\leftrightarrow v}(D\sqcup D^{\prime};t).

We now turn our attention to deletion: in what follows, the digraphs DD and D′D^{\prime} should be thought as deletions from the digraph D⊔D′D\sqcup D^{\prime}. The result is easier to understand than the contraction of Proposition 3.54 but only allows us to express partial acyclic polynomials Ψu→v\Psi^{u\to v} using partial acyclic polynomials of smaller digraphs.

Proposition 3.58.

Let G=H⊔H′G=H\sqcup H^{\prime} be a graph with a bipartition of the edges of GG such that N⁡(H)∩N⁡(H′)={u,v}N(H)\cap N(H^{\prime})=\{u,v\}, and D⊔D′D\sqcup D^{\prime} an orientation of GG. Then

Ψu→v​(D⊔D′,t)=(Ψu↮v​(D′,t)+Ψu→v​(D′,t))⋅Ψu→v​(D,t)=(Ψ⁡(D′,t)−t|E|⋅Ψu→v​(D′,1t))⋅Ψu→v​(D,t).\begin{array}[]{rcl}\Psi^{u\to v}(D\sqcup D^{\prime};t)&=&\bigl(\Psi^{u\not\leftrightarrow v}(D^{\prime};t)+\Psi^{u\to v}(D^{\prime};t)\bigr)\cdot\Psi^{u\to v}(D;t)\\ &=&\bigl(\Psi(D^{\prime};t)-t^{|E|}\cdot\Psi^{u\to v}(D^{\prime};\tfrac{1}{t})\bigr)\cdot\Psi^{u\to v}(D;t).\end{array}
Proof.

The set of acyclic orientations A⊔A′A\sqcup A^{\prime} of G=D⊔D′G=D\sqcup D^{\prime} such that A⁡(u,v)=1A(u,v)=1 is in bijection with the set of pairs (A,A′)∈𝒜​𝒪​(H)×𝒜​𝒪​(H′)(A,A^{\prime})\in{\mathcal{AO}}(H)\times{\mathcal{AO}}(H^{\prime}) such that A⁡(u,v)=1A(u,v)=1 and A′​(u,v)≠−1A^{\prime}(u,v)\neq-1. Consequently, since trkD⊔D′⁡A⊔A′=trkD⁡A⋅trkD′⁡A′t^{\rank_{D\sqcup D^{\prime}}A\sqcup A^{\prime}}=t^{\rank_{D}A}\cdot t^{\rank_{D^{\prime}}A^{\prime}}:

Ψu→v​(D⊔D′,t)=∑A⊔A′∈𝒜​𝒪​(G)A⁡(u,v)=1trkD⊔D′⁡A⊔A′=(∑A′∈𝒜​𝒪​(D′)A′​(u,v)∈{0,1}trkD′⁡A′)⋅(∑A∈𝒜​𝒪​(D)A⁡(u,v)=1trkD⁡A)\Psi^{u\to v}(D\sqcup D^{\prime};t)=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}A\sqcup A^{\prime}\in{\mathcal{AO}}(G)\\ A(u,v)=1\end{subarray}}t^{\rank_{D\sqcup D^{\prime}}A\sqcup A^{\prime}}=\left(\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}A^{\prime}\in{\mathcal{AO}}(D^{\prime})\\ A^{\prime}(u,v)\in\{0,1\}\end{subarray}}t^{\rank_{D^{\prime}}A^{\prime}}\right)\cdot\left(\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}A\in{\mathcal{AO}}(D)\\ A(u,v)=1\end{subarray}}t^{\rank_{D}A}\right)

The rightmost parenthesis is Ψu→v​(D,t)\Psi^{u\to v}(D;t), while the left parenthesis is

∑A′∈𝒜​𝒪​(D′)A′​(u,v)=0trkD′⁡A′+∑A′∈𝒜​𝒪​(D′)A′​(u,v)=1trkD′⁡A′=Ψu↮v​(D′,t)+Ψu→v​(D′,t).\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}A^{\prime}\in{\mathcal{AO}}(D^{\prime})\\ A^{\prime}(u,v)=0\end{subarray}}t^{\rank_{D^{\prime}}A^{\prime}}+\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}A^{\prime}\in{\mathcal{AO}}(D^{\prime})\\ A^{\prime}(u,v)=1\end{subarray}}t^{\rank_{D^{\prime}}A^{\prime}}=\Psi^{u\not\leftrightarrow v}(D^{\prime};t)+\Psi^{u\to v}(D^{\prime};t).

Using Proposition 3.43, we get the second formula. ∎

Remark 3.59.

Sadly, Propositions 3.54 and 3.58 do not allow us to compute Ψ⁡(D,t)\Psi(D;t) for any digraph DD via a deletion-contraction recursion. Not only is the choice of the bipartition G=H⊔H′G=H\sqcup H^{\prime} slightly restrictive, but also, although the formula for Ψu↮v​(D⊔D,t)\Psi^{u\not\leftrightarrow v}(D\sqcup D;t) only involves Ψ\Psi of smaller digraphs, the formula for Ψu→v​(D⊔D′,t)\Psi^{u\to v}(D\sqcup D^{\prime};t) involves some Ψu→v\Psi^{u\to v} for smaller digraphs, and we provide no method (except exhaustive enumeration of acyclic orientations) to compute such polynomials. Note that the polynomial Ψu→v​(D,t)\Psi^{u\to v}(D;t) cannot be recovered knowing Ψ⁡(D,t)\Psi(D;t) and Ψu↮v​(D,t)\Psi^{u\not\leftrightarrow v}(D;t) since it is not palindromic.

Remark 3.60.

In [40], Stanley proved that ψ(G)=ψ(G/u​v)+ψ(G∖uv)\psi(G)=\psi(G/_{uv})+\psi(G\smallsetminus uv) for all graphs GG and all edges u​vuv of GG, where ψ⁡(G)=Ψ⁡(D,1)\psi(G)=\Psi(D;1) for any orientation DD of GG. Considering the bipartition of edges G=H⊔H′G=H\sqcup H^{\prime} where H′H^{\prime} is a single edge between uu and vv, one can almost recover Stanley’s deletion-contraction recursion. Indeed, if u,vu,v have no common neighbors in GG, then evaluating Propositions 3.43, 3.54 and 3.58 at t=1t=1 yields:

Ψ⁡(D⊔D′,1)=Ψu↮v​(D⊔D′,1)+2⋅Ψu→v​(D⊔D′,1)=Ψ(D′;1)⋅Ψ(D/u​v;1)+2⋅(Ψu↮v(D′;1)+Ψu→v(D′;1))⋅Ψu→v(D;1)\begin{array}[]{rcl}\Psi(D\sqcup D^{\prime};1)&=&\Psi^{u\not\leftrightarrow v}(D\sqcup D^{\prime};1)+2\cdot\Psi^{u\to v}(D\sqcup D^{\prime};1)\\ &=&\Psi(D^{\prime};1)\cdot\Psi(D/_{uv};1)+2\cdot\bigl(\Psi^{u\not\leftrightarrow v}(D^{\prime};1)+\Psi^{u\to v}(D^{\prime};1)\bigr)\cdot\Psi^{u\to v}(D;1)\end{array}

where Ψ⁡(D′,1)=2\Psi(D^{\prime};1)=2, Ψu↮v​(D′,1)=0\Psi^{u\not\leftrightarrow v}(D^{\prime};1)=0, and Ψu→v​(D′,1)=1\Psi^{u\to v}(D^{\prime};1)=1, since D′D^{\prime} is only an (oriented) edge. Now, applying Propositions 3.43 and 3.54 to DD itself gives: Ψu→v(D;1)=12Ψ(D;1)−12Ψu↮v(D;1)=12Ψ(D;1)−12Ψ(D/u​v;1)\Psi^{u\to v}(D;1)=\frac{1}{2}\Psi(D;1)-\frac{1}{2}\Psi^{u\not\leftrightarrow v}(D;1)=\frac{1}{2}\Psi(D;1)-\frac{1}{2}\Psi(D/_{uv};1). Substituting in the above, we obtain: Ψ(D⊔D′;1)=Ψ(D/u​v;1)+Ψ(D;1)\Psi(D\sqcup D^{\prime};1)=\Psi(D/_{uv};1)+\Psi(D;1), which is precisely Stanley’s recursion, as desired.

However, as our Proposition 3.54 does not apply if uu and vv are not suspended over HH, one still needs to prove Stanley’s recursion in these cases, and cannot recover it from the deletion-contraction phenomenon that we presented.

3.3. Acyclic signature

We use the knowledge on the acyclic polynomial to compute the acyclic signature σ⁡(D)≔Ψ⁡(D,−1)\sigma(D)\coloneqq\Psi(D;-1) of (di)graphs. The actual value of the signature is not very important for the problem of Hamiltonicity of 𝒜​𝒪​(G){\mathcal{AO}}(G): we only care about whether σ⁡(D)\sigma(D) is 00 or not. Indeed, by the parity argument (see [37] or Lemma 2.9), if σ⁡(D)≠0\sigma(D)\neq 0 for some orientation DD or GG, then GG is not 𝒜​𝒪{\mathcal{AO}}-Hamiltonian. The reciprocal is false, yet it seems non-trivial to produce an interesting 22-connected graph with an even number of edges that would help to understand how far from characterizing 𝒜​𝒪{\mathcal{AO}}-Hamiltonicity the acyclic signature is.

3.3.1. Definition for (di)graphs, first examples and first properties

We have seen in Figure 3 that, up to a sign, the signature σ⁡(D)\sigma(D) for DD an orientation of K2,3K_{2,3} does not depend on DD. This is actually a general fact:

Proposition 3.61.

Let DD and D′D^{\prime} be two orientations of a graph GG, then: σ⁡(D′)=(−1)rkD⁡D′⋅σ⁡(D)\sigma(D^{\prime})=(-1)^{\rank_{D}D^{\prime}}\cdot\sigma(D).

Proof.

Suppose that D′=DYD^{\prime}=D^{Y} for some Y⊆2EY\subseteq 2^{E}, and let A=DXA=D^{X} be another orientation of GG. Thus, we have A=(D′)X​△​YA=(D^{\prime})^{X\triangle Y} where △\triangle denotes the symmetric difference operator. This implies that rkD′⁡A=|X​△​Y|=|X|+|Y​|−2|​X∩Y|=rkD⁡D′+rkD⁡A−2​|X∩Y|\rank_{D^{\prime}}A=|X\triangle Y|=|X|+|Y|-2|X\cap Y|=\rank_{D}D^{\prime}+\rank_{D}A-2|X\cap Y| which has the same parity as rkD⁡D′+rkD⁡A\rank_{D}D^{\prime}+\rank_{D}A, i.e. (−1)rkD′⁡A=(−1)rkD⁡D′⋅(−1)rkD⁡A(-1)^{\rank_{D^{\prime}}A}=(-1)^{\rank_{D}D^{\prime}}\cdot(-1)^{\rank_{D}A}. Consequently:

σ⁡(D′)=∑A∈𝒜​𝒪​(G)(−1)rkD′⁡A=(−1)rkD⁡D′⋅∑A∈𝒜​𝒪​(G)(−1)rkD⁡A=(−1)rkD⁡D′⋅σ⁡(D).∎\sigma(D^{\prime})=\sum_{A\in{\mathcal{AO}}(G)}(-1)^{\rank_{D^{\prime}}A}=(-1)^{\rank_{D}D^{\prime}}\cdot\sum_{A\in{\mathcal{AO}}(G)}(-1)^{\rank_{D}A}=(-1)^{\rank_{D}D^{\prime}}\cdot\sigma(D).~\qed

In view of Proposition 3.61, we define σ⁡(G){\sigma(G)} to be the absolute value of σ⁡(D)\sigma(D) for any orientation DD of the graph GG. We can directly use the explicit formulas given in Section 3.2 for Ψ⁡(D,t)\Psi(D;t) to obtain formulas for σ⁡(G)\sigma(G), see Table 1.

3.3.2. Towards a deletion-contraction algorithm

Looking at the formulas we developed for Ψ⁡(D,t)\Psi(D;t) in Section 3.2, one can see that some of them simplify drastically when evaluated at t=1t=1: this allows for recovering many key properties of the number of acyclic orientations ψ⁡(G)=Ψ⁡(D,1)\psi(G)=\Psi(D;1), as we did in Remark 3.60. Likewise, some of these formulas also simplify when evaluated at t=−1t=-1, yielding properties of the acyclic signature σ⁡(G)=|Ψ⁡(D,−1)|\sigma(G)=\bigl|\Psi(D;-1)\bigr|.

Corollary 3.62.

If GG has an odd number of edges, then σ⁡(G)=0\sigma(G)=0.

Proof.

By Corollary 3.44, Ψ⁡(D,t)\Psi(D;t) is palindromic of length |E||E| for any orientation DD of G=(N,E)G=(N,E), i.e. Ψ⁡(D,t)=t|E|​Ψ​(D,1t)\Psi(D;t)=t^{|E|}\Psi(D;\tfrac{1}{t}). Evaluating at t=−1t=-1 for |E||E| odd yields σ⁡(D)=−σ⁡(D)\sigma(D)=-\sigma(D), so σ⁡(D)=0\sigma(D)=0. ∎

For the case of graphs with an even number of edges, we can use the decomposition of Proposition 3.43 and the deletion-contraction phenomenon described in Propositions 3.54 and 3.58, but we need to work with σ⁡(D)\sigma(D) instead of σ⁡(G)\sigma(G) to keep track of signs.

Definition 3.63.

Let G=H⊔H′G=H\sqcup H^{\prime} be a graph with a bipartition of the edges of GG such that N⁡(H)∩N⁡(H′)={u,v}N(H)\cap N(H^{\prime})=\{u,v\}, and D⊔D′D\sqcup D^{\prime} an orientation of GG. We define the partial signatures as σu↮v​(D⊔D′)≔Ψu↮v​(D⊔D′,−1){\sigma^{u\not\leftrightarrow v}(D\sqcup D^{\prime})}\coloneqq\Psi^{u\not\leftrightarrow v}(D\sqcup D^{\prime};-1) and σu→v​(D⊔D′)≔Ψu→v​(D⊔D′,−1){\sigma^{u\to v}(D\sqcup D^{\prime})}\coloneqq\Psi^{u\to v}(D\sqcup D^{\prime};-1).

Theorem 3.64.

For GG a graph with an even number of edges, let G=H⊔H′G=H\sqcup H^{\prime} be a graph with a bipartition of the edges of GG such that N⁡(H)∩N⁡(H′)={u,v}N(H)\cap N(H^{\prime})=\{u,v\}, and D⊔D′D\sqcup D^{\prime} an orientation of GG. Then:

(3.2) σ⁡(D⊔D′)=σu↮v​(D⊔D′)+2⋅σu→v​(D⊔D′)\sigma(D\sqcup D^{\prime})=\sigma^{u\not\leftrightarrow v}(D\sqcup D^{\prime})+2\cdot\sigma^{u\to v}(D\sqcup D^{\prime})
(3.3) σu→v​(D⊔D′)=(σ⁡(D′)−σu→v​(D′))⋅σu→v​(D)\sigma^{u\to v}(D\sqcup D^{\prime})=\bigl(\sigma(D^{\prime})-\sigma^{u\to v}(D^{\prime})\bigr)\cdot\sigma^{u\to v}(D)

Moreover, if uu and vv are suspended over HH, then with the notations of Definition 3.52, and ε=1\varepsilon=1 if u​v∈E⁡(H)uv\in E(H) and ε=0\varepsilon=0 if u​v∉E⁡(H)uv\notin E(H), we get:

(3.4) σu↮v(D⊔D′)=(1−ε)⋅(−1)x⋅2x+y⋅σ(D′)⋅σ(D~/u​v)\sigma^{u\not\leftrightarrow v}(D\sqcup D^{\prime})=(1-\varepsilon)\cdot(-1)^{x}\cdot 2^{x+y}\cdot\sigma(D^{\prime})\cdot\sigma(\tilde{D}/_{uv})
Proof.

Direct applications of Propositions 3.43, 3.54 and 3.58 evaluated at t=−1t=-1 and |E||E| even. ∎

Lemma 3.65.

Let GG be a graph with nodes uu and vv which are suspended over GG. Then, we have

(3.5) σu→v(D)=12(σ(D)−(−1)x⋅2x+y⋅σ(D~/u​v)).\sigma^{u\to v}(D)=\frac{1}{2}\bigl(\sigma(D)-(-1)^{x}\cdot 2^{x+y}\cdot\sigma(\tilde{D}/_{uv})\bigr)\,.
Proof.

Write the bipartition of edges G=H⊔H′G=H\sqcup H^{\prime} where H′H^{\prime} is the graph with nodes u,vu,v and no edge between them, by Theorem 3.64 (3.2), we get: σ⁡(D)=σu↮v​(D)+2⋅σu→v​(D)\sigma(D)=\sigma^{u\not\leftrightarrow v}(D)+2\cdot\sigma^{u\to v}(D), so we have σu→v​(D)=12​(σ⁡(D)−σu↮v​(D))\sigma^{u\to v}(D)=\frac{1}{2}\bigl(\sigma(D)-\sigma^{u\not\leftrightarrow v}(D)\bigr). Besides, by (3.4) σu↮v(D)=(−1)x⋅2x+y⋅1⋅σ(D~/u​v)\sigma^{u\not\leftrightarrow v}(D)=(-1)^{x}\cdot 2^{x+y}\cdot 1\cdot\sigma(\tilde{D}/_{uv}). Thus,

σu→v(D)=12(σ(D)−(−1)x⋅2x+y⋅σ(D~/u​v))∎\sigma^{u\to v}(D)=\frac{1}{2}\bigl(\sigma(D)-(-1)^{x}\cdot 2^{x+y}\cdot\sigma(\tilde{D}/_{uv})\bigr)~~\qed
Remark 3.66 (Algorithm to compute the acyclic signature).

Constructing an algorithm to compute the acyclic signature of a graph GG is not always possible with our current formulas, but we describe how to do it for certain graphs.

First of all, if GG is not connected or not 22-connected Table 1 indicates that σ⁡(G)\sigma(G) can be written as a product of the signatures of the 22-connected components of GG. Secondly, if GG has an odd number of edges, then σ⁡(G)=0\sigma(G)=0 by Corollary 3.62.

Now, assume that GG is 22-connected with an even number of edges. Suppose there is a bipartition G=H⊔H′G=H\sqcup H^{\prime} of its edges such that N⁡(H)∩N⁡(H′)={u,v}N(H)\cap N(H^{\prime})=\{u,v\}, |E⁡(H)||E(H)| and |E⁡(H′)||E(H^{\prime})| are both even, and uu and vv are suspended over HH, then, combining Equations 3.2, 3.3, 3.4 and 3.5 yields:

(3.6) σ⁡(D⊔D′)=c⋅b+12⋅(c−d)⋅(a+b)\sigma(D\sqcup D^{\prime})=c\cdot b+\frac{1}{2}\cdot(c-d)\cdot(a+b)

where, with the notations of Definition 3.52 for x,y,D~x,y,\tilde{D} and x′,y′,D′~x^{\prime},y^{\prime},\tilde{D^{\prime}}:

a=σ⁡(D),b=(−1)x⋅2x+y⋅σ(D~/u​v),c=σ⁡(D′)​, and ​d=(−1)x′⋅2x′+y′⋅σ(D′~/u​v).\begin{array}[]{rclrclrclrcl}a&=&\sigma(D),~~b&=&(-1)^{x}\cdot 2^{x+y}\cdot\sigma(\tilde{D}/_{uv}),~~c&=&\sigma(D^{\prime})\text{, and }d&=&(-1)^{x^{\prime}}\cdot 2^{x^{\prime}+y^{\prime}}\cdot\sigma(\tilde{D^{\prime}}/_{uv})\end{array}\,.

Note that Equation 3.6 expresses the acyclic signature of GG using acyclic signatures of smaller (di)graphs, not using any partial signature. Hence, this is a genuine induction step. In particular, one can try dealing with the signatures aa, bb, cc and dd using the same method, or computing them directly via Table 1 or by exhaustive enumeration of acyclic orientations if the involved digraphs are tame enough. Note that the common neighbors of uu and vv are taken care of in this induction step.

3.3.3. Acyclic signature of multipaths

Definition 3.67.

A path Pℓ{P_{\ell}} of length ℓ≥1\ell\geq 1 is a graph composed of ℓ+1\ell+1 nodes  i1​…,iℓ+1i_{1}\dots,i_{\ell+1}, and edges ip​ip+1i_{p}i_{p+1} for p∈[ℓ]p\in[\ell]. A multipath is a graph composed of several (internally) disjoint paths between the same endpoints uu and vv, see Figure 5 for an illustration. Precisely, for a sequence of integers ℓ=(ℓ1,…,ℓs){\boldsymbol{\ell}}=(\ell_{1},\dots,\ell_{s}) with ℓ1≥1\ell_{1}\geq 1 and ℓi≥2\ell_{i}\geq 2 for all i≥2i\geq 2, the ℓ{\boldsymbol{\ell}}-multipath Pℓ{P_{{\boldsymbol{\ell}}}} is the graph obtained as the contraction of paths Pℓ1,…,PℓsP_{\ell_{1}},\dots,P_{\ell_{s}} at their endpoints, i.e. the graph with nodes uu, vv and i1,2,…,i1,ℓ1,…,is,2,…,is,ℓsi_{1,2},\dots,i_{1,\ell_{1}},\dots,i_{s,2},\dots,i_{s,\ell_{s}}, and edges u​ip,2ui_{p,2}, ip,ℓp​vi_{p,\ell_{p}}v for all p∈[s]p\in[s] and ip,m​ip,m+1i_{p,m}i_{p,m+1} for all p∈[s]p\in[s] and m∈[2,ℓp]m\in[2,\ell_{p}].

We denote Du→vℓ{D^{{\boldsymbol{\ell}}}_{u\to v}} the acyclic orientation of PℓP_{{\boldsymbol{\ell}}} “from uu to vv”, i.e. with arcs u​ip,2ui_{p,2}, ip,ℓp​vi_{p,\ell_{p}}v for all p∈[s]p\in[s] and ip,m​ip,m+1i_{p,m}i_{p,m+1} for all p∈[s]p\in[s] and m∈[2,ℓp]m\in[2,\ell_{p}].

Example 3.68.

The graph K2,3K_{2,3} is the multipath PℓP^{{\boldsymbol{\ell}}} with ℓ=(2,2,2){\boldsymbol{\ell}}=(2,2,2). Orientation of Figure 3 is the orientation Du→vℓD^{{\boldsymbol{\ell}}}_{u\to v}, and we have σ⁡(Du→vℓ)=+6=(−1)3+1⋅(23−2)\sigma(D^{{\boldsymbol{\ell}}}_{u\to v})=+6=(-1)^{3+1}\cdot(2^{3}-2).

The goal of this subsection is to compute the acyclic signature of multipaths. The proof should be read as a showcase of the algorithm of Remark 3.66.

Theorem 3.69.

Fix any ℓ=(ℓ1,…,ℓs){\boldsymbol{\ell}}=(\ell_{1},\dots,\ell_{s}) with ℓ1≥1\ell_{1}\geq 1 and ℓi≥2\ell_{i}\geq 2 for all i≥2i\geq 2. If ∑iℓi\sum_{i}\ell_{i} is odd, then σ⁡(Pℓ)=0\sigma(P^{{\boldsymbol{\ell}}})=0. If ∑iℓi\sum_{i}\ell_{i} is even, then denoting rr the number of i∈[s]i\in[s] such that ℓi\ell_{i} is even, we have:

σ⁡(Du→vℓ)={(−1)s+1⋅(2s−2) if ​ℓi​ is even for all ​i∈[s](−1)r⋅2 otherwise.\sigma(D^{{\boldsymbol{\ell}}}_{u\to v})=\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}(-1)^{s+1}\cdot(2^{s}-2)&\text{ if }\ell_{i}\text{ is even for all }i\in[s]\\ (-1)^{r}\cdot 2&\text{ otherwise}\end{array}\right.\,.
Proof.

If ∑iℓi\sum_{i}\ell_{i} is odd, then PℓP^{{\boldsymbol{\ell}}} has an odd number of edges, so by Corollary 3.62, we get σ⁡(Pℓ)=0\sigma(P^{{\boldsymbol{\ell}}})=0.

Suppose all ℓi\ell_{i} are even for i∈[s]i\in[s], let uu and vv be the two common endpoints of the multipath PℓP^{{\boldsymbol{\ell}}}, and let ℓ′=(ℓ1,…,ℓs){\boldsymbol{\ell}}^{\prime}=(\ell_{1},\dots,\ell_{s}). Assume by induction on ss that σ⁡(Du→vℓ′)=(−1)s⋅(2s−1−2)\sigma(D^{{\boldsymbol{\ell}}^{\prime}}_{u\to v})=(-1)^{s}\cdot(2^{s-1}-2), which holds true for s=1s=1 (where PℓP^{{\boldsymbol{\ell}}} is a path, hence a tree) and s=2s=2 (where PℓP^{{\boldsymbol{\ell}}} is an even cycle) by Table 1. Let xx be the number of i∈[s−1]i\in[s-1] such that ℓi=2\ell_{i}=2. Fix the bipartition Pℓ=Pℓ′⊔PℓsP^{{\boldsymbol{\ell}}}=P^{{\boldsymbol{\ell}}^{\prime}}\sqcup P^{\ell_{s}}. The deletion-contraction argument of Theorem 3.64 (see also Remark 3.66) gives:

σ⁡(Du→vℓ)=σu↮v​(Du→vℓ)+2⋅σu→v​(Du→vℓ)σu↮v​(Du→vℓ)=(−2)x⋅σ(Dℓsu→v)⋅σ(D~ℓu→v/u​v)σu→v​(Du→vℓ)=(σ⁡(Du→vℓs)−σu→v​(Du→vℓs))⋅σu→v​(Du→vℓ′)\begin{array}[]{rcl}\sigma(D^{{\boldsymbol{\ell}}}_{u\to v})&=&\sigma^{u\not\leftrightarrow v}(D^{{\boldsymbol{\ell}}}_{u\to v})+2\cdot\sigma^{u\to v}(D^{{\boldsymbol{\ell}}}_{u\to v})\\ \sigma^{u\not\leftrightarrow v}(D^{{\boldsymbol{\ell}}}_{u\to v})&=&(-2)^{x}\cdot\sigma(D^{\ell_{s}}_{u\to v})\cdot\sigma(\tilde{D}^{{\boldsymbol{\ell}}}_{u\to v}/_{uv})\\ \sigma^{u\to v}(D^{{\boldsymbol{\ell}}}_{u\to v})&=&\bigl(\sigma(D^{\ell_{s}}_{u\to v})-\sigma^{u\to v}(D^{\ell_{s}}_{u\to v})\bigr)\cdot\sigma^{u\to v}(D^{{\boldsymbol{\ell}}^{\prime}}_{u\to v})\end{array}

Since PℓsP^{\ell_{s}} is a path, it is a tree, so σ⁡(Du→vℓs)=0\sigma(D^{\ell_{s}}_{u\to v})=0 by Table 1. Moreover, there is a unique acyclic orientation of PℓsP^{\ell_{s}} which contains a directed path from uu to vv, namely Du→vℓsD^{\ell_{s}}_{u\to v}, so Ψu→v​(Du→vℓs,t)=1\Psi^{u\to v}(D^{\ell_{s}}_{u\to v};t)=1, and in particular σu→v​(Du→vℓs)=1\sigma^{u\to v}(D^{\ell_{s}}_{u\to v})=1. It remains to compute σu→v​(Du→vℓ′)\sigma^{u\to v}(D^{{\boldsymbol{\ell}}^{\prime}}_{u\to v}) which can be done using Lemma 3.65 (where y=0y=0 by construction) because uu and vv have no common neighbors in PℓP^{{\boldsymbol{\ell}}} except on paths of length 22: σu→v(Du→vℓ′)=12(σ(Du→vℓ′)−(−2)x⋅σ(D~u→vℓ′/u​v))\sigma^{u\to v}(D^{{\boldsymbol{\ell}}^{\prime}}_{u\to v})=\frac{1}{2}\bigl(\sigma(D^{{\boldsymbol{\ell}}^{\prime}}_{u\to v})-(-2)^{x}\cdot\sigma(\tilde{D}^{{\boldsymbol{\ell}}^{\prime}}_{u\to v}/_{uv})\bigr).

The graph D~ℓu→v/u​v\tilde{D}^{{\boldsymbol{\ell}}}_{u\to v}/_{uv} is a 11-sum of several cycles directed in a cyclic way of lengths ℓj\ell_{j} for j∈[s−1]j\in[s-1] such that ℓj≠2\ell_{j}\neq 2: these are s−1−xs-1-x even cycles. Thus σu→v​(Du→vℓ′)=(−2)s−1−x\sigma^{u\to v}(D^{{\boldsymbol{\ell}}^{\prime}}_{u\to v})=(-2)^{s-1-x} by Table 1. Putting everything back together, we get

σ⁡(Du→vℓ)=0+(0−1)⋅12​(σ⁡(Du→vℓ′)−(−2)x⋅(−2)s−1−x).\sigma(D^{{\boldsymbol{\ell}}}_{u\to v})=0+(0-1)\cdot\frac{1}{2}\bigl(\sigma(D^{{\boldsymbol{\ell}}^{\prime}}_{u\to v})-(-2)^{x}\cdot(-2)^{s-1-x}\bigr).

As we have assumed by induction that σ⁡(Du→vℓ′)=(−1)s⋅(2s−1−2)\sigma(D^{{\boldsymbol{\ell}}^{\prime}}_{u\to v})=(-1)^{s}\cdot(2^{s-1}-2), we indeed get σ⁡(Du→vℓ)=(−1)s+1⋅(2s−2)\sigma(D^{{\boldsymbol{\ell}}}_{u\to v})=(-1)^{s+1}\cdot(2^{s}-2) if ℓi\ell_{i} is even for all i∈[s]i\in[s].

Last but not least, if there is some j∈[s]j\in[s] such that ℓj\ell_{j} is odd, then, since ∑iℓi\sum_{i}\ell_{i} is even, it implies that there exists another index k∈[s]k\in[s], k≠jk\neq j such that ℓk\ell_{k} is odd. Without loss of generality, we can assume that ℓs−1\ell_{s-1} and ℓs\ell_{s} are odd, and if there exists some j∈[s]j\in[s] such that ℓj=1\ell_{j}=1 then ℓs=1\ell_{s}=1. We denote ℓ′=(ℓ1,…,ℓs−2){\boldsymbol{\ell}}^{\prime}=(\ell_{1},\dots,\ell_{s-2}). We consider the bipartition Pℓ=Pℓ′⊔P(ℓs−1,ℓs)P^{{\boldsymbol{\ell}}}=P^{{\boldsymbol{\ell}}^{\prime}}\sqcup P^{(\ell_{s-1},\ell_{s})}, and compute the corresponding (partial) signatures in a similar manner. Note that Du→v(ℓs−1,ℓs)D^{(\ell_{s-1},\ell_{s})}_{u\to v} is a cycle of even length whose orientation differs on the direction of an odd number of arcs (namely ℓs\ell_{s}) from the cyclic orientation, so σ⁡(Du→v(ℓs−1,ℓs))=+2\sigma(D^{(\ell_{s-1},\ell_{s})}_{u\to v})=+2. Besides, D~ℓ′u→v/u​v\tilde{D}^{{\boldsymbol{\ell}}^{\prime}}_{u\to v}/_{uv} is a 11-sum of cycles directed in a cyclic way: if there is j∈[s−2]j\in[s-2] such that ℓj\ell_{j} is odd, then one of these cycles is of odd length, so σ(D~u→vℓ′/u​v)=0\sigma(\tilde{D}^{{\boldsymbol{\ell}}^{\prime}}_{u\to v}/_{uv})=0, otherwise, σ(D~u→vℓ′/u​v)=(−2)s−x−2\sigma(\tilde{D}^{{\boldsymbol{\ell}}^{\prime}}_{u\to v}/_{uv})=(-2)^{s-x-2}. We could compute σu→v​(Du→v(ℓs−1,ℓs))\sigma^{u\to v}(D^{(\ell_{s-1},\ell_{s})}_{u\to v}) directly, but note that uu and vv have no common neighbors in Du→v(ℓs−1,ℓs)D^{(\ell_{s-1},\ell_{s})}_{u\to v}, so we can instead apply Lemma 3.65, where D~(ℓs−1,ℓs)u→v/u​v\tilde{D}^{(\ell_{s-1},\ell_{s})}_{u\to v}/_{uv} is a 11-sum of two odd cycles, so σ(D~u→v(ℓs−1,ℓs)/u​v)=0\sigma(\tilde{D}^{(\ell_{s-1},\ell_{s})}_{u\to v}/_{uv})=0. We now have all the pieces:

σu→v​(Du→v(ℓs−1,ℓs))=12(σ(D(ℓs−1,ℓs)u→v)−σ(D~(ℓs−1,ℓs)u→v/u​v))=12⋅(2−0)=1σ⁡(Du→vℓ)=(−2)x⋅2⋅σ(D~ℓ′u→v/u​v)+2⋅(2−1)⋅12(σ(Dℓ′u→v)−(−2)x⋅σ(D~ℓ′u→v/u​v))=(−2)x⋅σ(D~ℓ′u→v/u​v)+σ(Dℓ′u→v)\begin{array}[]{rcl}\sigma^{u\to v}(D^{(\ell_{s-1},\ell_{s})}_{u\to v})&=&\frac{1}{2}\bigl(\sigma(D^{(\ell_{s-1},\ell_{s})}_{u\to v})-\sigma(\tilde{D}^{(\ell_{s-1},\ell_{s})}_{u\to v}/_{uv})\bigr)=\frac{1}{2}\cdot(2-0)=1\\ \sigma(D^{{\boldsymbol{\ell}}}_{u\to v})&=&(-2)^{x}\cdot 2\cdot\sigma(\tilde{D}^{{\boldsymbol{\ell}}^{\prime}}_{u\to v}/_{uv})+2\cdot\bigl(2-1\bigr)\cdot\frac{1}{2}\bigl(\sigma(D^{{\boldsymbol{\ell}}^{\prime}}_{u\to v})-(-2)^{x}\cdot\sigma(\tilde{D}^{{\boldsymbol{\ell}}^{\prime}}_{u\to v}/_{uv})\bigr)\\ &=&(-2)^{x}\cdot\sigma(\tilde{D}^{{\boldsymbol{\ell}}^{\prime}}_{u\to v}/_{uv})+\sigma(D^{{\boldsymbol{\ell}}^{\prime}}_{u\to v})\end{array}

To finish, if ℓ′{\boldsymbol{\ell}}^{\prime} contains only even elements, then r=s−2r=s-2, σ(D~u→vℓ′/u​v)=(−2)s−x−2=(−2)r−x\sigma(\tilde{D}^{{\boldsymbol{\ell}}^{\prime}}_{u\to v}/_{uv})=(-2)^{s-x-2}=(-2)^{r-x}, and σ⁡(Du→vℓ′)=(−1)r+1​(2r−2)\sigma(D^{{\boldsymbol{\ell}}^{\prime}}_{u\to v})=(-1)^{r+1}(2^{r}-2) by induction: hence σ⁡(Du→vℓ)=(−2)r+(−1)r+1​(2r−2)=(−1)r⋅2\sigma(D^{{\boldsymbol{\ell}}}_{u\to v})=(-2)^{r}+(-1)^{r+1}(2^{r}-2)=(-1)^{r}\cdot 2. If ℓ′{\boldsymbol{\ell}}^{\prime} contains some odd elements, then σ(D~u→vℓ′/u​v)=0\sigma(\tilde{D}^{{\boldsymbol{\ell}}^{\prime}}_{u\to v}/_{uv})=0, and σ⁡(Du→vℓ′)=(−1)r⋅2\sigma(D^{{\boldsymbol{\ell}}^{\prime}}_{u\to v})=(-1)^{r}\cdot 2 by induction: hence σ⁡(Du→vℓ)=(−1)r⋅2\sigma(D^{{\boldsymbol{\ell}}}_{u\to v})=(-1)^{r}\cdot 2. This concludes the proof. ∎

Corollary 3.70.

For any ℓ=(ℓ1,…,ℓs){\boldsymbol{\ell}}=(\ell_{1},\dots,\ell_{s}) with ℓ1≥1\ell_{1}\geq 1 and ℓi≥2\ell_{i}\geq 2 for all i≥2i\geq 2, if PℓP^{{\boldsymbol{\ell}}} is 𝒜​𝒪{\mathcal{AO}}-Hamiltonian, then ∑i=1sℓi\sum_{i=1}^{s}\ell_{i} is odd.

Proof.

Direct consequence of Theorems 3.69 and 2.9. ∎

Remark 3.71.

One could decide whether the acyclic signature of multipaths is 00 or not via a more direct count of the number of acyclic orientations of multipaths. We prefer the proof of Theorem 3.69 since it emphasizes the properties of the acyclic signature and hints at ways to compute it for larger families of graphs, but the interested reader may have a look at Appendix C.

Remark 3.72.

Let HH be a graph with two nodes u,vu,v, and H′=PℓH^{\prime}=P^{{\boldsymbol{\ell}}} a multipath with endpoints u,vu,v such that ∑iℓi\sum_{i}\ell_{i} is even. One can deduce the acyclic signature of H⊔H′H\sqcup H^{\prime} from the acyclic signature of HH if HH has an even number of edges, and uu and vv do not have a common neighbor in HH except for nodes on induced paths of length 22 between uu and vv. Indeed, in this context, we can use Equation 3.6, where c=σ⁡(Du→vℓ)c=\sigma(D^{{\boldsymbol{\ell}}}_{u\to v}) is known from Theorem 3.69 and d=(−2)x′⋅σ(D~u→vℓ/u​v)d=(-2)^{x^{\prime}}\cdot\sigma(\tilde{D}^{{\boldsymbol{\ell}}}_{u\to v}/_{uv}) is equal to 00 if there is some j∈[s]j\in[s] such that ℓj\ell_{j} is odd, and is equal to (−2)s(-2)^{s} otherwise (since D~ℓu→v/u​v\tilde{D}^{{\boldsymbol{\ell}}}_{u\to v}/_{uv} is a 11-sum of cycles directed in a cyclic way).

4. 𝒜​𝒪{\mathcal{AO}}-Hamiltonicity: (multi)path gluing, and simplicial nodes

Our goal in this section is to construct a Hamiltonian cycle in 𝒜​𝒪​(G){\mathcal{AO}}(G) where GG is obtained from an 𝒜​𝒪{\mathcal{AO}}-Hamiltonian graph HH by adding a multipath between two nodes of HH.

We give an overview of the strategy for proving Hamiltonicity of graphs in a constructive way, in Section 4.1. We begin with a key element in the proof of Hamiltonicity of the graph of regions of supersolvable arrangements in [BrennerCardinalMcConvilleMerinoMutze25-CombinatorialGenerationVII].

Definition 4.1.

Denoting PℓP_{\ell} the path on ℓ\ell nodes with endpoints uu and vv for ℓ≥2\ell\geq 2, a graph GG is ℓ\ell-suspended over a graph H=(N,E)H=(N,E) if GG is a spanning graph of the Cartesian product H×PℓH\times P_{\ell}, such that G⁡[{x}×Pℓ]≃PℓG[\{x\}\times P_{\ell}]\simeq P_{\ell} for all x∈Nx\in N and G⁡[N×{u}]≃G⁡[N×{v}]≃HG[N\times\{u\}]\simeq G[N\times\{v\}]\simeq H.

This graph GG is well-behaved in terms of Hamiltonicity if the graph HH was Hamiltonian (see [BrennerCardinalMcConvilleMerinoMutze25-CombinatorialGenerationVII, Lemma 15]). This is illustrated in Figure 6.

The proof for supersolvable arrangements takes advantage of the fact that if we add new hyperplanes according to the modular chain witnessing supersovability, we subdivide each of the existing chambers in a very regular way, identical to all chambers. Thus, we only need to specify how to walk the new chambers subdividing the existing ones, and then zigzag through the existing chambers through the graphic suspension.

We want to analyze which operations on graphs we can perform, such that if the base graph is 𝒜​𝒪{\mathcal{AO}}-Hamiltonian, the resulting graph is also 𝒜​𝒪{\mathcal{AO}}-Hamiltonian. This means that we generalize this approach of graphic suspension to a case where the two graphs G⁡[N×{0}]G[N\times\{0\}] and G⁡[N×{ℓ}]G[N\times\{\ell\}] need not be copies of the same graph, but rather instances of graphs of the subdivisions of neighboring chambers of the original arrangement through the new hyperplanes. In this case, we find that it can be necessary to use the edges between two graphs G⁡[{v}×i]G[\{v\}\times i] and G⁡[{w}×i]G[\{w\}\times i], where {v,w}\{v,w\} is an edge in the original graph HH.

For our problem, what the authors of [BrennerCardinalMcConvilleMerinoMutze25-CombinatorialGenerationVII] proved implies that if GG is obtained from HH by adding a simplicial node on a clique of size bb, then 𝒜​𝒪​(G){\mathcal{AO}}(G) is bb-suspended over 𝒜​𝒪​(H){\mathcal{AO}}(H), so the zigzag method guarantees that if HH is 𝒜​𝒪{\mathcal{AO}}-Hamiltonian, then GG is also 𝒜​𝒪{\mathcal{AO}}-Hamiltonian. We will discuss this idea in Section 4.3 since we need more conditions on the nodes and certain sequences associated to them.

The question we are concerned with is what to do when GG is obtained from HH by an operation more complicated than adding a simplicial node, especially when 𝒜​𝒪​(G){\mathcal{AO}}(G) is not suspended over 𝒜​𝒪​(H){\mathcal{AO}}(H). We propose two generalizations of the zigzag method, namely Corollaries 4.4 and 4.5. Both are based on the following core idea: if G=H⊔H′G=H\sqcup H^{\prime} is a bipartition of the edges of GG, where H′H^{\prime} shall be thought of as the edges we add to HH, then 𝒜​𝒪​(G){\mathcal{AO}}(G) is an induced subgraph of 𝒜​𝒪​(H)×𝒜​𝒪​(H′){\mathcal{AO}}(H)\times{\mathcal{AO}}(H^{\prime}) (see Lemma 3.40). For each acyclic orientation AA of HH, we consider the graph of acyclic orientations of GG of the form A⊔A′A\sqcup A^{\prime} for all admissible A′∈𝒜​𝒪​(H′)A^{\prime}\in{\mathcal{AO}}(H^{\prime}): if we find a Hamiltonian path PAP_{A} through these acyclic orientations and if we manage to guarantee that we can “string together” the (PA,A∈𝒜​𝒪​(H))(P_{A}~;~A\in{\mathcal{AO}}(H)), then we would have a Hamiltonian path (or cycle) of 𝒜​𝒪​(G){\mathcal{AO}}(G). This is the idea of Theorem 4.5.

Yet, such a straightforward construction is usually not possible. Therefore, instead of just one single orientation, we consider entire sequences (A1,…,As)(A_{1},\dots,A_{s}) of adjacent acyclic orientations of HH (i.e. directed paths in 𝒜​𝒪​(H){\mathcal{AO}}(H)), and find a Hamiltonian path in the subgraph of 𝒜​𝒪​(G){\mathcal{AO}}(G) induced by all the acyclic orientations of the form Ai⊔A′A_{i}\sqcup A^{\prime} for i∈[s]i\in[s] and A′∈𝒜​𝒪​(H′)A^{\prime}\in{\mathcal{AO}}(H^{\prime}). We call such a Hamiltonian path a replacing pattern for (A1,…,As)(A_{1},\dots,A_{s}). To be able to “string together” these replacing patterns in order to construct a Hamiltonian path (or cycle) for 𝒜​𝒪​(G){\mathcal{AO}}(G), we develop a theory of lacing patterns, leading to Propositions 4.3 and 4.4.

We formalize these ideas, and apply them to gluing multipaths in Sections 4.2.2, 4.2.1 and 4.2.3.

4.1. How to lace patterns

Recall from Definition 3.39 that A⁡(u,v)A(u,v) is the direction induced by the acyclic orientation AA on the nodes u,vu,v (i.e. ±1\pm 1 if there is a directed path from uu to vv or from vv to uu in AA, and 00 otherwise), and that we denote 𝑨⁡(u,v)≔(A1​(u,v),…,Ar​(u,v)){\boldsymbol{A}}(u,v)\coloneqq\bigl(A_{1}(u,v),\dots,A_{r}(u,v)\bigr) for a sequence of acyclic orientations 𝑨=(A1,…,Ar){\boldsymbol{A}}=(A_{1},\dots,A_{r}).

Let G=H⊔H′G=H\sqcup H^{\prime} be a bipartition of the edges of the graph G=(N,E)G=(N,E). We have seen in Lemma 3.40 that 𝒜​𝒪​(G){\mathcal{AO}}(G) is the subgraph of the Cartesian product 𝒜​𝒪​(H)×𝒜​𝒪​(H′){\mathcal{AO}}(H)\times{\mathcal{AO}}(H^{\prime}) induced on the pairs of orientations (A,A′)(A,A^{\prime}) with A∈𝒜​𝒪​(H)A\in{\mathcal{AO}}(H) and A′∈𝒜​𝒪​(H′)A^{\prime}\in{\mathcal{AO}}(H^{\prime}) such that A⁡(u,v)⋅A′​(u,v)≠−1A(u,v)\cdot A^{\prime}(u,v)\neq-1 for all u,v∈Nu,v\in N. Hence, for an acyclic orientation AA of HH, we denote by 𝒜​𝒪​(H′|A){{\mathcal{AO}}(H^{\prime}|A)} the set of acyclic orientations A′A^{\prime} of H′H^{\prime} such that A⁡(u,v)⋅A′​(u,v)≠−1A(u,v)\cdot A^{\prime}(u,v)\neq-1 for all u,v∈Nu,v\in N.

Let 𝑨=(A1,…,As){\boldsymbol{A}}=(A_{1},\dots,A_{s}) be a directed path in 𝒜​𝒪​(H){\mathcal{AO}}(H). We denote by 𝒜​𝒪​(H′|𝑨){\mathcal{AO}}(H^{\prime}|{\boldsymbol{A}}) the subgraph of 𝒜​𝒪​(G){\mathcal{AO}}(G) induced on all the orientations Aj⊔Ak′A_{j}\sqcup A^{\prime}_{k} of GG for Ak′∈𝒜​𝒪​(H′|Aj)A^{\prime}_{k}\in{\mathcal{AO}}(H^{\prime}|A_{j}) with 1≤j≤s1\leq j\leq s.

Definition 4.2.

A replacing pattern 𝑷{\boldsymbol{P}} for 𝑨{\boldsymbol{A}} is a (directed) Hamiltonian path in 𝒜​𝒪​(H′|𝑨){\mathcal{AO}}(H^{\prime}|{\boldsymbol{A}}) that starts at some A1⊔A′A_{1}\sqcup A^{\prime} for some A′∈𝒜​𝒪​(H′|A1)A^{\prime}\in{\mathcal{AO}}(H^{\prime}|A_{1}) and ends at some As⊔B′A_{s}\sqcup B^{\prime} for some B′∈𝒜​𝒪​(H′|As)B^{\prime}\in{\mathcal{AO}}(H^{\prime}|A_{s}).

We denote by ωi𝑷{\omega_{i}^{{\boldsymbol{P}}}} the total order on 𝒜​𝒪​(H′|Ai){\mathcal{AO}}(H^{\prime}|A_{i}) (i.e. the bijection from 𝒜​𝒪​(H′|Ai){\mathcal{AO}}(H^{\prime}|A_{i}) to [m][m] with m≔|𝒜​𝒪​(H′|Ai)|m\coloneqq|{\mathcal{AO}}(H^{\prime}|A_{i})|) induced by the replacing pattern 𝑷{\boldsymbol{P}}, that is ωi𝑷​(A′)≤ωi𝑷​(B′)\omega_{i}^{{\boldsymbol{P}}}(A^{\prime})\leq\omega_{i}^{{\boldsymbol{P}}}(B^{\prime}) if Ai⊔A′A_{i}\sqcup A^{\prime} appears before Ai⊔B′A_{i}\sqcup B^{\prime} in the directed path 𝑷{\boldsymbol{P}}.

For a replacing pattern 𝑷{\boldsymbol{P}} on (A1,…,As)(A_{1},\dots,A_{s}) and i∈[s]i\in[s], we define the consecutive locus consi⁡(𝑷){\cons_{i}({\boldsymbol{P}})} to be the set of indices jj such that for the orientation A′∈𝒜​𝒪​(H′|Ai)A^{\prime}\in{\mathcal{AO}}(H^{\prime}|A_{i}) with ωi𝑷​(A′)=j\omega_{i}^{{\boldsymbol{P}}}(A^{\prime})=j, it holds that the node in 𝑷{\boldsymbol{P}} after Ai⊔A′A_{i}\sqcup A^{\prime} is of the form Ai⊔B′A_{i}\sqcup B^{\prime} for some B′∈𝒜​𝒪​(H′|Ai)B^{\prime}\in{\mathcal{AO}}(H^{\prime}|A_{i}).

Denoting m≔|𝒜​𝒪​(H′|As)|m\coloneqq|{\mathcal{AO}}(H^{\prime}|A_{s})|, two replacing patterns 𝑷{\boldsymbol{P}} on (A1,…,As)(A_{1},\dots,A_{s}) and 𝑸{\boldsymbol{Q}} on (As,…,At)(A_{s},\dots,A_{t}) can lace if ωs𝑷=ωs𝑸\omega_{s}^{{\boldsymbol{P}}}=\omega_{s}^{{\boldsymbol{Q}}} and conss⁡(𝑷)∪conss⁡(𝑸)=[m]\cons_{s}({\boldsymbol{P}})\cup\cons_{s}({\boldsymbol{Q}})=[m]. If they can lace, we write 𝑷{\boldsymbol{P}} as the concatenation of directed paths 𝑷0∪⋯∪𝑷m−1{{\boldsymbol{P}}_{0}}\cup\dots\cup{{\boldsymbol{P}}_{m-1}} where each 𝑷j{\boldsymbol{P}}_{j} is the directed sub-path from the node As⊔A′A_{s}\sqcup A^{\prime} with ωs𝑷​(A′)=j\omega_{s}^{{\boldsymbol{P}}}(A^{\prime})=j to the node As⊔B′A_{s}\sqcup B^{\prime} with ωs𝑷​(B′)=j+1\omega_{s}^{{\boldsymbol{P}}}(B^{\prime})=j+1 (by convention, 𝑷0{\boldsymbol{P}}_{0} starts at the starting node of 𝑷{\boldsymbol{P}}). Similarly, we write 𝑸{\boldsymbol{Q}} as the concatenation of directed paths 𝑸1∪⋯∪𝑸m{{\boldsymbol{Q}}_{1}}\cup\dots\cup{{\boldsymbol{Q}}_{m}} where each 𝑸j{\boldsymbol{Q}}_{j} is the directed sub-path from the node As⊔A′A_{s}\sqcup A^{\prime} with ωs𝑸​(A′)=j\omega_{s}^{{\boldsymbol{Q}}}(A^{\prime})=j to the node As⊔B′A_{s}\sqcup B^{\prime} with ωs𝑸​(B′)=j+1\omega_{s}^{{\boldsymbol{Q}}}(B^{\prime})=j+1 (by convention, 𝑸m{\boldsymbol{Q}}_{m} ends at the ending node of 𝑸{\boldsymbol{Q}}). Then, the lacing 𝑷∧𝑸{\boldsymbol{P}}\wedge{\boldsymbol{Q}} is the directed path obtained as the concatenation of 𝑷0∪𝑿1∪⋯∪𝑿m−1∪𝑸m{\boldsymbol{P}}_{0}\cup{\boldsymbol{X}}_{1}\cup\dots\cup{\boldsymbol{X}}_{m-1}\cup{\boldsymbol{Q}}_{m} where:

𝑿j={𝑷j if ​j∈conss⁡(𝑸)𝑸j otherwise.{\boldsymbol{X}}_{j}=\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}{\boldsymbol{P}}_{j}&\text{ if }j\in\cons_{s}({\boldsymbol{Q}})\\ {\boldsymbol{Q}}_{j}&\text{ otherwise}\end{array}\right..

Note that the condition conss⁡(𝑷)∪conss⁡(𝑸)=[m]\cons_{s}({\boldsymbol{P}})\cup\cons_{s}({\boldsymbol{Q}})=[m] ensures that the “otherwise” case implies j∈conss⁡(𝑷)j\in\cons_{s}({\boldsymbol{P}}).

Proposition 4.3.

Let 𝐏{\boldsymbol{P}} (resp. 𝐐{\boldsymbol{Q}}) be a replacing pattern for the subsequence (A1,…,As)(A_{1},\dots,A_{s}) (resp. (As,…,At)(A_{s},\dots,A_{t})). If 𝐏{\boldsymbol{P}} and 𝐐{\boldsymbol{Q}} can lace, then their lacing 𝐏∧𝐐{\boldsymbol{P}}\wedge{\boldsymbol{Q}} is a replacing pattern for (A1,…,At)(A_{1},\dots,A_{t}).

Proof.

Since 𝑷{\boldsymbol{P}} and 𝑸{\boldsymbol{Q}} can lace, we have ωs𝑷=ωs𝑸\omega_{s}^{{\boldsymbol{P}}}=\omega_{s}^{{\boldsymbol{Q}}}, so 𝑿j{\boldsymbol{X}}_{j} and 𝑿j+1{\boldsymbol{X}}_{j+1} meet on the node As⊔A′A_{s}\sqcup A^{\prime} with ωs​𝑷​(A′)=j+1=ωs𝑸​(A′)\omega_{s}{{\boldsymbol{P}}}(A^{\prime})=j+1=\omega_{s}^{{\boldsymbol{Q}}}(A^{\prime}). Hence, by construction of 𝑷∧𝑸{\boldsymbol{P}}\wedge{\boldsymbol{Q}}, it is a directed path inside 𝒜​𝒪​(H′|A1,…,As,…,At){\mathcal{AO}}(H^{\prime}|A_{1},\dots,A_{s},\dots,A_{t}). Moreover, 𝑷∧𝑸{\boldsymbol{P}}\wedge{\boldsymbol{Q}} starts at some A1⊔A′A_{1}\sqcup A^{\prime} for some A′∈𝒜​𝒪​(H′|A1)A^{\prime}\in{\mathcal{AO}}(H^{\prime}|A_{1}) (because its starting node is the same as the one of 𝑷{\boldsymbol{P}}), and ends at some At⊔B′A_{t}\sqcup B^{\prime} for some B′∈𝒜​𝒪​(H′|At)B^{\prime}\in{\mathcal{AO}}(H^{\prime}|A_{t}) (because its ending node is the same as the one of 𝑸{\boldsymbol{Q}}). Hence, it is enough to prove that all nodes of 𝒜​𝒪​(H′|A1,…,As,…,At){\mathcal{AO}}(H^{\prime}|A_{1},\dots,A_{s},\dots,A_{t}) appear in 𝑷∧𝑸{\boldsymbol{P}}\wedge{\boldsymbol{Q}}.

We use the notations presented in the definition of the lacing. Consider the restriction of 𝑷∧𝑸{\boldsymbol{P}}\wedge{\boldsymbol{Q}} to 𝒜​𝒪​(H′|A1,…,As){\mathcal{AO}}(H^{\prime}|A_{1},\dots,A_{s}): by construction, if 𝑷j⊄𝑷∧𝑸{\boldsymbol{P}}_{j}\not\subset{\boldsymbol{P}}\wedge{\boldsymbol{Q}}, then j∈conss⁡(𝑷)j\in\cons_{s}({\boldsymbol{P}}), so 𝑷j{\boldsymbol{P}}_{j} is composed of a single edge from As⊔A′A_{s}\sqcup A^{\prime} to As⊔B′A_{s}\sqcup B^{\prime} for some A′,B′∈𝒜​𝒪​(H′|As)A^{\prime},B^{\prime}\in{\mathcal{AO}}(H^{\prime}|A_{s}). Note that these two nodes As⊔A′A_{s}\sqcup A^{\prime} to As⊔B′A_{s}\sqcup B^{\prime} are in the path 𝑷∧𝑸{\boldsymbol{P}}\wedge{\boldsymbol{Q}} since they belong to 𝑸j{\boldsymbol{Q}}_{j}, only the edge is not there. Hence, all the nodes appearing in 𝑷{\boldsymbol{P}} (resp. 𝑸{\boldsymbol{Q}}) also appear in 𝑷∧𝑸{\boldsymbol{P}}\wedge{\boldsymbol{Q}}. As 𝑷{\boldsymbol{P}} (resp. 𝑸{\boldsymbol{Q}}) is a Hamiltonian path in 𝒜​𝒪​(H′|A1,…,As){\mathcal{AO}}(H^{\prime}|A_{1},\dots,A_{s}) (resp. in 𝒜​𝒪​(H′|As,…,At){\mathcal{AO}}(H^{\prime}|A_{s},\dots,A_{t})), we indeed get that 𝑷∧𝑸{\boldsymbol{P}}\wedge{\boldsymbol{Q}} is a Hamiltonian path in 𝒜​𝒪​(H′|A1,…,As,…,At){\mathcal{AO}}(H^{\prime}|A_{1},\dots,A_{s},\dots,A_{t}). ∎

Finally, a replacing pattern 𝑷{\boldsymbol{P}} for a directed cycle (A1,…,As)(A_{1},\dots,A_{s}) in 𝒜​𝒪​(H){\mathcal{AO}}(H) with As=A1A_{s}=A_{1} can self-lace if conss⁡(𝑷)={1,…,|𝒜​𝒪​(H′|As)|}\cons_{s}({\boldsymbol{P}})=\{1,\dots,|{\mathcal{AO}}(H^{\prime}|A_{s})|\} and for the orientation A∘′∈𝒜​𝒪​(H′|As)A^{\prime}_{\circ}\in{\mathcal{AO}}(H^{\prime}|A_{s}) such that ωs𝑷​(A∘′)=1\omega_{s}^{{\boldsymbol{P}}}(A^{\prime}_{\circ})=1 we also have ω1𝑷​(A∘′)=1\omega_{1}^{{\boldsymbol{P}}}(A^{\prime}_{\circ})=1. The self-lacing of 𝑷{\boldsymbol{P}}, denoted ∧𝑷{\wedge{\boldsymbol{P}}}, is defined as 𝑷{\boldsymbol{P}} without its edges from As⊔A′A_{s}\sqcup A^{\prime} to As⊔B′A_{s}\sqcup B^{\prime} for some A′,B′∈𝒜​𝒪​(H′|As)A^{\prime},B^{\prime}\in{\mathcal{AO}}(H^{\prime}|A_{s}).

Corollary 4.4.

Let G=H⊔H′G=H\sqcup H^{\prime} be a bipartition of the edges of GG. If 𝐀{\boldsymbol{A}} is a Hamiltonian cycle for 𝒜​𝒪​(H){\mathcal{AO}}(H) and 𝐏{\boldsymbol{P}} a replacing pattern for 𝐀{\boldsymbol{A}} that can self-lace, then ∧𝐏\wedge{\boldsymbol{P}} is a Hamiltonian cycle for 𝒜​𝒪​(G){\mathcal{AO}}(G).

Proof.

Since ωs𝑷\omega_{s}^{{\boldsymbol{P}}} and ω1𝑷\omega_{1}^{{\boldsymbol{P}}} have the same first element A∘′A^{\prime}_{\circ}, the first node of 𝑷{\boldsymbol{P}} is equal to the last node of 𝑷{\boldsymbol{P}} without its edges from As⊔A′A_{s}\sqcup A^{\prime} to As⊔B′A_{s}\sqcup B^{\prime} for some A′,B′∈𝒜​𝒪​(H′|As)A^{\prime},B^{\prime}\in{\mathcal{AO}}(H^{\prime}|A_{s}). Hence ∧𝑷\wedge{\boldsymbol{P}} is a (directed) cycle. Moreover, all the nodes of 𝒜​𝒪​(H′|A1,…​As−1){\mathcal{AO}}(H^{\prime}|A_{1},\dots A_{s-1}) appear in ∧𝑷\wedge{\boldsymbol{P}}, so because A1=AsA_{1}=A_{s}, the cycle ∧𝑷\wedge{\boldsymbol{P}} is a Hamiltonian cycle for 𝒜​𝒪​(G){\mathcal{AO}}(G). ∎

One can generalize Propositions 4.3 and 4.4 in order to weaken their hypotheses. As it makes the hypotheses less concise and handy, we keep both as stated above, for the more general statement see Appendix A.1.

Theorem 4.5.

Let G=H⊔H′G=H\sqcup H^{\prime} be a bipartition of the edges of GG. Suppose that there exists X′,Y′∈𝒜​𝒪​(H′)X^{\prime},Y^{\prime}\in{\mathcal{AO}}(H^{\prime}) and a Hamiltonian path 𝐀=(A1,…,As){\boldsymbol{A}}=(A_{1},\dots,A_{s}) in 𝒜​𝒪​(H){\mathcal{AO}}(H) such that:

  • •

    X′∈𝒜​𝒪​(H′|Ai)X^{\prime}\in{\mathcal{AO}}(H^{\prime}|A_{i}) and Y′∈𝒜​𝒪​(H′|Ai)Y^{\prime}\in{\mathcal{AO}}(H^{\prime}|A_{i}) for all i∈[s]i\in[s] (equivalently, X′​(u,v)=Y′​(u,v)=0X^{\prime}(u,v)=Y^{\prime}(u,v)=0 for all nodes u,vu,v connected in HH), and

  • •

    One can split the sequence 𝑨{\boldsymbol{A}} into splitting subsequences 𝑨j≔(Aij,Aij+1,…,Aij+1−1){\boldsymbol{A}}_{j}\coloneqq(A_{i_{j}},A_{i_{j}+1},\dots,A_{i_{j+1}-1}) for j∈[r]j\in[r] with i1=1i_{1}=1 and ir−1=si_{r}-1=s such that for each j∈[r]j\in[r], the sequence 𝑨j{\boldsymbol{A}}_{j} admits either:

    • –

      a replacing pattern which starts at Aij⊔Aj′A_{i_{j}}\sqcup A_{j}^{\prime} and ends at Aij+1−1⊔Bj′A_{i_{j+1}-1}\sqcup B_{j}^{\prime} either for {Aj′,Bj′}={X′,Y′}\{A_{j}^{\prime},B_{j}^{\prime}\}=\{X^{\prime},Y^{\prime}\}, or

    • –

      two replacing patterns which start at Aij⊔Aj′A_{i_{j}}\sqcup A_{j}^{\prime} and end at Aij+1−1⊔Bj′A_{i_{j+1}-1}\sqcup B_{j}^{\prime}, one for Aj′=Bj′=X′A_{j}^{\prime}=B_{j}^{\prime}=X^{\prime} and one for Aj′=Bj′=Y′A_{j}^{\prime}=B_{j}^{\prime}=Y^{\prime},

then there exists a Hamiltonian path in 𝒜​𝒪​(G){\mathcal{AO}}(G) obtained as a concatenation of some of these replacing patterns.

Moreover, if 𝐀{\boldsymbol{A}} is a Hamiltonian cycle of 𝒜​𝒪​(H){\mathcal{AO}}(H), and #⁡{j∈[r];Aj′≠Bj′}\#\{j\in[r]~;~A^{\prime}_{j}\neq B^{\prime}_{j}\} is even, then GG is 𝒜​𝒪{\mathcal{AO}}-Hamiltonian.

Proof.

We will concatenate replacing patterns. Note that one can reverse the direction of every arc in a replacing pattern to exchange its starting and ending nodes.

Let ςj=#⁡{k∈[j−1];Ak′≠Bk′}\varsigma_{j}=\#\{k\in[j-1]~;~A^{\prime}_{k}\neq B^{\prime}_{k}\}. We choose the replacing pattern 𝑷j{\boldsymbol{P}}_{j} as follows:

  • •

    if Aj′≠Bj′A^{\prime}_{j}\neq B^{\prime}_{j} and ςj\varsigma_{j} is even, then 𝑷j{\boldsymbol{P}}_{j} starts at Aij⊔X′A_{i_{j}}\sqcup X^{\prime} and ends at Aij+1−1⊔Y′A_{i_{j+1}-1}\sqcup Y^{\prime};

  • •

    if Aj′≠Bj′A^{\prime}_{j}\neq B^{\prime}_{j} and ςj\varsigma_{j} is odd, then 𝑷j{\boldsymbol{P}}_{j} starts at Aij⊔Y′A_{i_{j}}\sqcup Y^{\prime} and ends at Aij+1−1⊔X′A_{i_{j+1}-1}\sqcup X^{\prime};

  • •

    if Aj′=Bj′A^{\prime}_{j}=B^{\prime}_{j} and ςj\varsigma_{j} is odd, then 𝑷j{\boldsymbol{P}}_{j} starts at Aij⊔Y′A_{i_{j}}\sqcup Y^{\prime} and ends at Aij+1−1⊔Y′A_{i_{j+1}-1}\sqcup Y^{\prime};

  • •

    if Aj′=Bj′A^{\prime}_{j}=B^{\prime}_{j} and ςj\varsigma_{j} is even, then 𝑷j{\boldsymbol{P}}_{j} starts at Aij⊔X′A_{i_{j}}\sqcup X^{\prime} and ends at Aij+1−1⊔X′A_{i_{j+1}-1}\sqcup X^{\prime}.

For all j∈[r−1]j\in[r-1], by construction of ςj\varsigma_{j}, the orientation of HH of the last node of 𝑷j{\boldsymbol{P}}_{j} is Aij+1−1A_{i_{j+1}-1} and the orientation of HH of the first node of 𝑷j+1{\boldsymbol{P}}_{j+1} is Aij+1A_{i_{j+1}} and the orientation of H′H^{\prime} is the same (either X′X^{\prime} or Y′Y^{\prime}), so these two nodes are adjacent in 𝒜​𝒪​(G){\mathcal{AO}}(G). In particular, the concatenation (𝑷1,𝑷2,…,𝑷r)({\boldsymbol{P}}_{1},{\boldsymbol{P}}_{2},\dots,{\boldsymbol{P}}_{r}) is a Hamiltonian path in 𝒜​𝒪​(G){\mathcal{AO}}(G).

Moreover, if #⁡{j∈[r];Aj′≠Bj′}\#\{j\in[r]~;~A^{\prime}_{j}\neq B^{\prime}_{j}\} is even, then either ςr\varsigma_{r} is odd and Aj′≠Bj′A^{\prime}_{j}\neq B^{\prime}_{j}, so its last node is As⊔X′A_{s}\sqcup X^{\prime}, or ςr\varsigma_{r} is odd and Aj′=Bj′A^{\prime}_{j}=B^{\prime}_{j}, so its last node is As⊔X′A_{s}\sqcup X^{\prime}. If, in addition, AsA_{s} and A1A_{1} are adjacent in 𝒜​𝒪​(H){\mathcal{AO}}(H) (i.e. if 𝑨{\boldsymbol{A}} is a Hamiltonian cycle of 𝒜​𝒪​(H){\mathcal{AO}}(H)), then the last node of 𝑷r{\boldsymbol{P}}_{r} and the first node of 𝑷1{\boldsymbol{P}}_{1} are adjacent in 𝒜​𝒪​(G){\mathcal{AO}}(G) so (𝑷1,𝑷2,…,𝑷r)({\boldsymbol{P}}_{1},{\boldsymbol{P}}_{2},\dots,{\boldsymbol{P}}_{r}) is a Hamiltonian cycle in 𝒜​𝒪​(G){\mathcal{AO}}(G). ∎

As before, one can generalize Theorem 4.5 in order to weaken its hypotheses, for the more general statement, see Appendix A.2.

4.2. Multipath gluing and 0-even sequences

For a graph G=(N,E)G=(N,E) and two nodes  u,v∈Nu,v\in N, the path gluing of length ℓ\ell at u,vu,v, denoted ⊕u,vℓG{\oplus_{u,v}^{\ell}G}, is the graph obtained by adding ℓ−1\ell-1 nodes  to GG and constructing a path of length ℓ\ell between uu and vv, supported on these new nodes. Formally, using the notation we have introduced for gluings in Section 2.4, let PℓP_{\ell} be a path of length ℓ\ell with end nodes xx and yy, and let φ1:{u}→{x}\varphi_{1}:\{u\}\to\{x\} and φ2:{v}→{y}\varphi_{2}:\{v\}\to\{y\}, then ⊕u,vℓG≔G⊕φ1,φ2Pℓ\oplus_{u,v}^{\ell}G\coloneqq G\oplus_{\varphi_{1},\varphi_{2}}P_{\ell}.

The multipath gluing of length ℓ=(ℓ1,…,ℓm){\boldsymbol{\ell}}=(\ell_{1},\dots,\ell_{m}) at u,vu,v is then defined recursively for m≥2m\geq 2 as the graph ⊕u,vℓG≔⊕u,vℓm(⊕u,v(ℓ1,…,ℓm−1)G){\oplus_{u,v}^{{\boldsymbol{\ell}}}G}\coloneqq\oplus_{u,v}^{\ell_{m}}\bigl(\oplus_{u,v}^{(\ell_{1},\dots,\ell_{m-1})}G\bigr).

Definition 4.6.

A sequence of integers 𝒂=(a1,…,ar){\boldsymbol{a}}=(a_{1},\dots,a_{r}) is 00-even if, between any two non-zero entries of 𝒂{\boldsymbol{a}}, there is an even number of zeros in 𝒂{\boldsymbol{a}}.

4.2.1. Gluing a path of even length

Our main objective in this section is to prove Theorem 4.7. This motivates us to define special subsequences as well as a proposition on regularity of replacing patterns (see Proposition 4.8). The proof is delayed to page 4.2.1.

Theorem 4.7.

Let G=(N,E)G=(N,E) be a 𝒜​𝒪{\mathcal{AO}}-Hamiltonian graph with 𝐀=(A1,…,As){\boldsymbol{A}}=(A_{1},\dots,A_{s}) a Hamiltonian cycle in 𝒜​𝒪​(G){\mathcal{AO}}(G). For u,v∈Nu,v\in N in the same connected component of GG and an even number ℓ≥2\ell\geq 2, if 𝐀⁡(u,v){\boldsymbol{A}}(u,v) is 00-even, then ⊕u,vℓG\oplus_{u,v}^{\ell}G is 𝒜​𝒪{\mathcal{AO}}-Hamiltonian. Moreover, under these assumptions, there exists a Hamiltonian cycle 𝐁=(B1,…,Bt){\boldsymbol{B}}=(B_{1},\dots,B_{t}) in 𝒜𝒪(⊕u,vℓG){\mathcal{AO}}(\oplus_{u,v}^{\ell}G) such that 𝐁⁡(u,v){\boldsymbol{B}}(u,v) is 00-even.

Our proof will explicitly construct a new Hamiltonian cycle 𝑩{\boldsymbol{B}} for 𝒜𝒪(⊕u,vℓG){\mathcal{AO}}(\oplus_{u,v}^{\ell}G) with ℓ\ell even, from any Hamiltonian cycle 𝑨{\boldsymbol{A}} of 𝒜​𝒪​(G){\mathcal{AO}}(G) (such that 𝑨⁡(u,v){\boldsymbol{A}}(u,v) is 00-even) and any Hamiltonian cycle of the cube-graph QℓQ_{\ell}.

For the cube-graph QℓQ_{\ell}, fix a Hamiltonian cycle 𝑺≔(S1,…,S2ℓ){{\boldsymbol{S}}}\coloneqq(S_{1},\dots,S_{2^{\ell}}) of Qℓ≃𝒜​𝒪​(Pℓ)Q_{\ell}\simeq{\mathcal{AO}}(P_{\ell}) (see Example 2.4 for its existence), where we interpret each SpS_{p} as a subset of E⁡(Pℓ)E(P_{\ell}) (instead of a subset of [ℓ][\ell]). Without loss of generality, we can suppose that S2ℓ=[ℓ]≃E⁡(Pℓ){S_{2^{\ell}}=[\ell]\simeq E(P_{\ell})}, i.e. S2ℓ​(u,v)=−1S_{2^{\ell}}(u,v)=-1; and we denote by μ{\mu} the index in [2ℓ][2^{\ell}] such that Sμ=∅{S_{\mu}=\varnothing}, i.e. Sμ​(u,v)=1S_{\mu}(u,v)=1. Note that QℓQ_{\ell} is bipartite: ∅\varnothing and E⁡(Pℓ)E(P_{\ell}) belong to the same part if and only if ℓ\ell is even. Consequently, as we have supposed ℓ\ell even, this implies that μ\mu is even and not 00.

Let 𝑨=(A1,…,As){\boldsymbol{A}}=(A_{1},\dots,A_{s}) be a Hamiltonian cycle in 𝒜​𝒪​(G){\mathcal{AO}}(G) such that 𝑨⁡(u,v){\boldsymbol{A}}(u,v) is 00-even. Without loss of generality, we can suppose that A1​(u,v)=1A_{1}(u,v)=1. For a,b∈{−1,+1}a,b\in\{-1,+1\}, a (a→b)(a\to b)-subsequence of 𝑨{\boldsymbol{A}} is a sequence (Ap,Ap+1,…,Aq)(A_{p},A_{p+1},\dots,A_{q}) for some p≤qp\leq q considered modulo rr such that Ap​(u,v)=aA_{p}(u,v)=a and Aq​(u,v)=bA_{q}(u,v)=b and Aj​(u,v)=0A_{j}(u,v)=0 for all p<j<qp<j<q. If p=q−1p=q-1, then we call it a degenerate (a→b)(a\to b)-subsequence of 𝑨{\boldsymbol{A}}. This is the case if and only if the edge between uu and vv exists in GG.

Proposition 4.8.

Let G=(N,E)G=(N,E) be a 𝒜​𝒪{\mathcal{AO}}-Hamiltonian graph with 𝐀=(A1,…,As){\boldsymbol{A}}=(A_{1},\dots,A_{s}) a Hamiltonian cycle in 𝒜​𝒪​(G){\mathcal{AO}}(G). For u,v∈Nu,v\in N in the same connected component of GG and an even number ℓ≥2\ell\geq 2, if 𝐀⁡(u,v){\boldsymbol{A}}(u,v) is 00-even, then for any (a→b)(a\to b)-subsequence (Ap,…,Aq)(A_{p},\dots,A_{q}) of 𝐀{\boldsymbol{A}} with a,b∈{−1,+1}a,b\in\{-1,+1\}, there exists a replacing pattern 𝐏{\boldsymbol{P}} such that:

  1. (a)

    𝑷⁡(u,v){\boldsymbol{P}}(u,v) is 00-even, and

  2. (b)

    if b=1b=1 (resp. b=−1b=-1), then ωq𝑷=1 2​…​2ℓ−1\omega_{q}^{{\boldsymbol{P}}}=1\,2\,\dots 2^{\ell}-1 (resp. ωq𝑷=μ+1​μ+2​…​μ−1\omega_{q}^{{\boldsymbol{P}}}=\mu+1\,\mu+2\,\dots\mu-1), and

  3. (c)

    consp⁡(𝑷)⊇{S2​k;k∈[2ℓ]}\cons_{p}({\boldsymbol{P}})\supseteq\{S_{2k}~;~k\in[2^{\ell}]\} and consq⁡(𝑷)⊇{S2​k+1;k∈[2ℓ]}\cons_{q}({\boldsymbol{P}})\supseteq\{S_{2k+1}~;~k\in[2^{\ell}]\}, and

  4. (d)

    if 𝑨{\boldsymbol{A}} is not degenerate and Aq​(u,v)=1A_{q}(u,v)=1 (resp. Aq​(u,v)=−1A_{q}(u,v)=-1), then consq⁡(𝑷)=[2ℓ]∖{2ℓ}\cons_{q}({\boldsymbol{P}})=[2^{\ell}]\smallsetminus\{2^{\ell}\} (resp. consq⁡(𝑷)=[2ℓ]∖{μ}\cons_{q}({\boldsymbol{P}})=[2^{\ell}]\smallsetminus\{\mu\}).

Proof.

The proof is by sketching the relevant replacing patterns with the claimed properties.

For a non-degenerate (1→1)(1\to 1)-subsequence, Figure 7 illustrates a replacing pattern with the claimed properties. The node in the ithi^{\text{th}} row and the jthj^{\text{th}} column represents the orientation Ai⊔SjA_{i}\sqcup S_{j} for i∈[p,q]i\in[p,q] and j∈[2ℓ]j\in[2^{\ell}]. A node is drawn with a red star ⋆{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}\star} if Ai​(u,v)=1A_{i}(u,v)=1 or Sj​(u,v)=1S_{j}(u,v)=1; it is drawn with a blue circle ∘{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\circ} if Ai​(u,v)=−1A_{i}(u,v)=-1 or Sj​(u,v)=−1S_{j}(u,v)=-1; otherwise, it is drawn with a black bullet ∙\bullet. Hence, Ai⊔SjA_{i}\sqcup S_{j} is an acyclic orientation of ⊕u,vℓG\oplus_{u,v}^{\ell}G if and only if its associated node is not both a red star ⋆{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}\star} and a blue circle ∘{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\circ}. As 𝑨=(Ap,…,Aq){\boldsymbol{A}}=(A_{p},\dots,A_{q}) is a path in 𝒜​𝒪​(G){\mathcal{AO}}(G), and (S1,…,S2ℓ)(S_{1},\dots,S_{2^{\ell}}) is a cycle in 𝒜​𝒪​(Pℓ){\mathcal{AO}}(P_{\ell}), the graph 𝒜​𝒪​(H′|𝑨){\mathcal{AO}}(H^{\prime}|{\boldsymbol{A}}) contains (at least) edges between vertically adjacent nodes, and edges between horizontally adjacent nodes, and edges between the rightmost and the leftmost nodes of each row (which we represent by a dotted line).

We have chosen and oriented some of these edges in order to construct a replacing pattern 𝑷{\boldsymbol{P}}. A vertical arrow coming from above the first row indicates the starting node of 𝑷{\boldsymbol{P}}, while a vertical arrow going below the last row indicates its ending node. To prove that this pattern is 00-even, it is enough to show that each (maximal) path of consecutive black bullets ∙\bullet contains an even number of such black bullets ∙\bullet. This is ensured by the fact that μ\mu is even. To determine ωp𝑷\omega_{p}^{{\boldsymbol{P}}} (resp. ωq𝑷\omega_{q}^{{\boldsymbol{P}}}), one follows along the directed path 𝑷{\boldsymbol{P}} and each time one sees a new node of the first (resp. last) row, one records the number of its column. To determine consp⁡(𝑷)\cons_{p}({\boldsymbol{P}}) (resp. consq⁡(𝑷)\cons_{q}({\boldsymbol{P}})), one follows along the nodes of the first (resp. last) row in the order given by ωp𝑷\omega_{p}^{{\boldsymbol{P}}} (resp. ωq𝑷\omega_{q}^{{\boldsymbol{P}}}), i.e. left-to-right starting from the first column, and one records which node has an edge going horizontally to its right.

For a (1→−1)(1\to-1)-subsequence, the drawing is given in Figure 8, with the same conventions. Note that, here, consq⁡(𝑷)\cons_{q}({\boldsymbol{P}}) is determined following along the nodes of the last row from left to right starting from the (μ+1)th(\mu+1)^{\text{th}} column, and recording which node has an edge going horizontally to its right.

For degenerate (1→1)(1\to 1)-subsequences and degenerate (1→−1)(1\to-1)-subsequences, the drawings are given in Figures 9 and 10, with the same conventions.

The drawings for the (degenerate) (−1→−1)(-1\to-1)-subsequences and for the (degenerate) (−1→1)(-1\to 1)-subsequences can be obtained from the ones of Figures 7, 8, 9 and 10 by swapping red stars ⋆{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}\star} and blue circles ∘{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\circ}. ∎

Proof of Theorem 4.7.

Fix a Hamiltonian cycle 𝑨=(A1,…,As){\boldsymbol{A}}=(A_{1},\dots,A_{s}) of 𝒜​𝒪​(G){\mathcal{AO}}(G) with A1=AsA_{1}=A_{s} such that 𝑨⁡(u,v){\boldsymbol{A}}(u,v) is 00-even.

On the one hand, we suppose that there exists j∈[s]j\in[s] such that Aj​(u,v)=0A_{j}(u,v)=0. Without loss of generality, we can consider that A1​(u,v)=1A_{1}(u,v)=1 and As−1​(u,v)=0A_{s-1}(u,v)=0. Let p1,…,prp_{1},\dots,p_{r} be such that the (a→b)(a\to b)-subsequences of 𝑨{\boldsymbol{A}} for all possible a,b∈{−1,+1}a,b\in\{-1,+1\} are (Api,Api+1,…,Api+1)(A_{p_{i}},A_{p_{i}+1},\dots,A_{p_{i+1}}) for i∈[r]i\in[r] (in particular p1=1=pr+1p_{1}=1=p_{r+1}).

Fix i∈[r]i\in[r]. Let 𝑷i{\boldsymbol{P}}_{i} be a replacing pattern for (Api,Api+1,…,Api+1)(A_{p_{i}},A_{p_{i}+1},\dots,A_{p_{i+1}}) given by Proposition 4.8. If Api+1​(u,v)=1A_{p_{i+1}}(u,v)=1 (resp. Api+1​(u,v)=−1A_{p_{i+1}}(u,v)=-1), then by (b) we get ωpi+1𝑷i=ωpi+1𝑷i+1\omega_{p_{i+1}}^{{\boldsymbol{P}}_{i}}=\omega_{p_{i+1}}^{{\boldsymbol{P}}_{i+1}}, and by (c) we get conspi+1⁡(𝑷i)∪conspi+1⁡(𝑷i+1)=[2ℓ]∖{2ℓ}\cons_{p_{i+1}}({\boldsymbol{P}}_{i})\cup\cons_{p_{i+1}}({\boldsymbol{P}}_{i+1})=[2^{\ell}]\smallsetminus\{2^{\ell}\} (resp. conspi+1⁡(𝑷i)∪conspi+1⁡(𝑷i+1)=[2ℓ]∖{μ}\cons_{p_{i+1}}({\boldsymbol{P}}_{i})\cup\cons_{p_{i+1}}({\boldsymbol{P}}_{i+1})=[2^{\ell}]\smallsetminus\{\mu\}).

Thus by Proposition 4.3, 𝑷i{\boldsymbol{P}}_{i} and 𝑷i+1{\boldsymbol{P}}_{i+1} can lace for all i∈[r]i\in[r]. Thus 𝑩≔𝑷1∧⋯∧𝑷r{\boldsymbol{B}}\coloneqq{\boldsymbol{P}}_{1}\wedge\dots\wedge{\boldsymbol{P}}_{r} is a replacing pattern for 𝑨{\boldsymbol{A}}. It remains to prove that 𝑩{\boldsymbol{B}} can self-lace. As we have assumed that A1​(u,v)=1A_{1}(u,v)=1 and As−1​(u,v)=0A_{s-1}(u,v)=0, the last (a→1)(a\to 1)-subsequence (Apr−1,…,Apr)(A_{p_{r-1}},\dots,A_{p_{r}}) is not degenerate. Thus by (d), we have conss⁡(𝑩)=[2ℓ]∖{2ℓ}\cons_{s}({\boldsymbol{B}})=[2^{\ell}]\smallsetminus\{2^{\ell}\}. Combining this with ωs𝑩=1 2​…​ 2ℓ−1\omega_{s}^{{\boldsymbol{B}}}=1\,2\,\dots\,2^{\ell}-1 proves that 𝑩{\boldsymbol{B}} can self-lace. By Corollary 4.4, we get that 𝑩{\boldsymbol{B}} is a Hamiltonian cycle for 𝒜𝒪(⊕u,vℓG){\mathcal{AO}}(\oplus_{u,v}^{\ell}G).

On the other hand, assume that Aj​(u,v)≠0A_{j}(u,v)\neq 0 for all j∈[s]j\in[s] (equivalently, that GG contains the edge between uu and vv). Suppose that there are two consecutive Ai​(u,v)A_{i}(u,v) and Ai+1​(u,v)A_{i+1}(u,v) of the same sign, so we can assume that A1​(u,v)=1A_{1}(u,v)=1 and As−2​(u,v)=As−1​(u,v)=−1A_{s-2}(u,v)=A_{s-1}(u,v)=-1.

The reasoning is very similar, as consecutive (degenerate) (a→b)(a\to b)-subsequences can lace according to Proposition 4.8. However, we need to modify the last step of the chosen replacing patterns so that the resulting 𝑩{\boldsymbol{B}} can self-lace and yield a Hamiltonian cycle for 𝒜𝒪(⊕u,vℓG){\mathcal{AO}}(\oplus_{u,v}^{\ell}G). We swap the last replacing pattern for (As−2,As−1)(A_{s-2},A_{s-1}) by the one drawn in Figure 11 where the last vertical edge connects As−1⊔S1A_{s-1}\sqcup S_{1} to A1⊔S1A_{1}\sqcup S_{1}, closing the Hamiltonian cycle of 𝒜𝒪(⊕u,vℓG){\mathcal{AO}}(\oplus_{u,v}^{\ell}G).

Otherwise, 𝑨⁡(u,v){\boldsymbol{A}}(u,v) alternates between +1+1 and −1-1 say A2​k​(u,v)=1A_{2k}(u,v)=1 and A2​k+1​(u,v)=−1A_{2k+1}(u,v)=-1, then we can replace each (A2​k,A2​k+1)(A_{2k},A_{2k+1}) by the replacing pattern of Figure 12 to directly get a cycle in 𝒜𝒪(⊕u,vℓG){\mathcal{AO}}(\oplus_{u,v}^{\ell}G) (no lacing is needed).

4.2.2. Gluing two paths of odd lengths

The main objective of this section is to prove Theorem 4.9. As before we state it here, and delay the proof to page 4.2.2. The proof is very similar to Theorem 4.7, except that it is conceptually easier since no lacing is needed; but the sketches are more intricate since the replacing patterns are larger.

Theorem 4.9.

Let G=(N,E)G=(N,E) be a 𝒜​𝒪{\mathcal{AO}}-Hamiltonian graph with 𝐀=(A1,…,As){\boldsymbol{A}}=(A_{1},\dots,A_{s}) a Hamiltonian cycle in 𝒜​𝒪​(G){\mathcal{AO}}(G). For u,v∈Nu,v\in N in the same connected component of GG and two odd numbers ℓ1,ℓ2≥2\ell_{1},\ell_{2}\geq 2, if 𝐀⁡(u,v){\boldsymbol{A}}(u,v) is 00-even, then ⊕u,vℓ1,ℓ2G\oplus_{u,v}^{\ell_{1},\ell_{2}}G is 𝒜​𝒪{\mathcal{AO}}-Hamiltonian. Moreover, under these assumptions, there exists a Hamiltonian cycle 𝐁=(B1,…,Bt){\boldsymbol{B}}=(B_{1},\dots,B_{t}) in 𝒜𝒪(⊕u,vℓ1,ℓ2G){\mathcal{AO}}(\oplus_{u,v}^{\ell_{1},\ell_{2}}G) such that 𝐁⁡(u,v){\boldsymbol{B}}(u,v) is 00-even.

Proof of Theorem 4.9.

For odd ℓ1,ℓ2≥3\ell_{1},\ell_{2}\geq 3, this is a direct consequence of Theorems 4.5 and 4.10 using the splitting ij+1=iji_{j+1}=i_{j} if Aij​(u,v)≠0A_{i_{j}}(u,v)\neq 0, and ij+1=ij+1i_{j+1}=i_{j}+1 if Aij=0A_{i_{j}}=0. As the number of acyclic orientations A∈𝒜​𝒪​(G)A\in{\mathcal{AO}}(G) with A⁡(u,v)=+1A(u,v)=+1 is equal to the number of acyclic orientations A∈𝒜​𝒪​(G)A\in{\mathcal{AO}}(G) with A⁡(u,v)=−1A(u,v)=-1 by Lemma 3.41 (4), the quantity #⁡{j∈[r];Aj′≠Bj′}\#\{j\in[r]~;~A^{\prime}_{j}\neq B^{\prime}_{j}\} of Theorem 4.5 is even. Thus, we get a Hamiltonian cycle in 𝒜𝒪(⊕u,vℓ1,ℓ2G){\mathcal{AO}}(\oplus_{u,v}^{\ell_{1},\ell_{2}}G). The 00-even-ness of this cycle is ensured by the 00-even-ness of each replacing pattern of Proposition 4.10.

The remaining case is ℓ1=1\ell_{1}=1 and ℓ2≥3\ell_{2}\geq 3 is odd. For readability, we call S+′S^{\prime}_{+} and S−′S^{\prime}_{-} the two orientations of P1P_{1}, where S+′​(u,v)=+1S^{\prime}_{+}(u,v)=+1 and S−′​(u,v)=−1S^{\prime}_{-}(u,v)=-1. Also, we rename ℓ2\ell_{2} into simply ℓ\ell, and μ2\mu_{2} into μ\mu. The proof is mainly via the drawings of Figure 15 where the conventions are the same as in Figures 13 and 14. We cannot directly apply Theorem 4.5, but we can concatenate paths joining four families of orientations, namely A⊔S+′⊔Sμ−1′′A\sqcup S_{+}^{\prime}\sqcup S^{\prime\prime}_{\mu-1}, and A⊔S+′⊔Sμ+1′′A\sqcup S_{+}^{\prime}\sqcup S^{\prime\prime}_{\mu+1}, and A⊔S−′⊔S1′′A\sqcup S_{-}^{\prime}\sqcup S^{\prime\prime}_{1}, and A⊔S−′⊔S2ℓ−1′′A\sqcup S_{-}^{\prime}\sqcup S^{\prime\prime}_{2^{\ell}-1} for A∈𝒜​𝒪​(G)A\in{\mathcal{AO}}(G).

We again use the splitting subsequences of 𝑨{\boldsymbol{A}} defined by ij+1=iji_{j+1}=i_{j} if Aij​(u,v)≠0A_{i_{j}}(u,v)\neq 0, and ij+1=ij+1i_{j+1}=i_{j}+1 if Aij​(u,v)=0A_{i_{j}}(u,v)=0.
