4.2.3. Gluing a multipath of even total length

Using Theorems 4.7 and 4.9, we can prove the main result of this section.

Corollary 4.11.

Let G=(N,E)G=(N,E) be a 𝒜​𝒪{\mathcal{AO}}-Hamiltonian graph with 𝐀=(A1,…,As){\boldsymbol{A}}=(A_{1},\dots,A_{s}) a Hamiltonian cycle in 𝒜​𝒪​(G){\mathcal{AO}}(G). For u,v∈Nu,v\in N in the same connected component of GG and integers ℓ=(ℓ1,…,ℓm){\boldsymbol{\ell}}=(\ell_{1},\dots,\ell_{m}) for m≥1m\geq 1, if:

  • •

    ∑i=1mℓi\sum_{i=1}^{m}\ell_{i} is even (i.e. the number of odd ℓi\ell_{i}s is even), and

  • •

    𝑨⁡(u,v){\boldsymbol{A}}(u,v) is 00-even,

then ⊕u,vℓG\oplus_{u,v}^{{\boldsymbol{\ell}}}G is 𝒜​𝒪{\mathcal{AO}}-Hamiltonian.

Moreover, under these assumptions, there exists a Hamiltonian cycle 𝐁=(B1,…,Bt){\boldsymbol{B}}=(B_{1},\dots,B_{t}) in 𝒜𝒪(⊕u,vℓG){\mathcal{AO}}(\oplus_{u,v}^{{\boldsymbol{\ell}}}G) such that 𝐁⁡(u,v){\boldsymbol{B}}(u,v) is 00-even.

Proof.

Inductive application of Theorems 4.7 and 4.9: since each Theorem yields a Hamiltonian cycle whose sequence of directions on (u,v)(u,v) is 00-even, the induction runs. ∎

Corollary 4.11 has several interesting consequences. First of all, the 00-even-ness can be dropped if u​vuv is an edge of GG, since it is impossible that A⁡(u,v)=0A(u,v)=0 in this case.

Corollary 4.12.

Let G=(N,E)G=(N,E) be a 𝒜​𝒪{\mathcal{AO}}-Hamiltonian graph, and let u​v∈Euv\in E. For numbers ℓ=(ℓ1,…,ℓs){\boldsymbol{\ell}}=(\ell_{1},\dots,\ell_{s}) if ∑p=1sℓp\sum_{p=1}^{s}\ell_{p} is odd, then ⊕u,vℓG\oplus_{u,v}^{{\boldsymbol{\ell}}}G is 𝒜​𝒪{\mathcal{AO}}-Hamiltonian.

Proof.

As u​v∈Euv\in E, for any acyclic orientation AA of GG, there is a directed path from uu to vv or from vv to uu, i.e. A⁡(u,v)≠0A(u,v)\neq 0. Hence, for any Hamiltonian cycle 𝑨=(A1,…,Ar){\boldsymbol{A}}=(A_{1},\dots,A_{r}) of 𝒜​𝒪​(G){\mathcal{AO}}(G), the sequence 𝑨⁡(u,v){\boldsymbol{A}}(u,v) is 00-even. Applying Corollary 4.11 yields the claim. ∎

Secondly, since a single path is 𝒜​𝒪{\mathcal{AO}}-Hamiltonian, we can finish our characterization of 𝒜​𝒪{\mathcal{AO}}-Hamiltonian multipaths, proving Theorem B.

Corollary 4.13.

The (ℓ1,…,ℓs)(\ell_{1},\dots,\ell_{s})-multipath is 𝒜​𝒪{\mathcal{AO}}-Hamiltonian if and only if ∑pℓp\sum_{p}\ell_{p} is odd.

Proof.

The “only if” direction is proven in Corollary 3.70. For the “if” direction, consider the graph G∘=({u,v},∅)G_{\circ}=\bigl(\{u,v\},\varnothing\bigr) composed of 2 isolated nodes: Its 𝒜​𝒪​(G){\mathcal{AO}}(G) is composed of a single node. Even if one might not consider this 𝒜​𝒪​(G){\mathcal{AO}}(G) to be Hamiltonian, is it enough for applying Corollary 4.11: if ∑pℓp\sum_{p}\ell_{p} is odd, then the (ℓ1,…,ℓs)(\ell_{1},\dots,\ell_{s})-multipath ⊕u,vℓ1,…,ℓsG∘\oplus_{u,v}^{\ell_{1},\dots,\ell_{s}}G_{\circ} is 𝒜​𝒪{\mathcal{AO}}-Hamiltonian. ∎

Thirdly, we can characterize 𝒜​𝒪{\mathcal{AO}}-Hamiltonian graphs among certain families of graphs:

Example 4.14.

As an immediate consequence of Corollaries 4.12, 4.11 and 4.13, we get:

  1. (1)

    As proven in [37, Lem. 3.1 & Thm. 4.2], the cycle graph CnC_{n} is 𝒜​𝒪{\mathcal{AO}}-Hamiltonian if and only if nn is odd: Indeed CnC_{n} is isomorphic to (n−1, 1)(n-1,\,1)-multipath.

  2. (2)

    Any 22-sum of two cycle graphs CnC_{n} and CmC_{m} is 𝒜​𝒪{\mathcal{AO}}-Hamiltonian if and only if n+mn+m is even: Indeed Cn⊕2CmC_{n}\oplus_{2}C_{m} is isomorphic to the (n−1,m−1, 1)(n-1,\,m-1,\,1)-multipath.

  3. (3)

    For a tree T=([s],E)T=([s],E) and numbers n1,…,ns≥3n_{1},\dots,n_{s}\geq 3, a (T,n1,…,ns)(T,\,n_{1},\dots,n_{s})-tree of cycles is any graph isomorphic to a 22-sum H⊕2CnsH\oplus_{2}C_{n_{s}} where HH is a (T∖s,n1,…,ns−1)(T\smallsetminus s,\,n_{1},\dots,n_{s-1})-tree of cycles (of course for s=1s=1, a (T,n1)(T,\,n_{1})-tree of cycle is just a cycle graph Cn1C_{n_{1}}). By consecutive applications of Corollary 4.12, one shows that if npn_{p} is odd for all p∈[s]p\in[s], then any (T,n1,…,ns)(T,\,n_{1},\dots,n_{s})-tree of cycles is 𝒜​𝒪{\mathcal{AO}}-Hamiltonian, for any tree TT.

  4. (4)

    If u​v∈Euv\in E is an edge of G=(N,E)G=(N,E), and CnC_{n} is a cycle graph, then the 22-sum G⊕2CnG\oplus_{2}C_{n} is 𝒜​𝒪{\mathcal{AO}}-Hamiltonian if and only if nn is odd: Indeed this is the case s=1s=1 of Corollary 4.12.

4.3. Adding a simplicial node and 0-even sequences

Recall that a node xx in a graph GG is simplicial if the neighbors of xx form a clique, that is if every pair of neighbors of xx share an edge in GG. If KK is a clique in GG, the simplicial augmentation above KK, denoted ⊙KG{\odot_{K}G}, is the graph obtained by adding a new (simplicial) node to GG connected to all the nodes of KK, i.e. ⊙KG≔G⊕nKn+1\odot_{K}G\coloneqq G\oplus_{n}K_{n+1} where n=|K|n=|K| and Kn+1K_{n+1} is the clique on [n+1][n+1].

In the details of the proof of [37, Theorem 4.1] that chordal graphs are 𝒜​𝒪{\mathcal{AO}}-Hamiltonian, they prove the first sentence of the upcoming Theorem 4.15. We use the Steinhaus–Johnson–Trotter algorithm (see Example 2.5) in a similar way but we keep track of 00-evenness:

Theorem 4.15.

If GG is 𝒜​𝒪{\mathcal{AO}}-Hamiltonian, and KK is a clique of GG, then ⊙KG\odot_{K}G is 𝒜​𝒪{\mathcal{AO}}-Hamiltonian. Moreover, for any nodes u,vu,v of GG, if 𝐀{\boldsymbol{A}} is a Hamiltonian cycle of 𝒜​𝒪​(G){\mathcal{AO}}(G) and either 𝐀⁡(u,v){\boldsymbol{A}}(u,v) is 00-even or if |K||K| is odd, then 𝒜𝒪(⊙KG){\mathcal{AO}}(\odot_{K}G) admits a Hamiltonian cycle 𝐁{\boldsymbol{B}} such that 𝐁⁡(u,v){\boldsymbol{B}}(u,v) is 00-even.

Proof.

Let KK be a clique of G=(N,E)G=(N,E) with n=|K|n=|K|, and let v∘v_{\circ} be the added node. Since KK is a clique, any acyclic orientation AA of GG induces a total order on KK, denoted σA:K→[n]\sigma_{A}:K\to[n]. Reciprocally, to a total order τ\tau on K⊔{v∘}K\sqcup\{v_{\circ}\}, we associate the orientation 𝒪⁡(τ){\mathcal{O}}(\tau) of the neighboring edges of v∘v_{\circ} where we orient from v∘v_{\circ} to u∈Ku\in K if τ⁡(v∘)<τ⁡(u)\tau(v_{\circ})<\tau(u), and conversely from uu to v∘v_{\circ} if τ⁡(u)<τ⁡(v∘)\tau(u)<\tau(v_{\circ}).

As in Example 2.5, for i∈[n+1]i\in[n+1], we denote σA(i)\sigma_{A}^{(i)} the total order on K⊔{v∘}K\sqcup\{v_{\circ}\} defined by

σA(i)​(u)={σA​(u)if ​σA​(u)<iiif ​u=v∘σA​(u)+1if ​σA​(u)>i for ​u∈K⊔{v∘}.\sigma_{A}^{(i)}(u)=\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}\sigma_{A}(u)&\text{if }\sigma_{A}(u)<i\\ i&\text{if }u=v_{\circ}\\ \sigma_{A}(u)+1&\text{if }\sigma_{A}(u)>i\end{array}\right.\qquad\text{ for }u\in K\sqcup\{v_{\circ}\}.

There is a bijection between acyclic orientations A′A^{\prime} of ⊙KG\odot_{K}G and pairs (A,i)(A,i) with A∈𝒜​𝒪​(G)A\in{\mathcal{AO}}(G) and i∈[n+1]i\in[n+1] given by (A,i)↦A⊔𝒪⁡(σA(i))(A,i)\mapsto A\sqcup{\mathcal{O}}\bigl(\sigma_{A}^{(i)}\bigr). Indeed, the edges of ⊙KG\odot_{K}G are bipartite between the edges of GG and the edges adjacent to v∘v_{\circ}, and the orientation A⊔A′A\sqcup A^{\prime} of ⊙KG\odot_{K}G (split according to this bipartition) is acyclic if and only if the total order induced by A′A^{\prime} on K⊔{v∘}K\sqcup\{v_{\circ}\} which agrees on KK with the total order induced by AA on KK. Moreover, A⊔𝒪⁡(σA(i))A\sqcup{\mathcal{O}}\bigl(\sigma_{A}^{(i)}\bigr) is adjacent to B⊔𝒪⁡(σB(j))B\sqcup{\mathcal{O}}\bigl(\sigma_{B}^{(j)}\bigr) in 𝒜𝒪(⊙KG){\mathcal{AO}}(\odot_{K}G) if and only if either AA is adjacent to BB in 𝒜​𝒪​(G){\mathcal{AO}}(G) and i=ji=j, either A=BA=B and j∈{i−1,i+1}j\in\{i-1,i+1\}.

Consequently, given a Hamiltonian cycle 𝑨=(A1,…,As){\boldsymbol{A}}=(A_{1},\dots,A_{s}) of 𝒜​𝒪​(G){\mathcal{AO}}(G) (recall that ss is even by Lemma 3.41), the following is mapped to a Hamiltonian cycle 𝑩{\boldsymbol{B}} of 𝒜𝒪(⊙KG){\mathcal{AO}}(\odot_{K}G):

((A1,n+1),…,(A1,1),(A2,1),…,(A2,n+1),(A3,n+1),…,(A3,1),…,(As,1),…,(As,n+1)).\bigl((A_{1},n+1),\dots,(A_{1},1),(A_{2},1),\dots,(A_{2},n+1),(A_{3},n+1),\dots,(A_{3},1),\dots,(A_{s},1),\dots,(A_{s},n+1)\bigr)\,.

Note that in (Ak,i)(A_{k},i) there is no directed path between uu and vv if and only if there is no directed path between uu and vv in AkA_{k}. Hence, by construction, the number of non-zero entries of 𝑩⁡(u,v){\boldsymbol{B}}(u,v) between two non-zero entries is always n+1n+1 times the corresponding number for 𝑨⁡(u,v){\boldsymbol{A}}(u,v). Thus, if 𝑨⁡(u,v){\boldsymbol{A}}(u,v) is 00-even or if nn is odd, then 𝑩⁡(u,v){\boldsymbol{B}}(u,v). ∎

Example 4.16.

Consider the complete graph K3K_{3} and let K={2,3}K=\{2,3\} be a clique of K3K_{3}. The graph ⊙23K3\odot_{23}K_{3} is drawn in Figure 16. A Hamiltonian cycle of 𝒜​𝒪​(K3){\mathcal{AO}}(K_{3}) is given by 𝑨=(123,132,312,321,231,213){\boldsymbol{A}}=(123,132,312,321,\linebreak 231,213) where i​j​kijk correspond to the orientation of K3K_{3} with arcs i→ji\to j, j→kj\to k and i→ki\to k. The (generalized) Steinhaus–Johnson–Trotter presented in the proof of Theorem 4.15 yields a Hamiltonian cycle of 𝒜𝒪(⊙23K3){\mathcal{AO}}(\odot_{23}K_{3}) shown in Table 4. Note that all the sequences 𝑩⁡(u,v){\boldsymbol{B}}(u,v) are 00-even for u,v∈[4]u,v\in[4] except for {u,v}={1,4}\{u,v\}=\{1,4\}.

Remark 4.17.

For KK a clique of the graph GG, and any Hamiltonian cycle 𝑩{\boldsymbol{B}} of 𝒜𝒪(⊙KG){\mathcal{AO}}(\odot_{K}G), note that 𝑩⁡(u,x∘){\boldsymbol{B}}(u,x_{\circ}) is 00-even for all u∈Ku\in K, where x∘x_{\circ} denotes the added simplicial node. Indeed, there is an edge between uu and x∘x_{\circ} in ⊙KG\odot_{K}G, so 𝑩⁡(u,x∘){\boldsymbol{B}}(u,x_{\circ}) contains no 00.

We can combine Corollaries 4.11 and 4.15 into a single corollary. To this end, we introduce simplicial multi-augmentation of a graph GG above a clique-sequence 𝑲=(K1,…,Ks){\boldsymbol{K}}=(K_{1},\dots,K_{s}), defined as GG if s=0s=0, otherwise as ⊙𝑲G≔⊙Ks(⊙(K1,…,Ks−1)G)\odot_{{\boldsymbol{K}}}G\coloneqq\odot_{K_{s}}\bigl(\odot_{(K_{1},\dots,K_{s-1})}G\bigr) where KsK_{s} is a clique of ⊙(K1,…,Ks−1)G\odot_{(K_{1},\dots,K_{s-1})}G.

We are going to construct a sequence of graphs where we alternate between gluing a multipath and adding a simplicial node. To ease notation, we consider that we start by gluing a multipath, but one can easily start by adding a simplicial node instead. In each step, we just need to state a condition ensuring that we glue the multipath between two nodes where we can guarantee that the Hamiltonian cycle constructed thus far is 00-even. This way we prove (the general version of) Theorem C.

Corollary 4.18.

Let G0,…,GpG_{0},\dots,G_{p} be a sequence of graphs such that G2​i+1=⊕ℓiui,viG2​iG_{2i+1}=\oplus^{{\boldsymbol{\ell}}_{i}}_{u_{i},v_{i}}G_{2i} for some ui,vi∈N⁡(G2​i)u_{i},v_{i}\in N(G_{2i}) and some ℓi∈ℕ≥1ri{\boldsymbol{\ell}}_{i}\in\mathbb{N}_{\geq 1}^{r_{i}} with ri≥1r_{i}\geq 1 where ℓi{\boldsymbol{\ell}}_{i} contains at most one 11, and G2​i+2=⊙𝐊iG2​i+1G_{2i+2}=\odot_{{\boldsymbol{K}}_{i}}G_{2i+1} for some clique-sequence 𝐊i{\boldsymbol{K}}_{i} of length si≥0s_{i}\geq 0 on G2​i+1G_{2i+1}. If

  1. (1)

    𝒜​𝒪​(G0){\mathcal{AO}}(G_{0}) admits a Hamiltonian cycle 𝑨{\boldsymbol{A}} where 𝑨⁡(u0,v0){\boldsymbol{A}}(u_{0},v_{0}) is 00-even; and

  2. (2)

    for all ii we have that ∑j=1riℓi,j\sum_{j=1}^{r_{i}}\ell_{i,j} is even, that uiu_{i} and viv_{i} are in the same connected component of G2​iG_{2i}; and either:

    • •

      ui​vi∈E⁡(G2​i)u_{i}v_{i}\in E(G_{2i}); or

    • •

      si≥1s_{i}\geq 1 and there is jj such that |Ki,j||K_{i,j}| is odd, and, with mi=max⁡{j;|Ki,j|​ is odd}m_{i}=\max\{j~;~|K_{i,j}|\text{ is odd}\} and (xi,1,…,xi,si)(x_{i,1},\dots,x_{i,s_{i}}) the simplicial nodes added in ⊙𝑲iG2​i+1\odot_{{\boldsymbol{K}}_{i}}G_{2i+1}, we have ui,vi∈N⁡(G2​i)∖{xi,mi,xi,mi+1,…,xi,si}u_{i},v_{i}\in N(G_{2i})\smallsetminus\{x_{i,m_{i}},x_{i,m_{i}+1},\dots,x_{i,s_{i}}\};

then GpG_{p} is 𝒜​𝒪{\mathcal{AO}}-Hamiltonian.

Proof.

Direct combination of Corollaries 4.11, 4.12 and 4.15: the conditions ensure that 𝒜​𝒪​(Gi){\mathcal{AO}}(G_{i}) admits a Hamiltonian cycle 𝑨i{\boldsymbol{A}}_{i} such that 𝑨2​i​(ui,vi){\boldsymbol{A}}_{2i}(u_{i},v_{i}) is 00-even for all ii. ∎

4.4. Disconnected graphs, 1-sums, strongly even and internally even sequences

It is well-known that if HH and H′H^{\prime} are Hamiltonian graphs, then the Cartesian product H×H′H\times H^{\prime} is also Hamiltonian: for instance, it is the first sentence of [43]. Consequently, if GG has several connected components, each inducing a 𝒜​𝒪{\mathcal{AO}}-Hamiltonian graph, then GG itself is also 𝒜​𝒪{\mathcal{AO}}-Hamiltonian because it is straightforward to show that 𝒜​𝒪​(G){\mathcal{AO}}(G) is the Cartesian product of the graph of acyclic orientations of its connected components. Similarly, if G=H⊕1H′G=H\oplus_{1}H^{\prime} is a 11-sum, then 𝒜​𝒪​(G)=𝒜​𝒪​(H)×𝒜​𝒪​(H′){\mathcal{AO}}(G)={\mathcal{AO}}(H)\times{\mathcal{AO}}(H^{\prime}), so if HH and H′H^{\prime} are 𝒜​𝒪{\mathcal{AO}}-Hamiltonian, then GG is also 𝒜​𝒪{\mathcal{AO}}-Hamiltonian.

We can go further and keep track of the 00-evenness. For disconnected graphs, the question is trivial by definition: if uu and vv are not in the same connected component, then 𝑨⁡(u,v)=(0,0,…,0){\boldsymbol{A}}(u,v)=(0,0,\dots,0) for any sequence of orientations 𝑨{\boldsymbol{A}}, since no orientation can induce a directed path between uu and vv. (Note however that Corollary 4.11 does not apply if uu and vv are not in the same connected component.) The case of 11-sums is, strangely, richer. We need two notions to further control evenness.

Definition 4.19.

A sequence of integers 𝒂=(a1,…,ar){\boldsymbol{a}}=(a_{1},\dots,a_{r}) is strongly even if for all x∈{a1,…,ar}x\in\{a_{1},\dots,a_{r}\} with x≠0x\neq 0:

  • •

    if 1≤i<j≤r1\leq i<j\leq r are such that ai=aj≠0a_{i}=a_{j}\neq 0 and ak≠aia_{k}\neq a_{i} for all i<k<ji<k<j, then ii and jj have the same parity; and

  • •

    min⁡{i;ai=x}\min\{i~;~a_{i}=x\} is odd and max⁡{i;ai=x}\max\{i~;~a_{i}=x\} is even.

Definition 4.20.

A sequence of integers 𝒂=(a1,…,ar){\boldsymbol{a}}=(a_{1},\dots,a_{r}) is internally even if:

  • •

    for any x∈{a1,…,ar}x\in\{a_{1},\dots,a_{r}\} with x≠0x\neq 0, if 1≤i<j≤r1\leq i<j\leq r are such that ai=aj≠0a_{i}=a_{j}\neq 0 and ak≠aia_{k}\neq a_{i} for all i<k<ji<k<j, then ii and jj have the same parity; and

  • •

    the parity of min⁡{i;ai=x}\min\{i~;~a_{i}=x\} does not depend on x≠0x\neq 0; and the parity of max⁡{i;ai=x}\max\{i~;~a_{i}=x\} does not depend on x≠0x\neq 0.

Remark 4.21.

It could be that 𝒂{\boldsymbol{a}} is strongly even but not 00-even, e.g. 𝒂=(1,0,2,1,0,2){\boldsymbol{a}}=(1,0,2,1,0,2). On the other hand, strongly even implies internally even.

We first show that 11-summing a 𝒜​𝒪{\mathcal{AO}}-Hamiltonian graph with a strongly even 𝒜​𝒪{\mathcal{AO}}-Hamiltonian graph yields a 00-even 𝒜​𝒪{\mathcal{AO}}-Hamiltonian graph.

Proposition 4.22.

Let G=H⊕1H′G=H\oplus_{1}H^{\prime} be a 11-sum with w∈N⁡(H)∩N⁡(H′)w\in N(H)\cap N(H^{\prime}), and let any u∈N⁡(H)∖{w}u\in N(H)\smallsetminus\{w\} and v∈N⁡(H′)∖{w}v\in N(H^{\prime})\smallsetminus\{w\}. If H′H^{\prime} is 𝒜​𝒪{\mathcal{AO}}-Hamiltonian and 𝒜​𝒪​(H){\mathcal{AO}}(H) admits a Hamiltonian cycle 𝐀{\boldsymbol{A}} such that 𝐀⁡(u,w){\boldsymbol{A}}(u,w) is strongly even, then 𝒜​𝒪​(G){\mathcal{AO}}(G) admits a Hamiltonian cycle 𝐁{\boldsymbol{B}} such that 𝐁⁡(u,v){\boldsymbol{B}}(u,v) is both strongly even and 00-even.

Proof.

Let 𝑨′=(A1′,…,At′){\boldsymbol{A}}^{\prime}=(A^{\prime}_{1},\dots,A^{\prime}_{t}) be a Hamiltonian cycle of 𝒜​𝒪​(H′){\mathcal{AO}}(H^{\prime}) (where 𝑨′​(w,v){\boldsymbol{A}}^{\prime}(w,v) is not necessarily 00-even). We denote 𝑨=(A1,…,As){\boldsymbol{A}}=(A_{1},\dots,A_{s}). Since GG is the 11-sum H⊕1H′H\oplus_{1}H^{\prime}, any two acyclic orientations Ai∈𝑨A_{i}\in{\boldsymbol{A}}, Aj′∈𝑨′A^{\prime}_{j}\in{\boldsymbol{A}}^{\prime} give rise to an acyclic orientation of GG, so the acyclic orientations of GG are Ai⊔Aj′A_{i}\sqcup A^{\prime}_{j} for all i∈[s]i\in[s] and j∈[t]j\in[t]. Besides, since the total number of acyclic orientations of a graph is always even (see Lemma 3.41), both ss and tt are even. Consider 𝑩{\boldsymbol{B}} defined as:

(4.1) 𝑩=(A1⊔A′1,A2⊔A′1,…,As⊔A′1,As⊔A2′,As−1⊔A2′,…,A1⊔A2′,A1⊔A3′,A2⊔A3′,…,As⊔A3′,…,OPENAs⊔At′,As−1⊔At′,…,A1⊔At′).\begin{array}[]{rl}{\boldsymbol{B}}=&\bigl(A_{1}\sqcup A^{\prime}_{1},\,A_{2}\sqcup A^{\prime}_{1},\,\dots,\,A_{s}\sqcup A^{\prime}_{1},\\ &A_{s}\sqcup A^{\prime}_{2},\,A_{s-1}\sqcup A^{\prime}_{2},\,\dots,\,A_{1}\sqcup A^{\prime}_{2},\\ &A_{1}\sqcup A^{\prime}_{3},\,A_{2}\sqcup A^{\prime}_{3},\,\dots,\,A_{s}\sqcup A^{\prime}_{3},\\ &\dots,\\ &A_{s}\sqcup A^{\prime}_{t},\,A_{s-1}\sqcup A^{\prime}_{t},\,\dots,\,A_{1}\sqcup A^{\prime}_{t}\bigr)\,.\end{array}

By construction, 𝑩{\boldsymbol{B}} is a Hamiltonian cycle of 𝒜​𝒪​(G){\mathcal{AO}}(G). Moreover, (Ai⊔Aj′)​(u,v)≠0(A_{i}\sqcup A^{\prime}_{j})(u,v)\neq 0 if and only if Ai​(u,w)=Aj′​(w,v)≠0A_{i}(u,w)=A^{\prime}_{j}(w,v)\neq 0. If Aj′​(w,v)=0A^{\prime}_{j}(w,v)=0, then (Ai⊔Aj′)​(u,v)=0(A_{i}\sqcup A^{\prime}_{j})(u,v)=0, so in evaluating the above definition to get 𝑩⁡(u,v){\boldsymbol{B}}(u,v) the jthj^{\text{th}} row is (0,…,0)(0,\dots,0) (and it is of even length). If Aj′​(w,v)=+1A^{\prime}_{j}(w,v)=+1 (resp. −1-1), then (Ai⊔Aj′)​(u,v)=0(A_{i}\sqcup A^{\prime}_{j})(u,v)=0 except if Ai​(u,w)=+1A_{i}(u,w)=+1 (resp. −1-1), so the jthj^{\text{th}} row in the above is the sequence 𝑨⁡(u,w){\boldsymbol{A}}(u,w) with its −1-1 (resp. +1+1) replaced by 00: since 𝑨⁡(u,w){\boldsymbol{A}}(u,w) is strongly even, this sequence is formed by 11 (resp. −1-1) separated by an even number of zeros with an even number of zeros at the beginning and at the end. Therefore, by concatenation, the sequence 𝑩⁡(u,v){\boldsymbol{B}}(u,v) is 00-even.

Furthermore, 𝑩⁡(u,v){\boldsymbol{B}}(u,v) is strongly even. Indeed, if (Ai⊔Aj′)​(u,v)=+1(A_{i}\sqcup A^{\prime}_{j})(u,v)=+1 and (Ak⊔Aℓ′)​(u,v)=+1(A_{k}\sqcup A^{\prime}_{\ell})(u,v)=+1 are such that there is no Am⊔An′A_{m}\sqcup A^{\prime}_{n} in between in 𝑩{\boldsymbol{B}} with (Am⊔An′)​(u,v)=+1(A_{m}\sqcup A^{\prime}_{n})(u,v)=+1, then either j=ℓj=\ell and both orientations are on the same row and separated by an even number of zeros as we have seen; either j<ℓj<\ell and both orientations are separated by a certain number of rows (each of them of even length) and are an even number of zeros away from the endpoints of their respective rows. Besides, the second condition for strong evenness of 𝑩⁡(u,v){\boldsymbol{B}}(u,v) straightforwardly follows from the one for 𝑨⁡(u,v){\boldsymbol{A}}(u,v). ∎

Secondly, 11-summing a 00-even 𝒜​𝒪{\mathcal{AO}}-Hamiltonian graph with an internally even 𝒜​𝒪{\mathcal{AO}}-Hamiltonian graph preserves both 𝒜​𝒪{\mathcal{AO}}-Hamiltonicity and 00-evenness.

Proposition 4.23.

Let G=H⊕1H′G=H\oplus_{1}H^{\prime} be a 11-sum with w∈N⁡(H)∩N⁡(H′)w\in N(H)\cap N(H^{\prime}), and let any u∈N⁡(H)∖{w}u\in N(H)\smallsetminus\{w\} and v∈N⁡(H′)∖{w}v\in N(H^{\prime})\smallsetminus\{w\}. If 𝒜​𝒪​(H′){\mathcal{AO}}(H^{\prime}) admits a Hamiltonian cycle 𝐀′{\boldsymbol{A}}^{\prime} such that 𝐀′​(w,v){\boldsymbol{A}}^{\prime}(w,v) is 00-even and 𝒜​𝒪​(H){\mathcal{AO}}(H) admits a Hamiltonian cycle 𝐀{\boldsymbol{A}} such that 𝐀⁡(u,w){\boldsymbol{A}}(u,w) is internally even, then 𝒜​𝒪​(G){\mathcal{AO}}(G) admits a Hamiltonian cycle 𝐁{\boldsymbol{B}} such that 𝐁⁡(u,v){\boldsymbol{B}}(u,v) is both internally even and 00-even.

Proof.

The proof is very similar to the one of Proposition 4.22, only the last part of the argument needs to be modified.

We construct 𝑩{\boldsymbol{B}} as in Equation 4.1. We call the ithi^{\text{th}} row of 𝑩⁡(u,v){\boldsymbol{B}}(u,v) a 00-row if (Ak⊔Ai′)​(u,v)=0(A_{k}\sqcup A^{\prime}_{i})(u,v)=0 for all k∈[s]k\in[s]. Suppose that the ithi^{\text{th}} and the jthj^{\text{th}} rows of 𝑩⁡(u,v){\boldsymbol{B}}(u,v) are non-00-rows but that the kthk^{\text{th}} row is a 00-row for all i<k<ji<k<j. Since 𝑨⁡(u,w){\boldsymbol{A}}(u,w) is 00-even, the 00-rows come in consecutive sequences of even length: ii and jj have the same parity. Let fif_{i} be the number of final 00s in the ithi^{\text{th}} row of 𝑩⁡(u,v){\boldsymbol{B}}(u,v) and ℓj\ell_{j} the number of leading 00s in its jthj^{\text{th}} row. As ii and jj have the same parity, fif_{i} and ℓj\ell_{j} are either both a minimum kk such that Ak′​(w,v)≠0A^{\prime}_{k}(w,v)\neq 0 or both a maximum kk such that Ak′​(w,v)≠0A^{\prime}_{k}(w,v)\neq 0. Since 𝑨′​(w,v){\boldsymbol{A}}^{\prime}(w,v) is internally even, fif_{i} and ℓj\ell_{j} have the same parity (i.e. fi+ℓjf_{i}+\ell_{j} is even). Thus, the number of consecutive 00s between the last non-zero value of the ithi^{\text{th}} row of 𝑩⁡(u,v){\boldsymbol{B}}(u,v) and the first non-zero value of its jthj^{\text{th}} row is even. Consequently, 𝑩⁡(u,v){\boldsymbol{B}}(u,v) is 00-even.

A similar reasoning as in the proof of Proposition 4.22 for strong evenness shows that 𝑩⁡(u,v){\boldsymbol{B}}(u,v) is also internally even. ∎

With some case-by-case analysis, the reader can adapt Propositions 4.22 and 4.23 for 11-summing several graphs at once. We do not state a general theorem here since it is unbearably notation-heavy. However, we give the following corollary. To prove it, we need the following notion.

Definition 4.24.

For A∈𝒜​𝒪​(G)A\in{\mathcal{AO}}(G) and four nodes u,v,x,y∈Nu,v,x,y\in N, their combined direction is

A⁡(u,v)∧A⁡(x,y)≔{A⁡(u,v)if ​A​(u,v)=A⁡(x,y)0otherwise.{A(u,v)\wedge A(x,y)}\coloneqq\begin{cases}A(u,v)&\text{if }A(u,v)=A(x,y)\\ 0&\text{otherwise}\end{cases}\,.

As per usual, for a sequence of orientations 𝑨=(A1,…,Ar){\boldsymbol{A}}=(A_{1},\dots,A_{r}), we denote 𝑨⁡(u,v)∧𝑨⁡(x,y)≔(A1​(u,v)∧A1​(x,y),…,Ar​(u,v)∧Ar​(x,y)){\boldsymbol{A}}(u,v)\wedge{\boldsymbol{A}}(x,y)\coloneqq\bigl(A_{1}(u,v)\wedge A_{1}(x,y),\,\dots,\,A_{r}(u,v)\wedge A_{r}(x,y)\bigr).

Corollary 4.25.

Let G=(N,E)G=(N,E) be a 𝒜​𝒪{\mathcal{AO}}-Hamiltonian graph with 𝐀=(A1,…,As){\boldsymbol{A}}=(A_{1},\dots,A_{s}) a Hamiltonian cycle in 𝒜​𝒪​(G){\mathcal{AO}}(G) and let u,v∈Nu,v\in N such that 𝐀⁡(u,v){\boldsymbol{A}}(u,v) is 00-even. Let HH be the 11-sum at uu of GG with a path PmP_{m} with endpoint xx, and let G′G^{\prime} be the 11-sum at vv of HH with a path PnP_{n} with endpoint yy.

Then both HH and G′G^{\prime} are 𝒜​𝒪{\mathcal{AO}}-Hamiltonian. If, moreover, mm and nn have the same parity, then there exists a Hamiltonian cycle 𝐁=(B1,…,Bt){\boldsymbol{B}}=(B_{1},\dots,B_{t}) in 𝒜​𝒪​(G′){\mathcal{AO}}(G^{\prime}) such that 𝐁⁡(x,y){\boldsymbol{B}}(x,y) is 00-even.

Proof.

Since HH is a 11-sum, the graph 𝒜​𝒪​(H){\mathcal{AO}}(H) is isomorphic to 𝒜​𝒪​(G)×𝒜​𝒪​(Pm){\mathcal{AO}}(G)\times{\mathcal{AO}}(P_{m}), while the graph 𝒜​𝒪​(G′){\mathcal{AO}}(G^{\prime}) is isomorphic to 𝒜​𝒪​(G)×𝒜​𝒪​(Pm)×𝒜​𝒪​(Pn){\mathcal{AO}}(G)\times{\mathcal{AO}}(P_{m})\times{\mathcal{AO}}(P_{n}). The Cartesian product of Hamiltonian graphs being Hamiltonian, and 𝒜​𝒪​(Pk){\mathcal{AO}}(P_{k}) being isomorphic to the (Hamiltonian) cube-graph QkQ_{k}, we get that both HH and G′G^{\prime} are 𝒜​𝒪{\mathcal{AO}}-Hamiltonian.

Let 𝑺{\boldsymbol{S}} (resp. 𝑺′{\boldsymbol{S}}^{\prime}) be a Hamiltonian cycle in 𝒜​𝒪​(Pm){\mathcal{AO}}(P_{m}) with S1​(x,u)=1S_{1}(x,u)=1 and Sμ​(x,u)=−1S_{\mu}(x,u)=-1 (resp. S1′​(v,y)=1S^{\prime}_{1}(v,y)=1 and Sμ′′​(v,y)=−1S^{\prime}_{\mu^{\prime}}(v,y)=-1). Since mm and nn have the same parity, μ\mu and μ′\mu^{\prime} also have the same parity (which is the parity of m+1m+1). Consider the usual Hamiltonian cycle 𝑻{\boldsymbol{T}} in 𝒜​𝒪​(Pm)×𝒜​𝒪​(Pn){\mathcal{AO}}(P_{m})\times{\mathcal{AO}}(P_{n}) constructed via Equation 4.1 on 𝑺{\boldsymbol{S}} and 𝑺′{\boldsymbol{S}}^{\prime}. For an acyclic orientation A∈𝒜​𝒪​(G)A\in{\mathcal{AO}}(G), we have (A⊔S⊔S′)​(x,y)=1(A\sqcup S\sqcup S^{\prime})(x,y)=1 (resp. −1-1) if and only if S⁡(x,u)=A⁡(u,v)=S′​(v,y)=1S(x,u)=A(u,v)=S^{\prime}(v,y)=1 (resp. −1-1). The sequence (S(x,u)∧S′(v,y);S⊔S′∈𝑻)\bigl(S(x,u)\wedge S^{\prime}(v,y)~;~S\sqcup S^{\prime}\in{\boldsymbol{T}}\bigr) is internally even. Indeed, it has a unique 11 at the first position, and a unique −1-1 at position either m⋅(μ−1)+μ′m\cdot(\mu-1)+\mu^{\prime} if mm is even, or m⋅(μ−1)+n−μ′m\cdot(\mu-1)+n-\mu^{\prime} if mm is odd: this position is odd in both cases.

It is left to the reader as an exercise to prove that a variant of Proposition 4.23 implies that the Hamiltonian cycle 𝑩{\boldsymbol{B}} of 𝒜​𝒪​(G′){\mathcal{AO}}(G^{\prime}) constructed using Equation 4.1 on 𝑨{\boldsymbol{A}} and 𝑻{\boldsymbol{T}} satisfies that 𝑩⁡(u,v){\boldsymbol{B}}(u,v) is 00-even. This concludes the proof. ∎

Corollary 4.26.

Let G=(N,E)G=(N,E) be a 𝒜​𝒪{\mathcal{AO}}-Hamiltonian graph with 𝐀=(A1,…,As){\boldsymbol{A}}=(A_{1},\dots,A_{s}) a Hamiltonian cycle in 𝒜​𝒪​(G){\mathcal{AO}}(G) and let u,v∈Nu,v\in N such that 𝐀⁡(u,v){\boldsymbol{A}}(u,v) is 00-even. Let HH be the 11-sum at uu of GG with a path PmP_{m} with endpoint xx, and let G′G^{\prime} be the 11-sum at vv of HH with a path PnP_{n} with endpoint yy.

If mm and nn have the same parity and ∑kℓk\sum_{k}\ell_{k} is even, then ⊕x,yℓG′\oplus_{x,y}^{{\boldsymbol{\ell}}}G^{\prime} is 𝒜​𝒪{\mathcal{AO}}-Hamiltonian.

Proof.

Direct application of Corollaries 4.11 and 4.25. ∎

Corollary 4.26 is our third result (with Corollaries 4.12 and 4.18) explaining how we can glue a multipath at a pair of nodes (u,v)(u,v), then glue another multipath at another pair of nodes (x,y)(x,y). These three statements are of different nature and suggest the following problem for future research.

Question 4.27.

Find conditions (such as 00-even, strongly even and internally even) that a graph GG or (a Hamiltonian cycle in) its graph of acyclic orientations 𝒜​𝒪​(G){\mathcal{AO}}(G) should satisfy to ensure that one can glue multipaths at the different pairs of nodes of GG.

Note that this question is only an intermediate step. If one wants to exploit the (open) ear decomposition of 22-connected graphs in order to inductively certify whether a graph is 𝒜​𝒪{\mathcal{AO}}-Hamiltonian or not, then he or she would not only need to solve the above question where the pairs of nodes are taken in the same starting graph GG, but also to consider pairs of nodes where one or both lie on the glued ears (i.e. multipaths) of the previous steps.

Appendix A General statements about pattern lacing

A.1. Loose lacing

In this section, we state more general methods of pattern (self-)lacing as compared to Propositions 4.3 and 4.4. For a replacing pattern 𝑷{\boldsymbol{P}} of (A1,…,As)(A_{1},\dots,A_{s}) and a replacing pattern 𝑸{\boldsymbol{Q}} of (As,…,At)(A_{s},\dots,A_{t}), consider the graph, illustrated in Figure 17, whose node set is 𝒜​𝒪​(H′|As){\mathcal{AO}}(H^{\prime}|A_{s}) and where there are three types of edges:

  • •

    red edges between A′A^{\prime} and B′B^{\prime} such that ωs𝑷​(B′)=ωs𝑷​(A′)+1\omega^{{\boldsymbol{P}}}_{s}(B^{\prime})=\omega^{{\boldsymbol{P}}}_{s}(A^{\prime})+1 and ωs𝑷​(A′)∉conss⁡(𝑷)\omega^{{\boldsymbol{P}}}_{s}(A^{\prime})\notin\cons_{s}({\boldsymbol{P}}); and

  • •

    blue edges between A′A^{\prime} and B′B^{\prime} such that ωs𝑸​(B′)=ωs𝑸​(A′)+1\omega^{{\boldsymbol{Q}}}_{s}(B^{\prime})=\omega^{{\boldsymbol{Q}}}_{s}(A^{\prime})+1 and ωs𝑸​(A′)∉conss⁡(𝑸)\omega^{{\boldsymbol{Q}}}_{s}(A^{\prime})\notin\cons_{s}({\boldsymbol{Q}}); and

  • •

    green edges between A′A^{\prime} and B′B^{\prime} such that ωs𝑷​(B′)=ωs𝑷​(A′)+1\omega^{{\boldsymbol{P}}}_{s}(B^{\prime})=\omega^{{\boldsymbol{P}}}_{s}(A^{\prime})+1 and ωs𝑷​(A′)∈conss⁡(𝑷)\omega^{{\boldsymbol{P}}}_{s}(A^{\prime})\in\cons_{s}({\boldsymbol{P}}) or such that ωs𝑸​(B′)=ωs𝑸​(A′)+1\omega^{{\boldsymbol{Q}}}_{s}(B^{\prime})=\omega^{{\boldsymbol{Q}}}_{s}(A^{\prime})+1 and ωs𝑸​(A′)∈conss⁡(𝑸)\omega^{{\boldsymbol{Q}}}_{s}(A^{\prime})\in\cons_{s}({\boldsymbol{Q}}).

We say that 𝑷{\boldsymbol{P}} and 𝑸{\boldsymbol{Q}} can loosely lace if there exists a (directed) path 𝝆{\boldsymbol{\rho}} from A′A^{\prime} with ωs𝑷​(A′)=1\omega^{{\boldsymbol{P}}}_{s}(A^{\prime})=1 to B′B^{\prime} with ωs𝑸​(B′)=m\omega^{{\boldsymbol{Q}}}_{s}(B^{\prime})=m such that 𝝆{\boldsymbol{\rho}} contains all the red edges and all the blue edges (and some, perhaps none, of the green edges) of this graph. One has to be careful, since several such paths may exist. The loose lace of 𝑷{\boldsymbol{P}} and 𝑸{\boldsymbol{Q}} according to 𝝆{\boldsymbol{\rho}}, denoted 𝑷∧𝝆𝑸{{\boldsymbol{P}}\wedge_{{\boldsymbol{\rho}}}{\boldsymbol{Q}}}, is obtained by replacing each red arc (resp. blue arc) of 𝝆{\boldsymbol{\rho}} by the corresponding directed path in 𝑷{\boldsymbol{P}} (resp. in 𝑸{\boldsymbol{Q}}), keeping each green arc, and adding 𝑷0{\boldsymbol{P}}_{0} and 𝑸m{\boldsymbol{Q}}_{m} (defined in the usual lacing 𝑷∧𝑸{\boldsymbol{P}}\wedge{\boldsymbol{Q}}).

A proof similar to the proof of Proposition 4.3 ensures that: If 𝑷{\boldsymbol{P}} and 𝑸{\boldsymbol{Q}} can loosely lace, then any loose lace 𝑷∧𝝆𝑸{\boldsymbol{P}}\wedge_{{\boldsymbol{\rho}}}{\boldsymbol{Q}} is a replacing pattern of 𝒜​𝒪​(H′|A1,…,At){\mathcal{AO}}(H^{\prime}|A_{1},\dots,A_{t}).

In the case of usual lacing, the graph at stake is a path with two edges between consecutive nodes, one of them being green.

Besides, for a replacing pattern 𝑷{\boldsymbol{P}} of (A1,…,As)(A_{1},\dots,A_{s}) with A1=AsA_{1}=A_{s}, consider the graph whose node set is 𝒜​𝒪​(H′|A1){\mathcal{AO}}(H^{\prime}|A_{1}) and where there are four types of edges:

  • •

    red edges between A′A^{\prime} and B′B^{\prime} such that ωs𝑷​(B′)=ωs𝑷​(A′)+1\omega^{{\boldsymbol{P}}}_{s}(B^{\prime})=\omega^{{\boldsymbol{P}}}_{s}(A^{\prime})+1 and ωs𝑷​(A′)∉conss⁡(𝑷)\omega^{{\boldsymbol{P}}}_{s}(A^{\prime})\notin\cons_{s}({\boldsymbol{P}}); and

  • •

    blue edges between A′A^{\prime} and B′B^{\prime} such that ω1𝑷​(B′)=ω1𝑷​(A′)+1\omega^{{\boldsymbol{P}}}_{1}(B^{\prime})=\omega^{{\boldsymbol{P}}}_{1}(A^{\prime})+1 and ω1𝑷​(A′)∉cons1⁡(𝑷)\omega^{{\boldsymbol{P}}}_{1}(A^{\prime})\notin\cons_{1}({\boldsymbol{P}}); and

  • •

    purple edges between A′A^{\prime} and B′B^{\prime} if there is a path between A1⊔A′A_{1}\sqcup A^{\prime} and As⊔B′A_{s}\sqcup B^{\prime} in 𝑷{\boldsymbol{P}} and no A1⊔B′A_{1}\sqcup B^{\prime} nor As⊔B′A_{s}\sqcup B^{\prime} lie on this path; and

  • •

    green edges between A′A^{\prime} and B′B^{\prime} such that ωs𝑷​(B′)=ωs𝑷​(A′)+1\omega^{{\boldsymbol{P}}}_{s}(B^{\prime})=\omega^{{\boldsymbol{P}}}_{s}(A^{\prime})+1 and ωs𝑷​(A′)∈conss⁡(𝑷)\omega^{{\boldsymbol{P}}}_{s}(A^{\prime})\in\cons_{s}({\boldsymbol{P}}) or such that ω1𝑷​(B′)=ω1𝑷​(A′)+1\omega^{{\boldsymbol{P}}}_{1}(B^{\prime})=\omega^{{\boldsymbol{P}}}_{1}(A^{\prime})+1 and ω1𝑷​(A′)∈cons1⁡(𝑷)\omega^{{\boldsymbol{P}}}_{1}(A^{\prime})\in\cons_{1}({\boldsymbol{P}}).

We say that 𝑷{\boldsymbol{P}} can loosely self-lace if this graph is loop-free and admits a (directed) cycle using all its red, blue and purple edges (and some, perhaps none, of its green edges). The loose self-lacing according to 𝝆{\boldsymbol{\rho}}, denoted ∧𝝆𝑷{\wedge_{{\boldsymbol{\rho}}}{\boldsymbol{P}}} is defined accordingly.

A proof similar to the proof of Corollary 4.4 ensures that: If 𝑨{\boldsymbol{A}} is a Hamiltonian cycle for 𝒜​𝒪​(H){\mathcal{AO}}(H) and 𝑷{\boldsymbol{P}} a replacing pattern for 𝑨{\boldsymbol{A}} that can loosely self-lace, then any loose self-lace ∧𝝆𝑷\wedge_{{\boldsymbol{\rho}}}{\boldsymbol{P}} is a Hamiltonian cycle for 𝒜​𝒪​(G){\mathcal{AO}}(G).

In the case of usual self-lacing, the graph at stake contains no blue edges, but only is a path of green edges from some A′A^{\prime} to some B′B^{\prime} together with another path of red and green edges from the same A′A^{\prime} to B′B^{\prime}, and a unique purple edge between A′A^{\prime} and B′B^{\prime}.

A.2. Splitting subsequences with varying endpoints

One can easily generalize Theorem 4.5 as follows, in order to weaken its hypotheses.

Let G=H⊔H′G=H\sqcup H^{\prime} be a bipartition of the edges of GG. Suppose that there exist X1,…,Xr∈𝒜​𝒪​(H′)X_{1},\dots,X_{r}\in{\mathcal{AO}}(H^{\prime}) and a Hamiltonian path 𝑨=(A1,…,As)∈𝒜​𝒪​(H){\boldsymbol{A}}=(A_{1},\dots,A_{s})\in{\mathcal{AO}}(H) such that:

  • •

    one can split the sequence 𝑨{\boldsymbol{A}} into splitting subsequences 𝑨j=(Aij,Aij+1,…,Aij+1−1){\boldsymbol{A}}_{j}=(A_{i_{j}},A_{i_{j}+1},\dots,A_{i_{j+1}-1}) for j∈[r]j\in[r] with i1=1i_{1}=1 and ir−1=si_{r}-1=s; and

  • •

    Xj∈𝒜​𝒪​(H′|Aij)∩𝒜​𝒪​(H′|Aij−1)X_{j}\in{\mathcal{AO}}(H^{\prime}|A_{i_{j}})\cap{\mathcal{AO}}(H^{\prime}|A_{i_{j}-1}) is such that 𝑨j{\boldsymbol{A}}_{j} admits a replacing pattern which starts at Aij⊔XjA_{i_{j}}\sqcup X_{j} and ends at Aij+1−1⊔Xj+1A_{i_{j+1}-1}\sqcup X_{j+1}.

Then there exists a Hamiltonian path in 𝒜​𝒪​(G){\mathcal{AO}}(G) obtained as the concatenation of these replacing patterns. Moreover, if 𝑨{\boldsymbol{A}} is a Hamiltonian cycle of 𝒜​𝒪​(H){\mathcal{AO}}(H) and if Xr=X1X_{r}=X_{1}, then GG is 𝒜​𝒪{\mathcal{AO}}-Hamiltonian.

This version of Theorem 4.5 applies in a broader context, but has the drawback of making the pivotal orientations XjX_{j} depend on the splitting subsequences 𝑨j{\boldsymbol{A}}_{j}.

Appendix B A note on complete bipartite graphs

The complete bipartite graph Km,n{K_{m,n}} is the graph on nodes (a1,…,am)(a_{1},\dots,a_{m}) and (b1,…,bn)(b_{1},\dots,b_{n}) with edges ai​bja_{i}b_{j} for all i∈[m]i\in[m] and j∈[n]j\in[n]. The longstanding question of which Km,nK_{m,n} are 𝒜​𝒪{\mathcal{AO}}-Hamiltonian already appears in [37, Sections 3 & 5]. In particular, the authors proved that if Km,nK_{m,n} is 𝒜​𝒪{\mathcal{AO}}-Hamiltonian, then both mm and nn are odd, see [37, Theorem 3.3] where they essentially prove that σ⁡(Km,n)=0\sigma(K_{m,n})=0 if and only if both mm and nn are odd. We conjecture (as other authors conducting research on the subject) that the reciprocal is true, i.e. that the complete bipartite graph Km,nK_{m,n} is 𝒜​𝒪{\mathcal{AO}}-Hamiltonian if and only if both mm and nn are odd.

Example B.1.

As already explained in [37, below Thm. 3.3], the graphs K1,nK_{1,n} are stars (hence, trees), so the graph of acyclic orientations 𝒜​𝒪​(K1,n){\mathcal{AO}}(K_{1,n}) is isomorphic to the cube-graph QnQ_{n}. In particular, by Example 2.4, the graphs K1,nK_{1,n} are 𝒜​𝒪{\mathcal{AO}}-Hamiltonian.

The graph 𝒜​𝒪​(K3,5){\mathcal{AO}}(K_{3,5}) has 4 7184\,718 nodes and 20 61020\,610 edges, while the graph 𝒜​𝒪​(K5,5){\mathcal{AO}}(K_{5,5}) has 329 462329\,462 nodes and 1 902 7501\,902\,750 edges, so a powerful computer and a good implementation of Hamiltonian cycle search might decide whether K3,5K_{3,5} and K5,5K_{5,5} are 𝒜​𝒪{\mathcal{AO}}-Hamiltonian or not.

Via a computer experiment (on a normal laptop), we confirmed that K3,3K_{3,3} is 𝒜​𝒪{\mathcal{AO}}-Hamiltonian, which was left open in [37]: the graph 𝒜​𝒪​(K3,3){\mathcal{AO}}(K_{3,3}) has 230230 nodes and 702702 edges. To showcase the compactness of Gray codes, we give explicitly a Hamiltonian cycle in 𝒜​𝒪​(K3,3){\mathcal{AO}}(K_{3,3}), namely:

4 3 5 3 1 9 1 6 7 1 7 2 1 6 1 9 6 7 2 4 3 9 8 3 8 2 4 6 2 1 3 4 6 8 9 8 6 1 7 1 9 4 6 8 3 2 1 7 1 2 1 6 1

8 4 1 7 1 3 1 5 8 1 3 8 1 8 2 4 5 4]

To read this Hamiltonian cycle, one proceeds as follows. The ithi^{\text{th}} digit sis_{i} (read from left to right, i.e. s1=3s_{1}=3, s2=1s_{2}=1, etc.) of the above sequence corresponds to an acyclic orientation AiA_{i} defined by:

  • •

    A0A_{0} is the acyclic orientation depicted in Figure 18;

  • •

    AiA_{i} is obtained from Ai−1A_{i-1} by changing the orientation of the arc labeled sis_{i}.

Besides, to compute directly AiA_{i} from A0A_{0}, one can count for each j∈[9]j\in[9] how many times it appears among s1,…,sis_{1},\dots,s_{i}: if jj appears an even number of times, then the arcs labeled jj are oriented the same way in A0A_{0} and in AiA_{i}, otherwise they are not. One can check that A230A_{230} (defined from A229A_{229} by changing the arc labeled 44) is indeed A0A_{0}, so the above sequence is indeed a cycle.

Let 𝒫⁡(i,j){\mathcal{P}}(i,j) be the set of ordered partitions of [i][i] into jj parts. In [37], it is established that the acyclic orientations of the complete bipartite graph Km,nK_{m,n} are in one-to-one correspondence with triples (Q,Q′,δ)(Q,Q^{\prime},\delta) where δ∈{0,1}\delta\in\{0,1\}, Q∈𝒫⁡(m,k)Q\in{\mathcal{P}}(m,k), Q′∈𝒫⁡(n,k+ε)Q^{\prime}\in{\mathcal{P}}(n,k+\varepsilon) for some k≥1k\geq 1 and ε∈{0,1}\varepsilon\in\{0,1\}. Given an acyclic orientation AA of Km,nK_{m,n}, one obtains such a triple as follows (see illustration in Figure 19). Let S1S_{1} be the set of sources of AA, let S2S_{2} be the set of sources of A∖S1A\smallsetminus S_{1}, and recursively let SiS_{i} be the set of sources of A∖(S1∪⋯∪Si−1)A\smallsetminus(S_{1}\cup\dots\cup S_{i-1}) (where Si≠∅S_{i}\neq\varnothing since AA is acyclic), and let SκS_{\kappa} be the last (non-empty) source set. Note that each SiS_{i} must be contained exclusively in one of the two parts of Km,nK_{m,n} because Km,nK_{m,n} is the complete bipartite graph. We set ε=1\varepsilon=1 and k=κ−12k=\frac{\kappa-1}{2} if κ\kappa is odd, and ε=0\varepsilon=0 and k=κ2k=\frac{\kappa}{2} otherwise. We set δ=0\delta=0 if S1S_{1} is contained in the part of Km,nK_{m,n} of size mm, and δ=1\delta=1 otherwise. If δ=1\delta=1, then Q=(S1,S3,S5,…,S2​(k+ε)−1)Q=(S_{1},S_{3},S_{5},\dots,S_{2(k+\varepsilon)-1}) is our ordered partition of [m][m], and Q′=(S2,S4,S6,…,S2​k)Q^{\prime}=(S_{2},S_{4},S_{6},\dots,S_{2k}) is our ordered partition of [n][n]; if δ=1\delta=1, the opposite holds.

Equivalently, SiS_{i} is the set of elements of rank i+1i+1 in the poset induced by AA: this poset is ranked because Km,nK_{m,n} is the complete bipartite graph. The reciprocal bijection can be found in [37].

We call the sequence (S1,…,Sκ)(S_{1},\dots,S_{\kappa}) and its encoding as triple (Q,Q′,δ)(Q,Q^{\prime},\delta) a bicolored (m,n)(m,n)-partition. Two elements p∈[n]p\in[n], q∈[m]q\in[m] are neighboring in (S1,…,Sκ)(S_{1},\dots,S_{\kappa}) if there exists an index i∈[κ−1]i\in[\kappa-1], such that p∈Sip\in S_{i} and q∈Si+1q\in S_{i+1}.

In [37], the authors only focus on counting the number of bicolored (m,n)(m,n)-partitions because they want to discuss a parity argument. We go slightly further by describing the graph 𝒜​𝒪​(m,n){\mathcal{AO}}(m,n) thanks to bicolored (m,n)(m,n)-partitions.

Let ρ=(Q,Q′,δ)\rho=(Q,Q^{\prime},\delta) be a bicolored partition and p,qp,q be two neighboring elements in ρ\rho, with p∈Sip\in S_{i} and q∈Si+1q\in S_{i+1}. Consider the sequence 𝑺⁡(p,q)=(S1,…,Si−1,Si∖{p},{q},{p},Si+1∖{q},Si+2,…,Sκ).{\boldsymbol{S}}(p,q)=(S_{1},\dots,S_{i-1},S_{i}\smallsetminus\{p\},\{q\},\{p\},S_{i+1}\smallsetminus\{q\},S_{i+2},\dots,S_{\kappa})\,. This sequence 𝑺⁡(p,q){\boldsymbol{S}}(p,q) may contain some empty sets (possibly Si∖{p}S_{i}\smallsetminus\{p\} or Si+1∖{q}S_{i+1}\smallsetminus\{q\}), so we compress it by removing all its empty sets and then merging adjacent sets of the same color together, that is by replacing all sub-sequences (Sa−1,Sa,Sa+1)(S_{a-1},S_{a},S_{a+1}) where Sa=∅S_{a}=\varnothing by a sub-sequence (Sa−1∪Sa+1)(S_{a-1}\cup S_{a+1}).

Definition B.2.

Denoting ρ′\rho^{\prime} the compressed version of 𝑺⁡(p,q){\boldsymbol{S}}(p,q) as described above, we say that ρ,ρ′\rho,\rho^{\prime} differ by a flip at (p,q)(p,q). The graph of flips of bicolored (m,n)(m,n)-partitions is the graph whose nodes are the bicolored (m,n)(m,n)-partitions and where two nodes share an edge if they differ by some flip.

Lemma B.3.

The graph 𝒜​𝒪​(m,n){\mathcal{AO}}(m,n) is isomorphic to the graph of flips of bicolored (m,n)(m,n)-partitions.

Proof.

Let A∈𝒜​𝒪​(m,n)A\in{\mathcal{AO}}(m,n), and ρ=(Q,Q′,δ)\rho=(Q,Q^{\prime},\delta) the associated triple. We first need to show that flipping an edge (p,q)(p,q) where p,qp,q are neighboring in ρ\rho will not result in an oriented cycle. Let SiS_{i} be the block containing pp and Si+1S_{i+1} the neighboring block of the partition ρ\rho (Because of the orientation of (p,q)(p,q), pp comes before qq). If there were an oriented cycle after flipping this edge, then there would be a directed path from pp to qq in AA. Since the graph is bipartite, the path has length at least 33 and is thus of the form (p,r1,r2,q)(p,r_{1},r_{2},q). By construction of AA, this means that the node r1r_{1} is in a block between SiS_{i} and Si+1S_{i+1}, which is a contradiction.

Conversely, consider an edge (p,q)(p,q) between two non-neighboring blocks. It follows that there are at least two blocks between SiS_{i} containing pp and SjS_{j} containing qq. Take one node of each block, then these p,qp,q and these two nodes form an oriented path in AA and would therefore form an oriented 44-cycle with the edge (p,q)(p,q). This finishes the proof. ∎

Thus, the problem of finding a Hamiltonian cycle in 𝒜​𝒪​(Km,n){\mathcal{AO}}(K_{m,n}) is equivalent to finding a Gray code for these bicolored (m,n)(m,n)-partitions with respect to the flipping operation described above.

This latter problem has already been explored in the unlabeled case, so bicolored partitions where the elements in each block are not integers in [m][m] and [n][n], but rather indistinguishable elements. Such an unlabeled colored (m,n)(m,n)-partition is a string of m+nm+n elements, namely mm zeros and nn ones. Two such strings ss and s′s^{\prime} differ by a flip if and only if s′s^{\prime} is obtained from ss by swapping a (consecutive) sub-string 0101 for a (consecutive) sub-string 1010, or the converse22 2 Although this graph of flips has (m+nm)\binom{m+n}{m} elements, it is not the Johnson graph J⁡(m+n,m)J(m+n,m) since it is not regular..

For example, the two unlabeled partitions corresponding to the bicolored (m,n)(m,n)-partitions in Figure 19 are respectively 1010110101 and 0110101101.

Theorem B.4 ([8, 15] independently).

If n≤1n\leq 1 or m≤1m\leq 1 or both nn and mm are odd, then the graph of flips of unlabeled bicolored (m,n)(m,n)-partitions admits a Hamiltonian path starting at 11​…​100​…​011\dots 100\dots 0 and 00​…​011​…​100\dots 011\dots 1 with mm copies of 00 and nn copies of 11.

Note that the above Gray code must start and end at the combinations 11​…​100​…​011\dots 100\dots 0 and 00​…​011​…​100\dots 011\dots 1 with mm copies of 00 and nn copies of 11. Consequently, a possible strategy to get a Gray code for the unlabeled case by lacing patterns into this existing Gray code could, at best, produce a Hamiltonian path, not a Hamiltonian cycle. This strategy in general might not be fruitful, as the cardinality of unlabeled partitions is not easily relatable to the cardinality of the labeled case.

Question B.5.

Is there a Gray code for the labeled bicolored (m,n)(m,n)-partitions described above when both m,nm,n are odd? Equivalently, is Km,nK_{m,n} 𝒜​𝒪{\mathcal{AO}}-Hamiltonian when both mm and nn are odd?

Appendix C Parity argument via the count of acyclic orientations for multipaths

We refer to Section 3.3.3 for the definitions concerning multipaths, no result from Section 3.3.3 is needed. We give an alternative proof that if a multipath is 𝒜​𝒪{\mathcal{AO}}-Hamiltonian then its number of edges is even. The first step is to count the number of (a)cyclic orientations of a multipath according to their rank with respect to the usual orientation Du→vℓD^{{\boldsymbol{\ell}}}_{u\to v} from uu to vv.

Proposition C.1.

For ℓ=(ℓ1,…,ℓs){\boldsymbol{\ell}}=(\ell_{1},\dots,\ell_{s}), the number of acyclic orientations AA of PℓP^{{\boldsymbol{\ell}}} such that rkDu→vℓ⁡A=k\rank_{D^{{\boldsymbol{\ell}}}_{u\to v}}A=k is:

|𝒜​𝒪k​(Du→vℓ)|=(∑p=1sℓpk)−∑S,T⊆[s]S∩T=∅,S≠∅,T≠∅(−1)|S⊔T|⋅(∑p∉S⊔Tℓpk−∑p∈Sℓp)|{\mathcal{AO}}_{k}(D^{{\boldsymbol{\ell}}}_{u\to v})|=\binom{\sum_{p=1}^{s}\ell_{p}}{k}-\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}S,T\subseteq[s]\\ S\cap T=\varnothing,~S\neq\varnothing,~T\neq\varnothing\end{subarray}}(-1)^{|S\sqcup T|}\cdot\binom{\sum_{p\notin S\sqcup T}\ell_{p}}{k-\sum_{p\in S}\ell_{p}}
Proof.

Recall that 𝒜​𝒪k​(D)=𝒪k​(D)∖𝒞​𝒪k​(D){\mathcal{AO}}_{k}(D)={\mathcal{O}}_{k}(D)\smallsetminus{\mathcal{CO}}_{k}(D), and that |𝒪k​(D)|=(|E|k)|{\mathcal{O}}_{k}(D)|=\binom{|E|}{k} for all digraphs D=(N,E)D=(N,E). Hence, it is enough to count 𝒞​𝒪k​(Du→vℓ){\mathcal{CO}}_{k}(D^{{\boldsymbol{\ell}}}_{u\to v}), remembering that Du→vℓD^{{\boldsymbol{\ell}}}_{u\to v} has ∑p=1sℓp\sum_{p=1}^{s}\ell_{p} arcs.

We denote by EpE_{p} the set of edges of the path Pℓp=(u,ip,2,…,ip,ℓp,v)P^{\ell_{p}}=(u,i_{p,2},\dots,i_{p,\ell_{p}},v), for p∈[s]p\in[s]. For a subset XX of edges of Du→vℓD^{{\boldsymbol{\ell}}}_{u\to v}, the orientation (Du→vℓ)X(D^{{\boldsymbol{\ell}}}_{u\to v})^{X} is cyclic if and only if Ep⊆XE_{p}\subseteq X and Eq∩X=∅E_{q}\cap X=\varnothing for some p≠qp\neq q, i.e. if and only if one of the paths in the multipath is directed from uu to vv while another one is directed from vv to uu. We count such sets XX according to their size, using inclusion-exclusion.

For k≥0k\geq 0, and S,T⊆[s]S,T\subseteq[s] with S∩T=∅S\cap T=\varnothing, and S≠∅S\neq\varnothing and T≠∅T\neq\varnothing, let 𝒳k,S,T{\mathcal{X}}_{k,S,T} be the set of subsets XX of edges of Du→vℓD^{{\boldsymbol{\ell}}}_{u\to v} with |X|=k|X|=k such that Ep⊆XE_{p}\subseteq X for p∈Sp\in S and Eq∩X=∅E_{q}\cap X=\varnothing for q∈Tq\in T. Such a subset corresponds to picking ∑p∈Sℓp\sum_{p\in S}\ell_{p} prescribed edges, then choosing the remaining k−∑p∈Sℓpk-\sum_{p\in S}\ell_{p} among the edges that are not in ⨆p∈S⊔TEp\bigsqcup_{p\in{S\sqcup T}}E_{p}. Thus (by convention, if a<0a<0 or b<0b<0 or a<ba<b, then (ab)=0\binom{a}{b}=0): |𝒳k,S,T|=(∑p∉S⊔Tℓpk−∑p∈Sℓp)|{\mathcal{X}}_{k,S,T}|=\binom{\sum_{p\notin S\sqcup T}\ell_{p}}{k-\sum_{p\in S}\ell_{p}}.

The set of cyclic orientations of rank kk, namely 𝒞​𝒪k​(Du→vℓ){\mathcal{CO}}_{k}(D^{{\boldsymbol{\ell}}}_{u\to v}), is in bijection with ⋃S,T⊆[s]𝒳k,S,T\bigcup_{S,T\subseteq[s]}{\mathcal{X}}_{k,S,T} where the union is on all S,T⊆[s]S,T\subseteq[s] with S∩T=∅S\cap T=\varnothing, S≠∅S\neq\varnothing and T≠∅T\neq\varnothing. The latter union is not disjoint, but according to the inclusion-exclusion principle, we get the following, proving the claim:

|𝒞​𝒪k​(Du→vℓ)|=|⋃S,T⊆[s]S∩T=∅,S,T≠∅𝒳k,S,T|=∑S,T⊆[s]S∩T=∅,S,T≠∅(−1)|S⊔T|⋅|𝒳k,S,T|∎\Bigl|{\mathcal{CO}}_{k}(D^{{\boldsymbol{\ell}}}_{u\to v})\Bigr|=\left|\bigcup_{\begin{subarray}{c}S,T\subseteq[s]\\ S\cap T=\varnothing,~S,T\neq\varnothing\end{subarray}}{\mathcal{X}}_{k,S,T}\right|=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}S,T\subseteq[s]\\ S\cap T=\varnothing,~S,T\neq\varnothing\end{subarray}}(-1)^{|S\sqcup T|}\cdot|{\mathcal{X}}_{k,S,T}|\hskip 14.22636pt\qed
Proposition C.2.

If ∑pℓp\sum_{p}\ell_{p} is even, then the (ℓ1,…,ℓs)(\ell_{1},\dots,\ell_{s})-multipath is not 𝒜​𝒪{\mathcal{AO}}-Hamiltonian.

Proof.

Let ℓ=(ℓ1,…,ℓs){\boldsymbol{\ell}}=(\ell_{1},\dots,\ell_{s}). We will apply Lemma 2.9 (in the form discussed in Remark 2.10): if PℓP^{{\boldsymbol{\ell}}} is 𝒜​𝒪{\mathcal{AO}}-Hamiltonian, then ∑k(−1)k⋅|𝒞​𝒪k​(Du→vℓ)|=0\sum_{k}(-1)^{k}\cdot|{\mathcal{CO}}_{k}(D^{{\boldsymbol{\ell}}}_{u\to v})|=0. By Proposition C.1, we get:

∑k(−1)k⋅|𝒞​𝒪k​(Du→vℓ)|\displaystyle\sum_{k}(-1)^{k}\cdot|{\mathcal{CO}}_{k}(D^{{\boldsymbol{\ell}}}_{u\to v})| =∑S,T⊆[s]S∩T=∅,S,T≠∅(−1)|S⊔T|⋅(∑k(−1)k⋅(∑p∉S⊔Tℓpk−∑p∈Sℓp))\displaystyle=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}S,T\subseteq[s]\\ S\cap T=\varnothing,~S,T\neq\varnothing\end{subarray}}(-1)^{|S\sqcup T|}\cdot\left(\sum_{k}(-1)^{k}\cdot\binom{\sum_{p\notin S\sqcup T}\ell_{p}}{k-\sum_{p\in S}\ell_{p}}\right)
=∑S,T⊆[s]S∩T=∅,S,T≠∅(−1)|S⊔T|⋅(∑k(−1)k+∑p∈Sℓp⋅(∑p∉S⊔Tℓpk))\displaystyle=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}S,T\subseteq[s]\\ S\cap T=\varnothing,~S,T\neq\varnothing\end{subarray}}(-1)^{|S\sqcup T|}\cdot\left(\sum_{k}(-1)^{k+\sum_{p\in S}\ell_{p}}\cdot\binom{\sum_{p\notin S\sqcup T}\ell_{p}}{k}\right)

Recall that ∑k(−1)k⋅(mk)=0\sum_{k}(-1)^{k}\cdot\binom{m}{k}=0 if m≥1m\geq 1 and equals 11 if m=0m=0. Hence, the rightmost sum is non-zero if and only if S⊔T=[s]S\sqcup T=[s]. We obtain

∑k(−1)k⋅|𝒞​𝒪k​(Du→vℓ)|=∑S⊔T=[s]S∩T=∅,S,T≠∅(−1)|S⊔T|⋅(−1)∑p∈Sℓp=(−1)s⋅∑S⊆[s]S≠∅,S≠[s](−1)∑p∈Sℓp\sum_{k}(-1)^{k}\cdot|{\mathcal{CO}}_{k}(D^{{\boldsymbol{\ell}}}_{u\to v})|=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}S\sqcup T=[s]\\ S\cap T=\varnothing,~S,T\neq\varnothing\end{subarray}}(-1)^{|S\sqcup T|}\cdot(-1)^{\sum_{p\in S}\ell_{p}}=(-1)^{s}\cdot\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}S\subseteq[s]\\ S\neq\varnothing,~S\neq[s]\end{subarray}}(-1)^{\sum_{p\in S}\ell_{p}}

Note that (−1)∑p∈Sℓp=1(-1)^{\sum_{p\in S}\ell_{p}}=1 if and only if SS contains an even number of odd values ℓp\ell_{p}. Hence, denoting A≔{p∈[s];ℓp​ is odd}A\coloneqq\{p\in[s]~;~\ell_{p}\text{ is odd}\} and B≔{p∈[s];ℓp​ is even}B\coloneqq\{p\in[s]~;~\ell_{p}\text{ is even}\}, we get: ∑S⊆[s](−1)∑p∈Sℓp=∑X⊆AY⊆B(−1)|X|=2|B|⋅∑j=0|A|(|A|j)​(−1)j=2|B|⋅0=0\sum_{S\subseteq[s]}(-1)^{\sum_{p\in S}\ell_{p}}=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}X\subseteq A\\ Y\subseteq B\end{subarray}}(-1)^{|X|}=2^{|B|}\cdot\sum_{j=0}^{|A|}\binom{|A|}{j}(-1)^{j}=2^{|B|}\cdot 0=0. Substituting in the above, we obtain:

∑k(−1)k⋅|𝒞​𝒪k​(Du→vℓ)|\displaystyle\sum_{k}(-1)^{k}\cdot|{\mathcal{CO}}_{k}(D^{{\boldsymbol{\ell}}}_{u\to v})| =(−1)s⋅(∑S⊆[s](−1)∑p∈Sℓp−(−1)0−(−1)∑p=1sℓp)\displaystyle=(-1)^{s}\cdot\left(\sum_{S\subseteq[s]}(-1)^{\sum_{p\in S}\ell_{p}}~-~(-1)^{0}-(-1)^{\sum_{p=1}^{s}\ell_{p}}\right)
=(−1)s+1⋅(1+(−1)∑p=1sℓp)\displaystyle=(-1)^{s+1}\cdot\left(1+(-1)^{\sum_{p=1}^{s}\ell_{p}}\right)

By Lemma 2.9 (see Remark 2.10), if Du→vℓD^{{\boldsymbol{\ell}}}_{u\to v} is 𝒜​𝒪{\mathcal{AO}}-Hamiltonian, then ∑k(−1)k⋅|𝒞​𝒪k​(Du→vℓ)|=0\sum_{k}(-1)^{k}\cdot|{\mathcal{CO}}_{k}(D^{{\boldsymbol{\ell}}}_{u\to v})|=0, implying that (−1)∑p=1sℓp=−1(-1)^{\sum_{p=1}^{s}\ell_{p}}=-1, i.e. implying that ∑p=1sℓp\sum_{p=1}^{s}\ell_{p} is odd. ∎

Remark C.3.

Note that, contrarily to Section 3.3.3, the present reasoning does not allow computing the acyclic signature of multipaths, only determining whether it is 00 or not.

Appendix D Acyclic polynomials and 𝒜​𝒪{\mathcal{AO}}-Hamiltonicity of some small graphs

To motivate further research, for 2222 graphs (from the named-graph database of SageMath [36]), we computed the number of acyclic orientations ψ⁡(G)\psi(G), the acyclic signature σ⁡(G)\sigma(G), and the acyclic polynomial Ψ⁡(D,t)\Psi(D;t). The chosen orientation DD of the graph GG is obtained by orienting each edge i​jij of GG from ii to jj if i<ji<j. For each graph, we address 𝒜​𝒪{\mathcal{AO}}-Hamiltonicity. If σ⁡(G)≠0\sigma(G)\neq 0, then GG is not 𝒜​𝒪{\mathcal{AO}}-Hamiltonian; otherwise we need to construct the graph of acyclic orientations 𝒜​𝒪​(G){\mathcal{AO}}(G) and search for a Hamiltonian cycle in it. The latter is a NP-hard problem. Our computations took minutes for the Moser spindle, and did not finish within 24 hours for the Wagner graph.
